Kafka SDE-2 Handbook

Apache Kafka from first principles to SDE-2 depth in 21 modules, 10 case studies, and 19 hands-on labs. Every lesson opens with a question to try, flow diagrams step through one arrow at a time, labs run on a real cluster on your laptop, and a tracker brings designs back for spaced review.

How this handbook teaches

The goal is not to memorize configuration names. It is to understand what Kafka does at each step well enough to predict its behavior, choose settings on purpose, design with it, and debug it at 2 AM. So the handbook asks you to think before it explains, and to run things before you trust them.

  • Try before you read. Every lesson opens with a short question. Answer it on paper first; getting it wrong is what makes the explanation stick.
  • Analogy, then mechanism, then trade-off. Each idea starts with the problem it solves and a plain analogy, then how it works, then what it costs. Rarely needed details sit in folded "Go deeper" sections.
  • Step through every flow. Diagrams with a step bar reveal one arrow at a time. Predict the next arrow before pressing Next.
  • Run it. Labs use the official Apache Kafka Docker image and the command-line tools, so you see offsets, lag, rebalances, and failovers happen. Each lab ends with "Check what you saw".
  • Live tools. A key-to-partition explorer that uses Kafka's real murmur2 hash, a partition count calculator, a durability explorer for acks and min ISR, a consumer group playground, a cluster sizing calculator, and a lag drain calculator.
  • Notes for work and interviews. Green "In production" and "At work" boxes show how ideas appear in real systems, including payments. Purple "Interview signal" boxes say what interviewers listen for at SDE-2 and what a senior answer adds.

How to study one module

  1. Clear the revision queue above at the start of each session: redesign those systems from a blank page.
  2. Do the warm-up quiz without reading anything. Note what you missed.
  3. For each lesson: answer "Try it first", read, step through the figure, then say out loud what problem the idea solves and when it fails.
  4. Do the lab. Predict the output of each command before running it.
  5. Do the self-check quiz, then tick lessons as studied.
  6. Tick the mastery checklist only when each item is true with your notes closed.

How to do the labs

  • Set up once on the lab setup page: a single broker for most labs, a three-broker cluster for replication and failure labs.
  • Labs take 15 to 30 minutes. They are written for Kafka 4.3 in Docker, with commands you can paste.
  • Tick Done on a lab when you have run it and can explain the "Check what you saw" answers. The dashboard counts finished labs.
  • Break things on purpose: stop brokers, kill consumers, reset offsets. That is what the local cluster is for.

How to practice a case study

  1. Set a timer for the time on the case study and design it on paper first: requirements, estimates, topics and keys, the diagram, then the hard parts.
  2. Open the case study and compare section by section. Answer each guided deep dive before revealing it.
  3. Set an honest status at the top of the page. The handbook schedules a review.
  4. When it comes due, redesign it from memory, faster each time. Then try related practice prompts in the tracker.

Where your progress is saved

Lesson ticks, lab ticks, mastery checks, readiness checks, and design statuses save automatically to your account, privately: nobody else who opens this page sees them, and they follow you to other devices. The indicator in the top bar shows where the latest change went. If the page cannot reach your account (for example in a private window), it saves in this browser instead, and the tracker has a backup and restore box.

Version and scope

Version note

Written for Apache Kafka 4.3 (October 2026) and checked against its source and documentation. Kafka 4.x runs only in KRaft mode: ZooKeeper was removed in 4.0. Where behavior changed in a recent release (the new consumer group protocol, share groups, linger.ms defaults, eligible leader replicas), a version note says so, so you can recognize older setups at work.

Covered: everything a backend engineer needs to build, run, and debug Kafka-based systems, and what SDE-2 interviews test about Kafka and event-driven design: the data model, producers, consumers, delivery semantics, internals that explain behavior, transactions, schemas, Connect, Streams and Flink at design level, Spring for Apache Kafka, tuning, operations, and troubleshooting.

Left out on purpose: ZooKeeper-mode administration, vendor-specific products in depth, Kafka's source code internals beyond what explains behavior, and non-Java client details (except where they behave differently, such as librdkafka's default partitioner).

Lab setup

Every module has hands-on labs. Set up once here: a single broker for most labs, a three-broker cluster for replication and failure labs, and a Java project for the client code. Everything runs locally in Docker with the official Apache Kafka image.

On this page

  1. What you need
  2. A single broker
  3. A three-broker cluster
  4. A Java project
  5. Optional tools
  6. Command-line tools you will use

What you need

  • Docker 20.10.4 or newer (Docker Desktop on macOS or Windows, Docker Engine on Linux), with about 4 GB of memory for the three-broker cluster.
  • For the Java examples: JDK 17 or newer and Maven or Gradle. Kafka 4.x clients need Java 11 or newer; brokers and tools need Java 17 or newer.
  • About 2 GB of free disk.
Version note

Labs use Apache Kafka 4.3 (the current release in October 2026) and its option names. Kafka 4.2 renamed some console tool options; on 4.1 or older, use --property instead of --reader-property and --formatter-property, and --producer-property or --consumer-property instead of --command-property.

A single broker

One container runs a combined broker and controller with default settings, listening on localhost:9092.

Terminal
docker run -d --name broker -p 9092:9092 apache/kafka:4.3.0

Kafka's command-line tools live in /opt/kafka/bin inside the container. Open a shell there and run tools with ./:

Terminal
docker exec -it --workdir /opt/kafka/bin broker sh
./kafka-topics.sh --bootstrap-server localhost:9092 --list

Stop and delete it when you are done (this also deletes its data):

Terminal
docker rm -f broker

A three-broker cluster

Used in Modules 3, 5, 12, and 20. Save this as docker-compose.yml. It is the official Apache Kafka combined-mode example with three nodes; each node is both a broker and a controller. Inside the Docker network, nodes talk on port 19092; from your laptop, use localhost:29092, localhost:39092, and localhost:49092.

docker-compose.yml
x-kafka-env: &kafka-env
  KAFKA_PROCESS_ROLES: 'broker,controller'
  KAFKA_LISTENER_SECURITY_PROTOCOL_MAP: 'CONTROLLER:PLAINTEXT,PLAINTEXT:PLAINTEXT,PLAINTEXT_HOST:PLAINTEXT'
  KAFKA_CONTROLLER_QUORUM_VOTERS: '1@kafka-1:9093,2@kafka-2:9093,3@kafka-3:9093'
  KAFKA_LISTENERS: 'PLAINTEXT://:19092,CONTROLLER://:9093,PLAINTEXT_HOST://:9092'
  KAFKA_INTER_BROKER_LISTENER_NAME: 'PLAINTEXT'
  KAFKA_CONTROLLER_LISTENER_NAMES: 'CONTROLLER'
  CLUSTER_ID: '4L6g3nShT-eMCtK--X86sw'
  KAFKA_GROUP_INITIAL_REBALANCE_DELAY_MS: 0
  KAFKA_LOG_DIRS: '/tmp/kraft-combined-logs'

services:
  kafka-1:
    image: apache/kafka:4.3.0
    hostname: kafka-1
    container_name: kafka-1
    ports: ["29092:9092"]
    environment:
      <<: *kafka-env
      KAFKA_NODE_ID: 1
      KAFKA_ADVERTISED_LISTENERS: 'PLAINTEXT://kafka-1:19092,PLAINTEXT_HOST://localhost:29092'
  kafka-2:
    image: apache/kafka:4.3.0
    hostname: kafka-2
    container_name: kafka-2
    ports: ["39092:9092"]
    environment:
      <<: *kafka-env
      KAFKA_NODE_ID: 2
      KAFKA_ADVERTISED_LISTENERS: 'PLAINTEXT://kafka-2:19092,PLAINTEXT_HOST://localhost:39092'
  kafka-3:
    image: apache/kafka:4.3.0
    hostname: kafka-3
    container_name: kafka-3
    ports: ["49092:9092"]
    environment:
      <<: *kafka-env
      KAFKA_NODE_ID: 3
      KAFKA_ADVERTISED_LISTENERS: 'PLAINTEXT://kafka-3:19092,PLAINTEXT_HOST://localhost:49092'

Start it, then define a helper that runs any tool on kafka-1 against the cluster:

Terminal
docker compose up -d
k() { tool=$1; shift; docker exec -it kafka-1 /opt/kafka/bin/$tool --bootstrap-server kafka-1:19092 "$@"; }
k kafka-topics.sh --list

The helper puts --bootstrap-server right after the tool name, which every Kafka tool accepts. Internal topics such as __consumer_offsets use replication factor 3 by default, which this cluster satisfies. Stop and remove everything with docker compose down.

A Java project

Add the Kafka client library. The client version can be newer than your brokers; Kafka 4.x clients work with brokers 2.1 and newer.

pom.xml (Maven)
<dependency>
  <groupId>org.apache.kafka</groupId>
  <artifactId>kafka-clients</artifactId>
  <version>4.3.0</version>
</dependency>
build.gradle (Gradle)
implementation 'org.apache.kafka:kafka-clients:4.3.0'

For Spring Boot (Module 18), add org.springframework.kafka:spring-kafka and let Spring Boot manage its version.

Optional tools

  • A web UI helps you browse topics and consumer groups. Open-source options include Kafbat UI, AKHQ, and Redpanda Console. None is required; every lab uses the bundled command-line tools.
  • kcat (formerly kafkacat) is a fast command-line producer and consumer, handy for scripts.

Command-line tools you will use

Tool Used for First appears
kafka-topics.sh Create, describe, alter, delete topics Module 2
kafka-console-producer.sh, kafka-console-consumer.sh Write and read records by hand Module 2
kafka-consumer-groups.sh Group members, offsets, lag, offset resets Module 7
kafka-configs.sh Read and change topic, broker, and client configs Module 5
kafka-producer-perf-test.sh, kafka-consumer-perf-test.sh Load tests Module 4
kafka-dump-log.sh Inspect segment files on disk Module 11
kafka-leader-election.sh, kafka-reassign-partitions.sh Move leadership and replicas Modules 3, 20
kafka-metadata-quorum.sh Controller quorum status Module 3
kafka-transactions.sh List and abort transactions Module 14

Phase 1: FoundationsCoreStart here

Module 1: Why Kafka exists

Before configs and APIs, learn the problem Kafka solves. This module shows what breaks when services call each other directly, what a log is, how Kafka gives you both a queue and pub/sub, where it fits in real systems, and when it is the wrong tool.

9 lessons3 figures6 mastery checks

On this page

  2. 1.2The log: Kafka's core idea

Warm-upWarm-up: one line each
  1. Checkout calls email, fraud, and analytics over HTTP, one after another. Analytics gets slow. What happens to checkout, and what is the event-driven fix?
    Reveal

    Checkout becomes as slow as its slowest dependency and fails when any of them fails. Publish one PaymentCompleted event to Kafka instead; email, fraud, and analytics each consume it at their own pace, and checkout returns as soon as the event is written.

  2. After a consumer reads a message from Kafka, is the message deleted?
    Reveal

    No. It stays until the topic's retention removes it (7 days by default). Other consumers, and the same consumer later, can read it again.

  3. Ten independent services must each receive every order event. Do you need ten copies of the topic?
    Reveal

    No. Each service uses its own consumer group, and every group reads the whole topic independently.

  4. Name one job Kafka is a poor fit for.
    Reveal

    Synchronous request-reply where the caller needs the answer now; per-message delays or priorities; storing large files; or a small job queue where a managed queue is simpler to run.

  5. What makes Kafka fast enough for millions of messages per second?
    Reveal

    Appending to sequential files, batching many records per request, compression, serving reads from the operating system's page cache, and spreading partitions across many brokers.

1.1The problem: services calling each other

Try it first2 minutes

The payments service must notify email, fraud scoring, the ledger, and analytics. Today it calls each one over HTTP. List three things that go wrong as traffic and the number of consumers grow.

Reveal the answer
  • Latency adds up: the payment waits for four calls in a row.
  • Availability multiplies: four services at 99.5% each give at most 0.995^4, about 98.0%, which is roughly a week of failed payments a year.
  • Failures spread: if the ledger is down, the payment either fails or needs custom retry code.
  • Bursts overload the slowest service: a sale doubles traffic and analytics falls over.
  • Every new consumer means changing and redeploying payments.
  • No history: if fraud scoring had a bug yesterday, there is nothing to replay.
Idea

Put a durable log between the services. Producers write each event once; consumers read it whenever they are ready. Neither side needs to know the other exists or be up at the same time.

Analogy

Instead of phoning every department about a new hire, HR pins one notice to a board that keeps every notice in order. Each department reads it when it can, and a department that opens next year can still read the old notices.

What you gain

Decoupling, burst absorption, independent scaling, many consumers for one event, and a replayable history.

What you pay

Results arrive later (eventual consistency), consumers must handle duplicates, and you run one more distributed system.

Commands vs events. A command asks for something to happen ("SendEmail") and has one intended handler. An event states a fact ("PaymentCompleted") that any number of services can react to. Kafka works best with events, because the producer does not need to know who listens, so adding a consumer never touches the producer.

1.2The log: Kafka's core idea

Try it first2 minutes

A bank passbook only gets new lines at the bottom, every line has a number, and you can re-read from any line. Which properties let you and the bank reconcile your balance independently?

Reveal the answer

It is append-only (old lines never change), ordered with positions (line numbers), and readable from any position without affecting anyone else. Two readers can each remember "I have checked up to line 40" and compare later.

Idea

A log is an append-only, ordered sequence of records. Each record gets a position called an offset. Writers add to the end; each reader remembers its own offset.

Analogy

The passbook, or an accounting ledger. Entries are never edited; a correction is a new entry.

Why it matters

Readers do not interfere with each other, any reader can replay history, and the current state of something (a balance) can be rebuilt by reading its events from the start.

Kafka is a distributed commit log. It takes this simple structure and splits each log into partitions spread across many servers, with copies on several servers so a crash loses nothing. Databases already use a log internally (the write-ahead log); Kafka makes the log itself the product that other systems read.

  • Events are facts: PaymentAuthorized, CardBlocked. They are immutable.
  • State is derived: a balance is the sum of its events. Module 13 shows topics that keep only the latest value per key, which turns a log into a table.

1.3Queue, pub/sub, and log

Try it first2 minutes

You want 20 workers to share image-resize jobs. Separately, email, search, and audit must each receive every new-user event. Which messaging shape fits each need?

Reveal the answer

Resize jobs need a queue: each job goes to exactly one worker. New-user events need pub/sub: every subscriber gets its own copy. Kafka covers both: put the 20 workers in one consumer group (they split the work) and give email, search, and audit one group each (each group gets everything).

Queue Pub/sub Log (Kafka)
Who gets a message One consumer Every subscriber Every consumer group; one member per partition inside a group
After it is read Deleted Deleted per subscriber Kept until retention expires
Replay No Usually no Yes: move the offset back
Ordering Weak once workers run in parallel Per subscriber, often none Strict within a partition
Examples RabbitMQ queues, Amazon SQS Amazon SNS, RabbitMQ fanout Kafka, Amazon Kinesis, Pulsar
Key idea

One mechanism gives both behaviors: inside a group, partitions are divided (queue); across groups, everything is shared (pub/sub). Module 7 covers groups in depth.

1.4What Kafka is, on one page

Term One-line meaning Module
Record (event, message) Key, value, headers, timestamp 2
Topic A named stream of records 2
Partition One ordered, append-only log; a topic has many 2
Offset A record's position in its partition 2, 8
Broker A Kafka server that stores partitions and serves clients 3
Controller (KRaft) The nodes that manage cluster metadata and leader elections 3
Replica, leader, follower Copies of a partition; the leader takes writes, followers copy it 3, 12
Producer Client that writes records 4 to 6
Consumer, consumer group Client that reads; a group splits partitions among its members 7 to 10
Kafka Connect Framework that moves data between Kafka and other systems 16
Kafka Streams Java library for processing streams with state 17

Four properties come out of this design:

  • Durable: records are written to disk on several brokers before they count as committed.
  • Scalable: more partitions spread load across more brokers and more consumers.
  • Ordered where it matters: strict order within a partition, chosen by the record key.
  • Replayable: records stay for the retention period, so any consumer can re-read history.

1.5Where Kafka fits

  • Event-driven microservices: services publish facts; others react. New features subscribe without changing the producer.
  • Activity tracking and analytics: clicks, page views, and app events at very high volume.
  • Log and metrics pipelines: agents ship logs to Kafka, which buffers them for search and storage systems.
  • Data integration and change data capture (CDC): stream every database change to caches, search indexes, and the data warehouse.
  • Stream processing: compute running totals, detect fraud patterns in time windows, and join streams as events arrive.
  • Audit trail and event sourcing: an ordered, immutable history of what happened.
  • Buffering: absorb bursts between fast producers and slow sinks.
In production

In a card platform, the authorization service publishes every authorization to one topic keyed by card ID. Fraud scoring, the ledger, customer notifications, rewards, and the data warehouse each consume it with their own consumer group. A new team (say, spend analytics) subscribes on day one and replays last week's events to backfill.

1.6When not to use Kafka

Try it first2 minutes

For each, Kafka or something else? (a) A mobile app needs a balance check that returns in 50 ms. (b) Send a reminder exactly 24 hours after signup. (c) Store 200 MB scanned KYC documents. (d) Five background jobs a minute for a small team on AWS.

Reveal the answer

(a) Something else: synchronous request-reply belongs on HTTP or gRPC. (b) Kafka has no per-message delay; use a scheduler, or a delay pattern (Module 10, Case study 8). (c) Store files in object storage and send a reference in the event (claim check, Module 15). (d) A managed queue such as SQS is simpler; Kafka is overkill unless it is already your platform.

  • Request-reply that needs an answer now. You can build it on Kafka, but it adds latency and complexity for no gain.
  • Per-message delays, priorities, or complex routing rules. RabbitMQ and SQS have these built in; on Kafka you build them from topics (Module 10 and Case study 8).
  • Large payloads. The default limit is about 1 MB per record batch. Put big objects in object storage.
  • Ad hoc queries. Kafka has no index by key or field. You cannot ask "all events for account 42" efficiently; sink the data into a database for that.
  • Global ordering at high throughput. Total order means one partition, which caps throughput at what one partition can handle.
  • Tiny workloads or no team to run it. Use a managed service (Confluent Cloud, Amazon MSK, Aiven) or a simpler queue.
Version note

Kafka 4.2 made share groups ("queues for Kafka") production-ready: many consumers share one partition and acknowledge records one at a time. That narrows the gap with classic job queues (Module 9).

1.7Kafka compared with other brokers

Kafka RabbitMQ Amazon SQS Apache Pulsar
Model Partitioned, replicated log Broker with exchanges and queues Fully managed queue Log with storage in Apache BookKeeper
Retention and replay Days, weeks, or forever; replay by offset Deleted on ack (streams add replay) 1 minute to 14 days, no replay Configurable; replay by cursor
Ordering Per partition Per queue with a single consumer FIFO queues: per message group Per partition or key
Scaling consumers Up to the partition count per group (share groups go beyond) Competing consumers on a queue Automatic Shared and key-shared subscriptions
Delays and priorities Not built in Priorities; delays via plugin Delay up to 15 minutes Delayed delivery built in
You operate Brokers and controllers (or use managed) Broker cluster Nothing Brokers and BookKeeper

1.8Common mistakes

Common mistakes

  • Treating Kafka as a database: expecting lookups by key or field. Sink data into a store built for queries.
  • Using Kafka for synchronous calls and then fighting timeouts with request-reply topics.
  • Assuming a message disappears after it is read, then being surprised by replays and duplicates.
  • Assuming one global order across a multi-partition topic.
  • Sending large files through Kafka instead of a reference to object storage.
  • Adding Kafka to a small system that one managed queue would serve.

1.9Self-check

Self-checkFive more, after the lessons
  1. In one sentence, what is a log in Kafka's sense?
    Reveal

    An append-only, ordered sequence of records where each record has an offset, writers append to the end, and each reader tracks its own position.

  2. How does Kafka act as a queue and as pub/sub at the same time?
    Reveal

    Within one consumer group, partitions are split among members, so each record is processed by one member (queue). Different groups read independently, so each group gets every record (pub/sub).

  3. Why does putting Kafka between services reduce coupling?
    Reveal

    Producers write events without knowing who reads them, and consumers read at their own pace. Neither must be up, fast, or even exist at the same time as the other.

  4. Give two costs of moving from synchronous calls to events.
    Reveal

    Effects happen later (eventual consistency) and consumers must handle duplicates and retries; also, you operate another distributed system and debugging spans asynchronous hops.

  5. A product manager asks to "query Kafka for all transactions of user 7 last March". What do you say?
    Reveal

    Kafka is not indexed by user. Stream the topic into a database or warehouse (Kafka Connect makes this easy) and query there.

Module 2: Events, topics, partitions, and offsets

The four words you will use every day. A record is an event; a topic is a named stream of records; a partition is one ordered log inside a topic; an offset is a record's position in that log. Get these exact and the rest of Kafka follows.

Warm-upWarm-up: one line each
  1. A record has no key. Which partition does it go to?
    Reveal

    The producer spreads keyless records across partitions (it fills a batch for one partition, then moves to another). There is no ordering between them.

  2. A topic has 4 partitions. Is there one global order across the topic?
    Reveal

    No. Order exists only within each partition.

  3. Are offsets numbered per topic or per partition?
    Reveal

    Per partition. Each partition has its own sequence starting at 0.

  4. Consumer A has read up to offset 100 in a partition. Can consumer B read offset 50 of the same partition?
    Reveal

    Yes. Readers are independent; each tracks its own position.

  5. Retention is 7 days and a consumer was down for 8 days. What happens when it returns?
    Reveal

    Records older than about 7 days were deleted, so its committed offset may now point before the start of the log. It jumps to the earliest or latest offset according to auto.offset.reset, and the deleted records are lost to it.

2.1Events and records

Try it first2 minutes

Write the record you would publish when a card payment is authorized. What is the key? What goes in the value? Which headers would you add?

Reveal the answer

Key: the card ID (or account ID), the entity whose events must stay in order. Value: an event ID for deduplication, amount, currency, merchant, authorization code, and the time it happened. Headers: event type, schema version, trace ID, and source service. Headers carry metadata; they do not affect routing.

Idea

An event says "something happened". Kafka stores it as a record: key, value, headers, and a timestamp.

Analogy

A printed receipt. Once printed it never changes; a refund is a new receipt, not an edit.

Rule

Records are immutable. You never update one in place; you append a new record.

  • Key and value are bytes. Producers turn objects into bytes with serializers and consumers turn them back with deserializers (Module 15). The key is optional.
  • Headers are key-value pairs of metadata, such as a trace ID or an event type.
  • Timestamp: by default the producer sets it when it creates the record (CreateTime). A topic can switch to broker time with message.timestamp.type=LogAppendTime. Since Kafka 4.0 the broker rejects CreateTime timestamps more than one hour in the future by default (message.timestamp.after.max.ms).
  • Size: the default broker limit is about 1 MB per record batch (message.max.bytes). Large payloads belong in object storage (Module 15).

2.2Topics

Try it first2 minutes

Should payment events and refund events share one topic?

Reveal the answer

It depends on ordering. If a consumer must see a refund after the payment it reverses, put both in one topic keyed by account or payment ID, because order only exists within a partition of one topic. If no consumer needs that cross-type order, separate topics are simpler to understand and secure.

  • A topic is a named stream: payments, card.authorizations.v1. Many producers can write to it and many consumers can read it.
  • Topic configs override broker defaults per topic: retention.ms, cleanup.policy, min.insync.replicas, max.message.bytes, and more.
  • Create topics explicitly with chosen partitions, replication, and retention. Brokers auto-create topics on first use by default (auto.create.topics.enable=true); most production clusters turn that off so a typo does not create a topic with one partition and one replica.
  • Name topics consistently, for example <domain>.<entity>.<event>.v<version>. Names are case-sensitive and cannot be changed later; you create a new topic and migrate.

2.3Partitions

Try it first2 minutes

A topic must take 50 MB/s and, on your hardware, one partition handles about 10 MB/s. What is the minimum partition count, and why do more partitions help?

Reveal the answer

At least 5, and more for headroom. Each partition is an independent log that can live on a different broker and be read by a different consumer, so partitions let writes, storage, and reads run in parallel.

Idea

A partition is one ordered, append-only log. A topic is a set of partitions.

Analogy

Supermarket checkout lanes. More lanes serve more customers, each lane is served in order, and there is no order between lanes.

Why it matters

The partition is the unit of parallelism, ordering, storage, and replication.

  • Writes only append to the end of a partition. The leader assigns the next offset.
  • Each partition replica lives on one broker, so one partition's throughput and size are bounded by one machine. More partitions spread a topic across machines.
  • Partition count is chosen at creation. You can increase it later but never decrease it, and increasing it remaps keys (Module 6).
  • Consumers: within one consumer group, each partition is read by at most one member at a time, so the partition count caps a group's parallelism (Module 7).

2.4Keys and ordering

  • The producer picks the partition from the key: by default murmur2(key bytes) modulo the partition count (Module 6). Same key, same partition, same order.
  • No key means the producer spreads records across partitions with no ordering promise.
  • Choose the key as the entity whose events must stay in order: account, card, order, or chat conversation. That gives per-entity order and lets different entities process in parallel.
Key idea

Kafka's ordering guarantee is per partition. Choose the key so that everything that must stay in order shares a partition, and accept that different keys interleave.

2.5Offsets

Try it first1 minute

In partition 2 your consumer processed every record up to offset 6, then committed offset 7 and restarted. Which record does it read first?

Reveal the answer

Offset 7. A committed offset is the next record to read, not the last one processed.

  • An offset is a record's position within its partition. The leader assigns it on append; it only increases and is never reused.
  • Offsets can have gaps. Compaction removes records, and transaction markers take up offsets (Module 14). Do not count records by subtracting offsets when exactness matters.
  • Consumers own their position. A consumer group commits offsets to Kafka (the internal __consumer_offsets topic) so a restart resumes where it left off (Module 8).
  • Consumers can move: to the beginning, the end, a specific offset, or the first offset at or after a timestamp.

2.6Retention: how long records live

  • With the default cleanup.policy=delete, records are removed when they are older than retention.ms (7 days by default) or when a partition exceeds retention.bytes (unlimited by default).
  • Reading never deletes. Deletion removes whole log segments, so data can stay a little longer than the retention setting (Module 11).
  • Retention can be infinite (retention.ms=-1) for event-sourced or audit topics; budget disk or use tiered storage (Module 11).
  • cleanup.policy=compact keeps the latest record per key instead (Module 13).

Choose retention from three questions: how long can a consumer be down and still recover? How far back will you replay? What do cost and compliance allow?

Watch out

If a consumer falls further behind than retention, it silently loses records: its offset becomes invalid and it resets to the earliest or latest offset. Alert on consumer lag measured in time, not only in messages.

2.7Lab: your first topic

LabCreate a topic, produce keyed records, read partitions and offsets15 minutes

Start the single broker from Lab setup, then open a shell in it:

Terminal
docker exec -it --workdir /opt/kafka/bin broker sh

Create a topic with three partitions and look at it:

Terminal
./kafka-topics.sh --bootstrap-server localhost:9092 --create --topic payments \
  --partitions 3 --replication-factor 1
./kafka-topics.sh --bootstrap-server localhost:9092 --describe --topic payments

Start a producer that reads key:value lines:

Terminal
./kafka-console-producer.sh --bootstrap-server localhost:9092 --topic payments \
  --reader-property parse.key=true --reader-property key.separator=:

Type these six lines, then press Ctrl-C:

Text
acct-5:deposit 100
acct-4:deposit 50
acct-5:withdraw 30
acct-1:deposit 70
acct-5:withdraw 10
acct-4:withdraw 20

Read everything, printing partition, offset, and key:

Terminal
./kafka-console-consumer.sh --bootstrap-server localhost:9092 --topic payments --from-beginning \
  --formatter-property print.partition=true \
  --formatter-property print.offset=true \
  --formatter-property print.key=true

Press Ctrl-C, then read only partition 0 starting at offset 1:

Terminal
./kafka-console-consumer.sh --bootstrap-server localhost:9092 --topic payments \
  --partition 0 --offset 1 \
  --formatter-property print.offset=true --formatter-property print.key=true
Check what you saw
  • acct-5 lands in partition 0 at offsets 0, 1, 2 in the order you typed; acct-4 in partition 1; acct-1 in partition 2. The key explorer in Module 6 computes the same partitions.
  • With --from-beginning, the consumer may print partitions in any interleaving, but within each partition the offsets are in order.
  • The last command prints withdraw 30 and withdraw 10 (offsets 1 and 2): you chose where to start.
  • Run the full read again: the records are still there. Reading did not delete them.

2.8Common mistakes

Common mistakes

  • Expecting global order across a multi-partition topic.
  • Picking a key that does not match the ordering need, for example keying by merchant when per-account order is what matters.
  • Relying on broker auto-creation and ending up with a one-partition, one-replica topic in production.
  • Treating the committed offset as the last processed record: it is the next one to read.
  • Setting retention shorter than the longest consumer outage you must survive.
  • Doing arithmetic on offsets and assuming they are contiguous.

2.9Self-check

Self-checkFive more, after the lessons
  1. What is the difference between a topic and a partition?
    Reveal

    A topic is a named stream; a partition is one ordered, append-only log inside it. A topic has one or more partitions spread across brokers.

  2. Why is the partition, not the topic, the unit of ordering?
    Reveal

    Each partition is appended by one leader in one sequence. Different partitions are independent logs on different brokers with no shared sequence.

  3. Which fields does the producer set, and which does the broker assign?
    Reveal

    The producer sets key, value, headers, and (by default) the timestamp. The broker assigns the partition's next offset; the partition itself is chosen by the producer's partitioner.

  4. Can you decrease a topic's partition count?
    Reveal

    No. You can only increase it, and doing so changes which partition a key maps to. To shrink, create a new topic and migrate.

  5. A consumer committed offset 500 in partition 3. What does that mean?
    Reveal

    It has processed everything before offset 500 in partition 3, and on restart it reads offset 500 next.

Module 3: Brokers, clusters, and KRaft

Where partitions physically live and who decides who leads them. This module covers brokers and replicas, the KRaft controller quorum that replaced ZooKeeper, how clients discover the right broker, the listener settings that trip up every first Docker setup, and the internal topics you will see in any cluster.

9 lessons4 figures1 lab6 mastery checks

On this page

  1. 3.1Brokers and the cluster
  2. 3.2Replication in brief

  4. 3.4How clients find the right broker
  5. 3.5Listeners and advertised listeners
  6. 3.6Internal topics you will see
  7. 3.7Lab: a three-broker cluster and a failure
  8. 3.8Common mistakes

Warm-upWarm-up: one line each
  1. A topic has replication factor 3. How many replica failures can committed data survive?
    Reveal

    Two, as long as the surviving replica was in sync. Writes with acks=all may stop earlier, depending on min.insync.replicas.

  2. A producer sends a record for partition 2. Which broker receives it?
    Reveal

    The current leader of partition 2. Clients learn leaders from metadata and send directly to them.

  3. What did ZooKeeper do for Kafka, and what replaced it?
    Reveal

    It stored cluster metadata and elected the controller. KRaft, a quorum of Kafka controllers using the Raft protocol, replaced it; Kafka 4.0 removed ZooKeeper support.

  4. bootstrap.servers lists one broker, but the cluster has 12. Does the client use all 12?
    Reveal

    Yes. The bootstrap address is only for the first metadata request, which returns every broker. List two or three for redundancy.

  5. A laptop producer reaches Kafka in Docker, but sends fail with "unknown host kafka". What is wrong?
    Reveal

    The broker's advertised listener tells clients to connect to kafka:9092, a name only the Docker network can resolve.

3.1Brokers and the cluster

Try it first2 minutes

Three brokers, a topic with 6 partitions and replication factor 1. One broker dies. What happens?

Reveal the answer

The two partitions stored on that broker go offline: their reads and writes fail until it returns, because no other broker has a copy. The other four partitions keep working. This is why production topics use replication factor 3.

Idea

A broker is one Kafka server process. It stores partition replicas on its disks and serves produce and fetch requests for them. A cluster is a group of brokers that share metadata.

Analogy

Bank branches. Each ledger has its master copy at one branch and photocopies at two others. Customers go to the branch with the master copy.

  • Each broker has a unique node.id. A broker can host thousands of partition replicas.
  • Partitions and their leaders are spread across brokers so load is shared.
  • Leaders do the work: producers write to the leader; consumers read from the leader by default. Followers fetch from the leader to stay in sync.

3.2Replication in brief

  • Replication factor (RF): how many copies of each partition exist, counting the leader. RF 3 is the production norm.
  • In-sync replicas (ISR): the replicas that are fully caught up with the leader. A follower that falls behind for longer than replica.lag.time.max.ms (30 seconds by default) is removed from the ISR.
  • Failover: if a leader's broker dies, the controller picks a new leader from the ISR, so no committed record is lost.
  • The production recipe is RF 3, min.insync.replicas=2, and producers with acks=all. Module 5 explains each part; Module 12 covers replication internals.
Replication factor Copies Typical use
1 One; a broker loss takes the partition offline and can lose data Local development only
2 Survives one failure, but writes with min.insync.replicas=2 stop when one replica is down Rare
3 Survives one failure with writes continuing, two failures without losing committed data Production default

3.3The controller and KRaft

Try it first2 minutes

Why can't each broker decide by itself which replica of a partition is the leader?

Reveal the answer

Two brokers could each believe they are the leader (split brain) and accept conflicting writes. Leadership must come from one source of truth that every broker agrees on, which needs a consensus protocol.

Idea

Controllers manage cluster metadata: which brokers are alive, each partition's leader and ISR, and topic configs. In KRaft mode they agree on that metadata with the Raft consensus protocol.

Analogy

An air traffic control tower. Planes fly themselves, but the tower assigns runways and every pilot follows the tower.

  • Roles: each node runs as a broker, a controller, or both (process.roles=broker,controller, called combined mode, fine for development but not recommended for critical production).
  • Quorum size: run 3 or 5 controllers. A majority must be alive: 3 tolerate one failure, 5 tolerate two.
  • Active controller: the Raft leader among the controllers. It writes every metadata change to the __cluster_metadata log; standbys replicate it and can take over immediately.
  • Brokers fetch the metadata log to keep their cache current and send heartbeats. A broker that misses heartbeats for broker.session.timeout.ms (9 seconds by default) is fenced, and its partitions get new leaders.
Version note

ZooKeeper mode was removed in Kafka 4.0. A ZooKeeper-based cluster must first migrate to KRaft on a 3.x release (3.9 is the recommended bridge) before upgrading to 4.x. Interview answers about "ZooKeeper stores offsets" are a decade out of date: offsets have lived in the __consumer_offsets topic since the Java consumer arrived in Kafka 0.9.

3.4How clients find the right broker

  • bootstrap.servers is only for first contact. List two or three brokers, or one DNS name that resolves to several, so a single dead broker does not block startup.
  • Clients route themselves. The producer picks the partition and sends to its leader; there is no proxy in the data path. Every client must be able to reach every broker directly.
  • Metadata refresh happens periodically (metadata.max.age.ms, 5 minutes) and immediately after errors such as NOT_LEADER_OR_FOLLOWER. Clients retry these errors automatically.

3.5Listeners and advertised listeners

  • listeners: where the broker binds, one entry per named listener, for example INTERNAL://:19092,EXTERNAL://:9092,CONTROLLER://:9093.
  • advertised.listeners: the address the broker hands to clients in metadata, per listener. It must be resolvable and reachable from the clients that use that listener.
  • listener.security.protocol.map maps each name to PLAINTEXT, SSL, SASL_PLAINTEXT, or SASL_SSL. inter.broker.listener.name and controller.listener.names say which listener brokers and controllers use among themselves.
server.properties (one broker, reachable from Docker and from the host)
listeners=INTERNAL://:19092,EXTERNAL://:9092,CONTROLLER://:9093
advertised.listeners=INTERNAL://kafka:19092,EXTERNAL://localhost:9092
listener.security.protocol.map=INTERNAL:PLAINTEXT,EXTERNAL:PLAINTEXT,CONTROLLER:PLAINTEXT
inter.broker.listener.name=INTERNAL
controller.listener.names=CONTROLLER
At work

In Kubernetes, external clients need a reachable address for each broker (a per-broker service or load balancer). One shared load balancer works for bootstrap only; after metadata, clients connect to individual brokers.

3.6Internal topics you will see

Topic Holds Notes
__consumer_offsets Committed offsets and group metadata 50 partitions by default, compacted
__transaction_state Transaction coordinator state Used by transactional producers (Module 14)
__share_group_state Share group delivery state Created on first use of share groups
__cluster_metadata KRaft metadata log Lives on controllers; not a regular topic
connect-configs, connect-offsets, connect-status Kafka Connect state Names are configurable (Module 16)
<app>-...-changelog, <app>-...-repartition Kafka Streams state and reshuffles Created by the Streams app (Module 17)
_schemas Confluent Schema Registry storage Part of the ecosystem, not Apache Kafka

Never write to or delete internal topics by hand.

3.7Lab: a three-broker cluster and a failure

LabWatch leadership move when a broker dies20 minutes

Start the three-node cluster from Lab setup. Define a helper so commands stay short:

Terminal
k() { tool=$1; shift; docker exec -it kafka-1 /opt/kafka/bin/$tool --bootstrap-server kafka-1:19092 "$@"; }

Create a replicated topic and describe it:

Terminal
k kafka-topics.sh --create --topic orders --partitions 6 --replication-factor 3
k kafka-topics.sh --describe --topic orders

Stop one node, describe again, and list under-replicated partitions:

Terminal
docker stop kafka-2
k kafka-topics.sh --describe --topic orders
k kafka-topics.sh --describe --under-replicated-partitions

Bring it back, wait 30 seconds, then restore preferred leaders and check the controller quorum:

Terminal
docker start kafka-2
k kafka-topics.sh --describe --topic orders
k kafka-leader-election.sh --election-type preferred --all-topic-partitions
k kafka-metadata-quorum.sh describe --status
Check what you saw
  • Before the stop, each partition shows Replicas: a,b,c and Isr: with all three nodes, and leaders are spread across nodes 1, 2, 3.
  • After docker stop kafka-2, node 2 disappears from every Isr list, and partitions it led now show leader 1 or 3. The topic keeps working.
  • After the restart, node 2 rejoins the ISR once caught up, but it leads nothing until the preferred leader election (or the automatic rebalance, auto.leader.rebalance.enable, which runs every 5 minutes by default) moves leadership back to the first replica in each list.
  • describe --status shows the controller leader, the voters, and the high watermark of the metadata log. These are combined nodes, so stopping one node also stopped one of three controllers; the quorum survived because two of three remained.

3.8Common mistakes

Common mistakes

  • Replication factor 1 or 2 in production, or relying on auto-created topics that use default.replication.factor=1.
  • Wrong advertised.listeners: clients connect for bootstrap and then fail on every request.
  • A load balancer in front of brokers for data traffic. Clients must reach each broker directly.
  • An even number of controllers: 4 controllers tolerate one failure, the same as 3.
  • Combined broker-controller nodes in a critical production cluster, so a busy broker can starve the controller.
  • Describing ZooKeeper's role in a modern cluster: Kafka 4.x has none.

3.9Self-check

Self-checkFive more, after the lessons
  1. What does the active controller do?
    Reveal

    It is the Raft leader of the controller quorum. It records metadata changes (topics, partition leaders, ISR, configs, broker registrations) in the metadata log and decides leader elections; brokers follow that log.

  2. Why 3 or 5 controllers, never 4?
    Reveal

    Raft needs a majority. 4 nodes need 3 alive, tolerating one failure, the same as 3 nodes, while costing more and adding a vote to wait for.

  3. What happens to a partition's leadership when its leader's broker stops heartbeating?
    Reveal

    After broker.session.timeout.ms, the controller fences the broker and elects a new leader from the partition's ISR, then publishes the change; clients refresh metadata and move.

  4. Why must every client reach every broker?
    Reveal

    Clients send each request to the leader of the target partition, which can be any broker. Only bootstrap can go through a shared address.

  5. What is the difference between listeners and advertised.listeners?
    Reveal

    listeners is where the broker binds and accepts connections. advertised.listeners is the address it tells clients to use; it must be reachable from those clients.

Module 4: The producer, end to end

What actually happens between producer.send() and a record sitting on a broker. You will learn the send path, batching with batch.size and linger.ms, compression, the timeouts that bound every send, which errors are retried for you, and how to write a producer you can trust in production.

8 lessons2 figures1 lab6 mastery checks

On this page

  1. 4.1What send() does
  2. 4.2Writing a producer
  3. 4.3Batching: batch.size and linger.ms
  4. 4.4Compression
  5. 4.5Timeouts and errors
  6. 4.6Lab: measure batching and compression
  7. 4.7Common mistakes
  8. 4.8Self-check
Warm-upWarm-up: one line each
  1. Does producer.send() block until the broker has the record?
    Reveal

    No. It appends the record to an in-memory batch and returns a Future immediately. A background thread sends batches; the callback or future completes when the broker replies.

  2. Should you create a new KafkaProducer for each HTTP request?
    Reveal

    No. A producer is thread-safe and expensive to create (connections, buffers, metadata). Share one per application and close it on shutdown.

  3. What do linger.ms and batch.size control?
    Reveal

    When a batch is sent: as soon as it reaches batch.size bytes, or after waiting linger.ms for more records, whichever comes first.

  4. Your callback receives an exception. Has the producer already retried?
    Reveal

    For retriable errors, yes: it retries until delivery.timeout.ms (2 minutes by default) runs out. An exception in the callback means retries are exhausted or the error cannot be retried.

  5. Where does compression happen: producer, broker, or consumer?
    Reveal

    The producer compresses whole batches, the broker stores them compressed (with the default topic setting), and the consumer decompresses.

4.1What send() does

Try it first2 minutes

Your service calls send() 10,000 times per second for 3 partitions. If each call made its own network request to the broker, what would hurt? What would you do instead?

Reveal the answer

Ten thousand small requests per second means per-request overhead (headers, syscalls, acknowledgments) dominates and the broker's request threads saturate. Instead, buffer records per partition and send them in batches: one request can carry hundreds of records. That is exactly what the producer does.

Idea

send() does the cheap work on your thread (serialize, pick a partition, append to a batch) and returns. A background sender thread does the network work in batches.

Analogy

A post office counter. You drop letters in the bin for each city and walk away; a van leaves for a city when its bin is full or on a timer, carrying many letters per trip.

  1. Interceptors (optional) can inspect or modify each record, for example to add tracing headers.
  2. Serializers turn the key and value into bytes. A serialization error is thrown from send() itself.
  3. The partitioner picks the partition (Module 6). This needs topic metadata; if it is missing, send() waits up to max.block.ms (60 seconds).
  4. The record accumulator appends the record to the open batch for that partition. Memory for all batches is capped by buffer.memory (32 MB); when it is full, send() blocks up to max.block.ms and then fails the record with a TimeoutException, reported to the callback and the returned Future.
  5. The sender thread drains ready batches, groups them by the broker that leads each partition, and sends one produce request per broker.
  6. The response completes each record's Future and runs its callback, on the producer's I/O thread.

4.2Writing a producer

PaymentProducer.java
import org.apache.kafka.clients.producer.*;
import org.apache.kafka.common.serialization.StringSerializer;
import java.util.Properties;

public class PaymentProducer {
    public static void main(String[] args) {
        Properties props = new Properties();
        props.put(ProducerConfig.BOOTSTRAP_SERVERS_CONFIG, "localhost:9092");
        props.put(ProducerConfig.KEY_SERIALIZER_CLASS_CONFIG, StringSerializer.class.getName());
        props.put(ProducerConfig.VALUE_SERIALIZER_CLASS_CONFIG, StringSerializer.class.getName());
        // acks=all and idempotence are already the defaults; stating them documents intent
        props.put(ProducerConfig.ACKS_CONFIG, "all");
        props.put(ProducerConfig.ENABLE_IDEMPOTENCE_CONFIG, true);
        props.put(ProducerConfig.LINGER_MS_CONFIG, 10);
        props.put(ProducerConfig.COMPRESSION_TYPE_CONFIG, "lz4");

        try (Producer<String, String> producer = new KafkaProducer<>(props)) {
            ProducerRecord<String, String> record =
                new ProducerRecord<>("payments", "acct-42", "{\"type\":\"DEBIT\",\"amt\":1250}");
            record.headers().add("event-type", "PaymentDebited".getBytes());

            producer.send(record, (metadata, exception) -> {
                if (exception != null) {
                    // retries are exhausted or the error is not retriable
                    System.err.println("send failed: " + exception);
                } else {
                    System.out.printf("stored in %s-%d at offset %d%n",
                        metadata.topic(), metadata.partition(), metadata.offset());
                }
            });
        } // close() sends everything still buffered and waits for responses
    }
}
  • Asynchronous with a callback (above) is the normal style. Keep callbacks short: they run on the producer's only I/O thread, so a slow callback delays every other send. Never call flush() inside a callback (Kafka 4.1+ rejects it).
  • Synchronous: producer.send(record).get() blocks until the broker answers. It is simple and correct, but it sends one record per round trip. Use it in scripts, tests, or when you must confirm before replying to a caller, and expect much lower throughput.
  • One producer per application, shared across threads. Sharing also helps batching.
  • flush() sends everything buffered and waits. Use it when you must be sure records are written before a next step, such as committing a consumer offset in a non-transactional pipeline.

4.3Batching: batch.size and linger.ms

Try it first2 minutes

A producer sends 200 records per second, about 1 KB each, to one partition. With linger.ms=0, roughly how many records go in each request? With linger.ms=20?

Reveal the answer

At 200 records per second, records arrive about every 5 ms. With linger.ms=0, a batch is sent as soon as the sender is free, so most requests carry one record. With linger.ms=20, the producer waits up to 20 ms, so a batch collects about 4 records: four times fewer requests for at most 20 ms of extra latency.

  • batch.size (16 KB by default) is the maximum size of one partition's batch. A full batch is sent at once.
  • linger.ms (5 ms by default since Kafka 4.0, previously 0) is how long a batch may wait for more records before it is sent anyway.
  • Under heavy load batches fill before linger.ms expires, so linger adds no latency. Under light load a small linger groups records that would otherwise go one per request.
  • Typical high-throughput settings: batch.size 64 KB to 256 KB and linger.ms 10 to 50 ms. Measure; Module 19 covers tuning.

4.4Compression

compression.type Ratio CPU When to use
none (default) 1x None Already compressed or tiny payloads
lz4 Good Very low Common default choice for throughput
zstd Best Low to moderate Large JSON or text, network or disk bound
snappy Moderate Low Older setups
gzip High High Rarely the best choice today
  • Compression works on whole batches, so bigger batches compress better: batching and compression reinforce each other.
  • The broker keeps the producer's compression when the topic's compression.type is producer (the default). If a topic forces a different codec, the broker must recompress every batch, which costs broker CPU.
  • Consumers decompress automatically; nothing to configure.

4.5Timeouts and errors

Try it first2 minutes

A leader election takes 8 seconds. The producer has delivery.timeout.ms=120000. What does the application see?

Reveal the answer

Nothing, apart from some latency. The producer gets NOT_LEADER_OR_FOLLOWER or timeouts, refreshes metadata, and retries on the new leader. As long as the record succeeds within 120 seconds, the callback reports success.

  • delivery.timeout.ms (120 s) is the upper bound on how long a record may take from send() returning to its callback: time waiting in the batch, every retry, and time in flight. When it expires the callback gets a TimeoutException.
  • request.timeout.ms (30 s) bounds one request to the broker.
  • retries defaults to the maximum integer: in practice delivery.timeout.ms decides when to give up. Retries back off from retry.backoff.ms (100 ms) up to retry.backoff.max.ms (1 s).
Error Retriable? What it means
NotLeaderOrFollowerException Yes Leadership moved; metadata refresh fixes it
NotEnoughReplicasException Yes Fewer in-sync replicas than min.insync.replicas (Module 5)
TimeoutException (request) Yes Broker slow or unreachable
UnknownTopicOrPartitionException Yes Topic missing or metadata stale
RecordTooLargeException No Record bigger than max.request.size or the topic's limit
SerializationException No Thrown by send() itself
TopicAuthorizationException No The client lacks permission
Key idea

When the callback reports a failure, the record is not in Kafka. Decide deliberately: fail the user's request, keep the event in a database outbox and publish later (Module 14), or alert. Logging and moving on silently loses data.

4.6Lab: measure batching and compression

LabProducer throughput with different linger.ms and compression15 minutes

In the single-broker container shell, create a topic and run the producer load test three times:

Terminal
./kafka-topics.sh --bootstrap-server localhost:9092 --create --topic perf --partitions 6 --replication-factor 1

./kafka-producer-perf-test.sh --bootstrap-server localhost:9092 --topic perf \
  --num-records 500000 --record-size 1000 --throughput -1 \
  --command-property linger.ms=0 --command-property batch.size=16384

./kafka-producer-perf-test.sh --bootstrap-server localhost:9092 --topic perf \
  --num-records 500000 --record-size 1000 --throughput -1 \
  --command-property linger.ms=20 --command-property batch.size=131072

./kafka-producer-perf-test.sh --bootstrap-server localhost:9092 --topic perf \
  --num-records 500000 --record-size 1000 --throughput -1 \
  --command-property linger.ms=20 --command-property batch.size=131072 \
  --command-property compression.type=lz4

Compare the final line of each run: records/sec, MB/sec, and the average and 99th percentile latency.

Check what you saw
  • The second run usually shows clearly higher throughput than the first: larger, fuller batches mean fewer requests.
  • The test sends random bytes, which barely compress, so lz4 changes little here. With real JSON payloads, compression often shrinks data several times and raises throughput further.
  • Latency numbers include time spent waiting in batches, so a larger linger can raise average latency even while throughput improves. Under this full load the batches fill quickly, so the effect is small.
  • Your exact numbers depend on your laptop. The point is the direction of each change.

4.7Common mistakes

Common mistakes

  • Creating a producer per request or per message, which wastes connections and kills batching.
  • Calling .get() on every send in a hot path, turning a batching client into one record per round trip.
  • Ignoring the callback's exception, so failed sends vanish silently.
  • Doing slow work in the callback, which stalls the producer's I/O thread.
  • Never closing the producer, which drops buffered records on shutdown.
  • Setting linger.ms=0 everywhere out of habit and getting tiny batches under normal load.

4.8Self-check

Self-checkFive more, after the lessons
  1. List the steps a record takes inside the producer before it leaves the machine.
    Reveal

    Interceptors, key and value serialization, partition selection, append to that partition's batch in the record accumulator, then the sender thread drains ready batches into one request per leader broker.

  2. When is a batch sent?
    Reveal

    When it reaches batch.size, when it has waited linger.ms, or when something forces it out (flush(), close(), or a full buffer).

  3. What happens when buffer.memory is exhausted?
    Reveal

    send() blocks for up to max.block.ms, then fails the record with a TimeoutException (through the callback and Future). It means the producer cannot send as fast as you produce, often because brokers are slow or unreachable. Because send() can block, lower max.block.ms in threads that must never stall, such as an event loop.

  4. Which timeout decides when the producer gives up on a record?
    Reveal

    delivery.timeout.ms, which covers batching, all retries, and in-flight time.

  5. Why does compression get better with larger batches?
    Reveal

    The codec compresses a whole batch at once, so it finds more repetition across many similar records.

Module 5: Durability and ordering on the write path

When can a producer trust that a record is safe, and will records stay in order? This module covers acks, min.insync.replicas, why retries create duplicates, how the idempotent producer removes them, how in-flight requests interact with ordering, and the safe producer configuration you should be able to recite.

9 lessons3 figures1 lab6 mastery checks

On this page

  1. 5.1acks: when the leader answers
  2. 5.2min.insync.replicas: a floor for acks=all
  3. 5.3Retries and the duplicate problem
  4. 5.4The idempotent producer
  5. 5.5Ordering with retries in flight
  6. 5.6The safe producer configuration
  7. 5.7Lab: min.insync.replicas in action
  8. 5.8Common mistakes
  9. 5.9Self-check
Warm-upWarm-up: one line each
  1. With acks=1, when does the producer get its acknowledgment?
    Reveal

    As soon as the leader has written the record to its own log, before any follower has copied it.

  2. Replication factor 3, min.insync.replicas=2, acks=all. Two brokers holding replicas go down. Can you still write?
    Reveal

    No. Only one replica is in sync, fewer than 2, so writes fail with NotEnoughReplicasException. Reads still work and no acknowledged record is lost.

  3. Why can a producer retry create a duplicate?
    Reveal

    The broker may have written the batch and only the acknowledgment was lost. The producer cannot tell, so it sends the batch again.

  4. What does enable.idempotence=true add to each batch?
    Reveal

    A producer ID and a per-partition sequence number, so the broker can recognize and drop a batch it has already written.

  5. You set acks=1 and leave enable.idempotence unset. Is the producer idempotent?
    Reveal

    No. Idempotence needs acks=all; when a conflicting setting is present and idempotence was not set explicitly, the client silently disables it.

5.1acks: when the leader answers

Try it first2 minutes

For each, choose acks=0, 1, or all: (a) debug logs you can afford to lose, (b) clickstream for a dashboard, (c) card authorizations feeding the ledger.

Reveal the answer

(a) acks=0 or 1: loss is acceptable and latency is lowest. (b) acks=1 is common, though all costs little with batching. (c) acks=all with min.insync.replicas=2: an acknowledged authorization must survive a broker crash.

acks Producer waits for Can an acknowledged record be lost? Latency
0 Nothing Yes, and failures are not even reported Lowest
1 The leader's own write Yes, if the leader dies before followers copy it Low
all (or -1) Every in-sync replica No, while one in-sync replica survives and unclean election is off Higher by one replication round trip

acks=all has been the default since Kafka 3.0. "All" means all replicas currently in the ISR, not all replicas that exist. That is why it needs a floor, which is the next lesson.

5.2min.insync.replicas: a floor for acks=all

Try it first2 minutes

Replication factor 3, acks=all, and min.insync.replicas=1. Two followers fall out of the ISR. The leader acknowledges a write and then its disk dies. What happened?

Reveal the answer

With only the leader in the ISR, "all in-sync replicas" was just the leader, so the write was acknowledged with a single copy, and that copy is gone. min.insync.replicas=2 would have refused the write instead of pretending it was safe.

  • min.insync.replicas is a topic config (with a broker or cluster default) and only matters for producers using acks=all.
  • If the ISR is smaller than this number, the leader rejects the write with NotEnoughReplicasException. If the ISR shrinks after the leader appended but before the acknowledgment, the producer gets NotEnoughReplicasAfterAppendException. Both are retriable, so the producer keeps trying until delivery.timeout.ms.
  • The standard recipe is replication factor 3 with min.insync.replicas=2: writes continue with one broker down, and every acknowledged record exists on at least two brokers.
Durability and availability simulatorOne partition. Click a broker to cycle it through in sync, lagging (alive but out of the ISR), and down.

Model: in-sync replicas hold every committed record; lagging replicas are missing recent ones. The high watermark rule shown here (it stops while the ISR is below min.insync.replicas) applies since Kafka 3.7.

RF, min ISR Brokers down acks=all writes Acknowledged data
3, 2 0 or 1 Accepted Safe
3, 2 2 Rejected (NotEnoughReplicas) Safe; reads still served
3, 1 2 Accepted on the leader alone At risk if the leader then fails
3, 3 1 Rejected Safe, but any single failure stops writes
Version note

Since Kafka 3.7, a leader also stops advancing the high watermark while the ISR is smaller than min.insync.replicas. Records written with acks=1 in that state are accepted but stay invisible to consumers until the ISR recovers. Module 12 explains the high watermark.

5.3Retries and the duplicate problem

  • A timeout is ambiguous: the request may have failed, or it may have succeeded with the response lost. The producer must retry to avoid loss, and retries risk duplicates.
  • At-least-once is what you get from retries alone: nothing lost, duplicates possible.
  • The idempotent producer removes the duplicates that its own retries create.

5.4The idempotent producer

Idea

Each producer gets a producer ID (PID) from the broker and numbers its batches per partition. The leader remembers the last few sequence numbers per PID and partition and rejects anything it has already written.

Analogy

Numbered cheques. A bank that has cleared cheque 107 from your account will not clear another cheque 107, even if the courier delivers it twice.

  • On by default since Kafka 3.0. It requires acks=all, retries above 0, and max.in.flight.requests.per.connection of 5 or less. If you set acks to 0 or 1, or retries=0, without explicitly enabling idempotence, the client quietly turns idempotence off (with enable.idempotence=true set explicitly, it refuses to start instead). An in-flight limit above 5 fails at startup unless you explicitly disable idempotence.
  • Cost: almost none. Keep it on.
  • Scope: one producer instance (one PID), per partition. It does not protect against:
    • your own code catching a failed send and calling send() again (a new record with a new sequence number),
    • a producer that restarts and resends records it was unsure about (a new PID),
    • two producer instances sending the same business event.
  • For those cases you need transactions (a stable transactional.id, Module 14) or idempotent consumers keyed by a business ID (Module 10).

5.5Ordering with retries in flight

Try it first2 minutes

max.in.flight.requests.per.connection=5 lets the producer send 5 requests to a broker before hearing back. Without idempotence, how can that reorder records within one partition?

Reveal the answer

Request 1 fails with a retriable error while request 2 succeeds. The producer retries request 1, which lands after request 2. The partition now holds batch 2 before batch 1.

  • With idempotence on, the broker requires sequence numbers to arrive in order. Batch 2 is rejected until batch 1 is written, so ordering holds with up to 5 requests in flight.
  • With idempotence off, the only way to guarantee order with retries is max.in.flight.requests.per.connection=1, which costs throughput. This was common advice before Kafka 3.0.

5.6The safe producer configuration

producer.properties (what each line protects)
# durability: wait for every in-sync replica (default since 3.0)
acks=all
# no duplicates from the producer's own retries, ordering kept (default since 3.0)
enable.idempotence=true
# keep retrying transient errors for up to 2 minutes (defaults)
retries=2147483647
delivery.timeout.ms=120000
# up to 5 is safe with idempotence (default)
max.in.flight.requests.per.connection=5
topic and broker settings that complete the picture
replication.factor=3
min.insync.replicas=2
unclean.leader.election.enable=false

And in your code: handle the callback's exception. A record whose callback reports failure is not in Kafka, whatever the settings say.

Interview signal

"How do you make sure a payment event is never lost and never duplicated by the producer?" A strong answer names all of it: acks=all, replication factor 3, min.insync.replicas=2, unclean election off, idempotence on, callbacks that handle failure, and for duplicates beyond one producer session, a business ID that consumers deduplicate on.

5.7Lab: min.insync.replicas in action

LabMake acks=all writes fail safely while acks=1 still succeeds15 minutes

Use the three-broker cluster and the k helper from Lab setup. To see the effect with only one node down (so the controller quorum keeps its majority), set the floor to 3 for this experiment:

Terminal
k kafka-topics.sh --create --topic ledger --partitions 1 --replication-factor 3 \
  --config min.insync.replicas=3
k kafka-topics.sh --describe --topic ledger

Note the leader, then stop one of the other two nodes. For example, if the leader is 1:

Terminal
docker stop kafka-3
k kafka-topics.sh --describe --topic ledger

Try a write with acks=all, then with acks=1. Type one line in each, then press Ctrl-C. (retries=0 is only there so the first error shows at once instead of after two minutes of retries.)

Terminal
docker exec -it kafka-1 /opt/kafka/bin/kafka-console-producer.sh \
  --bootstrap-server kafka-1:19092 --topic ledger \
  --command-property acks=all --command-property retries=0

docker exec -it kafka-1 /opt/kafka/bin/kafka-console-producer.sh \
  --bootstrap-server kafka-1:19092 --topic ledger --command-property acks=1

Restart the node when you are done: docker start kafka-3.

Check what you saw
  • After the stop, describe shows an ISR of two nodes, below the topic's min.insync.replicas=3.
  • The acks=all producer reports a NotEnoughReplicasException: the leader refuses a write it cannot place on enough replicas. With normal retries the producer would keep trying until delivery.timeout.ms. No acknowledged data was put at risk.
  • The acks=1 producer reports no error: the leader accepted the record with fewer copies than the topic demands. Because the ISR is below min.insync.replicas, the high watermark does not advance, so consumers will not see this record until the third replica rejoins.
  • With the production setting min.insync.replicas=2, the same thing happens when two of three replicas are unavailable.

5.8Common mistakes

Common mistakes

  • acks=all with min.insync.replicas=1: "all" can mean just the leader.
  • min.insync.replicas equal to the replication factor: one broker restart stops all writes.
  • Turning off idempotence by setting acks=1 without noticing.
  • Believing idempotence gives end-to-end exactly-once: it only covers one producer's own retries.
  • Retrying failed sends in application code without a business ID for deduplication.
  • Raising max.in.flight.requests.per.connection above 5, which is incompatible with idempotence (Kafka 4.0 no longer falls back silently).

5.9Self-check

Self-checkFive more, after the lessons
  1. What exactly does acks=all wait for?
    Reveal

    For the record to be written by every replica that is in the partition's ISR at that moment, and only if the ISR has at least min.insync.replicas members.

  2. Why does the standard setup use RF 3 and min.insync.replicas=2 rather than 3 and 3?
    Reveal

    With 2, writes continue through one broker failure and every acknowledged record is on two brokers. With 3, any single broker restart blocks all writes.

  3. How does the broker detect a duplicate batch from an idempotent producer?
    Reveal

    It tracks the producer ID, epoch, and the last sequence numbers it wrote for each partition. A batch whose sequence it has already written is acknowledged without being written again.

  4. Why is max.in.flight.requests.per.connection limited to 5 with idempotence?
    Reveal

    The broker keeps metadata for the last 5 batches per producer and partition to detect duplicates and enforce order; more in-flight batches than that could not be checked.

  5. Name two duplicate sources the idempotent producer does not prevent.
    Reveal

    Application code that re-sends after a failure, and a restarted producer that resends records it was unsure about. Each produces records with new sequence numbers or a new producer ID.
