Module 6: Keys and partitioning

The key you choose decides ordering, load balance, and how far a topic can scale. This module shows exactly how the producer picks a partition, how to choose a key, how to spot and fix hot partitions, what changes when you add partitions, and how to size the partition count.

10 lessons3 figures1 lab6 mastery checks

On this page

  1. 6.1How the producer picks a partition
  2. 6.2Choosing a key
  3. 6.3Hot partitions
  4. 6.4The key-to-partition explorer
  5. 6.5Changing the partition count
  6. 6.6How many partitions
  7. 6.7Custom partitioners
  8. 6.8Lab: predict partitions, then add one
  9. 6.9Common mistakes
  10. 6.10Self-check
Warm-upWarm-up: one line each
  1. Two records have the same key. Will they always land in the same partition?
    Reveal

    Yes, as long as the partition count does not change and both producers hash the same serialized key bytes the same way.

  2. Why might a Java producer and a Python (librdkafka) producer put the same key in different partitions?
    Reveal

    librdkafka's default partitioner hashes keys with CRC32, while the Java client uses murmur2. Set librdkafka's partitioner=murmur2_random to match Java.

  3. One merchant produces 60% of all payment events and the key is merchant_id. Will adding partitions help?
    Reveal

    No. One key always maps to one partition, so that partition, its broker, and its consumer still carry 60% of the load. Change or extend the key.

  4. You grow a keyed topic from 6 to 8 partitions. What breaks?
    Reveal

    Most keys now hash to a different partition. A key's old records stay in the old partition and its new records go to the new one, so a consumer can process new events before old ones.

  5. What caps how many consumers in one group can work in parallel?
    Reveal

    The number of partitions. Extra consumers sit idle (share groups are the exception).

6.1How the producer picks a partition

  • Keyed records: partition = toPositive(murmur2(serialized key bytes)) % numPartitions. Same bytes, same partition.
  • Keyless records: the producer sticks to one partition until about batch.size bytes have gone to it, then switches. (Sticky partitioning arrived in Kafka 2.4; the current byte-based, adaptive version in 3.3. Before that, keyless records went round robin.) This builds full batches instead of many tiny ones. With partitioner.adaptive.partitioning.enable=true (the default) it sends more to partitions whose brokers are keeping up.
  • The hash runs on bytes, not on your object. Changing the key serializer (for example from String to Avro) changes the partition for the same logical key.
  • partitioner.ignore.keys=true makes keyed records use the sticky behavior too. That gives up per-key ordering.

6.2Choosing a key

Try it first3 minutes

Pick a key for each topic: (a) card authorizations where a card's events must be processed in order, (b) app click events for analytics where order does not matter, (c) chat messages that must appear in order per conversation, (d) inventory updates per SKU in a flash sale with one viral product.

Reveal the answer

(a) card_id. (b) No key, or a random one: maximum spread. (c) conversation_id. (d) sku_id gives per-SKU order, but the viral SKU becomes a hot key; see the next lesson for options.

A good key has three properties:

  1. It matches the ordering need. Everything that must be processed in order shares the key, and nothing more.
  2. It has many distinct values, far more than the partition count, so load spreads evenly.
  3. It has no giants. No single value should carry a large share of traffic.
Need Key Notes
Per-entity order (account, card, order, user) That entity's ID The common case
Per-tenant order in a multi-tenant system tenant_id Watch for one huge tenant
No ordering need null Best spread, best batching
Joins in stream processing The join key Both topics need the same key and partition count (Module 17)

6.3Hot partitions

  • Symptoms: one partition's consumer lag grows while others are near zero; one broker has much higher bytes in; one consumer instance is at 100% CPU.
  • More partitions do not help a single hot key. All of that key's records still map to one partition.
  • Fixes, from least to most invasive:
    • Pick a finer key that still meets the ordering need, such as card_id instead of merchant_id.
    • Salt the hot key: merchant-42#0 to merchant-42#7 spreads one key over 8 partitions. You lose per-merchant order, so only do this when downstream can reorder or does not care (such as counting).
    • Route known giants to a dedicated topic with its own scaling.
    • Speed up per-record processing on the hot partition, for example by batching writes downstream.

6.4The key-to-partition explorer

Type any key to see the partition the Java producer chooses, then simulate many keys and one hot key.

Key to partition explorerRuns the same murmur2 hash as the Java producer's default partitioner, so the partition shown here is the one Kafka picks for a String key.

Many keys and one hot key. Keys are generated as prefix + 1, prefix + 2, and so on. The first key gets the hot share of traffic.

6.5Changing the partition count

  • You can only add partitions, with kafka-topics.sh --alter --partitions N. Existing records never move.
  • Keyed topics change mapping: after the change, many keys go to different partitions. Old records of a key stay behind, so during the transition a consumer may handle a key's new records before its old ones.
  • Compacted topics are worse: a key's old value sits in one partition and its new value in another, and compaction never reconciles them. Readers that rebuild a table from the topic can end up with a stale value.
  • Stream processing joins need both inputs to have the same partition count; changing one breaks the join (Module 17).
  • Safe ways to grow a keyed topic:
    • Size it for years of growth up front; partitions are cheap compared with a migration.
    • Create a new topic with more partitions, dual-write or replay into it, and move consumers over once they have caught up.
    • Drain first: stop producers, let consumers finish, add partitions, then resume. Order across the change is then preserved.

6.6How many partitions

Try it first3 minutes

Peak is 30,000 messages per second, 1 KB each. One consumer instance processes 2,000 messages per second. A partition comfortably absorbs 10 MB/s of writes on your brokers. How many partitions, with 2x headroom?

Reveal the answer

Consumers need 30,000 / 2,000 = 15. Writes need 30 MB/s / 10 MB/s = 3. The larger is 15; with 2x headroom, 30. Rounding to a number that divides evenly across brokers and consumer counts, 32 or 36 is a sensible choice.

Partition count calculatorPartitions cap consumer parallelism and spread write load. Measure the two per-unit rates on your own hardware; the defaults are only placeholders.

Rule: partitions = max(peak rate / per-consumer rate, peak MB/s / per-partition MB/s), times headroom. You can add partitions later, but keyed topics then remap keys, so size for growth up front.

Too few partitions cap consumer parallelism and per-topic throughput. Too many cost something too:

  • Each partition replica means open files and memory on its broker, and work for the controller during failures and reassignments.
  • Producers keep a batch per partition, so many partitions mean smaller, emptier batches for the same traffic, which lowers compression and raises request counts.
  • Consumers get more partitions to fetch and more to move in a rebalance.

KRaft handles far more partitions per cluster than the ZooKeeper era did, but the batching cost is unchanged. Most topics are fine with tens of partitions; go into the hundreds only when the throughput math says so.

6.7Custom partitioners

A custom partitioner is rarely needed. Valid uses: give one huge tenant dedicated partitions, or keep a region's data in partitions whose leaders sit in that region's racks.

TenantPartitioner.java
import org.apache.kafka.clients.producer.Partitioner;
import org.apache.kafka.common.Cluster;
import org.apache.kafka.common.utils.Utils;
import java.util.Map;

public class TenantPartitioner implements Partitioner {
    @Override
    public int partition(String topic, Object key, byte[] keyBytes,
                         Object value, byte[] valueBytes, Cluster cluster) {
        int n = cluster.partitionCountForTopic(topic);
        if ("tenant-big".equals(key)) {
            return 0;                                   // reserved for the giant tenant
        }
        return 1 + Utils.toPositive(Utils.murmur2(keyBytes)) % (n - 1);
    }
    @Override public void configure(Map<String, ?> configs) { }
    @Override public void close() { }
}

Register it with partitioner.class. Every producer writing to the topic must use the same partitioner, or keys scatter.

6.8Lab: predict partitions, then add one

LabVerify the hash, then watch keys move15 minutes

On the single broker, create a topic and produce nine keys:

Terminal
./kafka-topics.sh --bootstrap-server localhost:9092 --create --topic accounts --partitions 3 --replication-factor 1
./kafka-console-producer.sh --bootstrap-server localhost:9092 --topic accounts \
  --reader-property parse.key=true --reader-property key.separator=:
Text
acct-1:a
acct-2:a
acct-3:a
acct-4:a
acct-5:a
acct-6:a
acct-7:a
acct-8:a
acct-9:a

Before reading them back, predict each key's partition with the explorer above (3 partitions). Then check:

Terminal
./kafka-console-consumer.sh --bootstrap-server localhost:9092 --topic accounts --from-beginning \
  --formatter-property print.partition=true --formatter-property print.key=true

Now grow the topic to 4 partitions. Then run the same producer command, type the nine keys again with value b (acct-1:b and so on), and read everything again:

Terminal
./kafka-topics.sh --bootstrap-server localhost:9092 --alter --topic accounts --partitions 4
Check what you saw
  • With 3 partitions: acct-5, acct-6, acct-9 in partition 0; acct-4, acct-7, acct-8 in partition 1; acct-1, acct-2, acct-3 in partition 2. These match the explorer because it runs the same murmur2.
  • With 4 partitions the b records go to: acct-4, acct-5, acct-7 in 0; acct-6, acct-8 in 1; acct-1, acct-9 in 2; acct-2, acct-3 in 3.
  • acct-6's a is in partition 0 and its b in partition 1. A consumer reading partition 1 before partition 0 sees b before a: the ordering break, made visible.

6.9Common mistakes

Common mistakes

  • Keying by a low-cardinality field (country, status, merchant) and creating hot partitions.
  • Adding partitions to a keyed or compacted topic in place without planning for the remapping.
  • Mixing producers with different partitioners (Java murmur2 and librdkafka's default CRC32) on one keyed topic.
  • Changing the key serializer and silently moving every key.
  • Expecting more partitions to fix a single hot key.
  • Choosing hundreds of partitions "just in case" for a low-traffic topic, then getting tiny batches.

6.10Self-check

Self-checkFive more, after the lessons
  1. Write the formula the Java producer uses for a keyed record.
    Reveal

    toPositive(murmur2(keyBytes)) % numPartitions, where keyBytes is the serialized key.

  2. What does the producer do with keyless records, and why?
    Reveal

    It sticks to one partition until roughly a batch worth of data has gone there, then switches (adaptively favoring faster brokers). This builds full batches instead of scattering tiny ones.

  3. Name three properties of a good key.
    Reveal

    It matches the ordering requirement, it has many distinct values, and no single value carries a large share of traffic.

  4. How do you grow a keyed topic without breaking per-key order?
    Reveal

    Either drain it first (stop producers, let consumers finish, then add partitions), or create a new, larger topic and migrate producers and consumers to it.

  5. Give the partition count formula from throughput.
    Reveal

    The larger of peak rate divided by one consumer's rate and peak MB/s divided by one partition's write MB/s, multiplied by a growth factor.

Module 7: The consumer and consumer groups

Consumers pull records in a loop you write, and consumer groups spread partitions across instances. This module covers the poll loop, how groups divide partitions, subscribe versus assign, where a new group starts reading, the fetch settings, and how to add threads without breaking ordering.

10 lessons3 figures1 lab6 mastery checks

On this page

  1. 7.1Pull, not push
  2. 7.2The poll loop
  3. 7.3Consumer groups
  4. 7.4subscribe or assign
  5. 7.5Where a group starts reading
  6. 7.6Fetch settings
  7. 7.7Threads and ordering
  8. 7.8Lab: a consumer group in action
  9. 7.9Common mistakes
  10. 7.10Self-check
Warm-upWarm-up: one line each
  1. Does Kafka push records to consumers?
    Reveal

    No. Consumers pull by calling poll(), which lets each consumer go at its own pace and fetch in large batches.

  2. Can two threads share one KafkaConsumer?
    Reveal

    No. The consumer is not thread-safe. Use one consumer per thread; only wakeup() may be called from another thread.

  3. A new consumer group subscribes to a topic with a week of data. Where does it start with default settings?
    Reveal

    At the end (auto.offset.reset=latest), so it sees only new records. Set earliest to read the history.

  4. Two consumer groups read the same topic. Do they compete for records?
    Reveal

    No. Each group gets every record and keeps its own committed offsets.

  5. A group has 3 consumers and the topic has 12 partitions. How many partitions does each consumer get?
    Reveal

    About 4 each. Partitions are spread across the members, and each partition belongs to exactly one member.

7.1Pull, not push

Try it first2 minutes

Why might a pull model suit Kafka better than having brokers push records to consumers?

Reveal the answer

Each consumer controls its own pace, so a slow consumer does not need the broker to track and throttle it. Consumers fetch large batches when they are ready, which is efficient, and replay is natural: a consumer simply fetches from an older offset.

  • Consumers send fetch requests to partition leaders. Long polling avoids busy loops: the broker holds a fetch until fetch.min.bytes of data is available (1 byte by default) or fetch.max.wait.ms passes (500 ms).
  • The client prefetches in the background, so poll() usually returns records already in memory.

7.2The poll loop

BillingConsumer.java
import org.apache.kafka.clients.consumer.*;
import org.apache.kafka.common.serialization.StringDeserializer;
import java.time.Duration;
import java.util.List;
import java.util.Properties;

public class BillingConsumer {
    public static void main(String[] args) {
        Properties props = new Properties();
        props.put(ConsumerConfig.BOOTSTRAP_SERVERS_CONFIG, "localhost:9092");
        props.put(ConsumerConfig.GROUP_ID_CONFIG, "billing");
        props.put(ConsumerConfig.KEY_DESERIALIZER_CLASS_CONFIG, StringDeserializer.class.getName());
        props.put(ConsumerConfig.VALUE_DESERIALIZER_CLASS_CONFIG, StringDeserializer.class.getName());
        props.put(ConsumerConfig.AUTO_OFFSET_RESET_CONFIG, "earliest");
        props.put(ConsumerConfig.ENABLE_AUTO_COMMIT_CONFIG, false);

        try (KafkaConsumer<String, String> consumer = new KafkaConsumer<>(props)) {
            consumer.subscribe(List.of("payments"));
            while (true) {
                ConsumerRecords<String, String> records = consumer.poll(Duration.ofMillis(500));
                for (ConsumerRecord<String, String> r : records) {
                    System.out.printf("p%d o%d %s=%s%n", r.partition(), r.offset(), r.key(), r.value());
                }
                consumer.commitSync();   // commit what this poll returned, after processing it
            }
        }
    }
}
  • poll(Duration) returns up to max.poll.records (500) records, possibly from several partitions; records from one partition arrive in offset order.
  • Process, then commit, then poll again. Module 8 covers commit strategies; Module 10 covers clean shutdown with wakeup().
  • Keep the loop moving. If the time between two poll() calls exceeds max.poll.interval.ms (5 minutes), the consumer is considered stuck and leaves the group (Module 9).

7.3Consumer groups

Try it first2 minutes

A topic has 4 partitions. Your group runs 6 instances to "go faster". What happens, and what would actually help?

Reveal the answer

Four instances each get one partition and two sit idle. To use 6 instances, the topic needs at least 6 partitions, or each record's processing must get faster. (Share groups, Module 9, can use more consumers than partitions when per-key order does not matter.)

  • All consumers with the same group.id form one group. Kafka assigns each partition to exactly one member, so members never process the same record at the same time.
  • Groups are independent: billing, fraud, and analytics each get every record.
  • When members join or leave, partitions move (a rebalance, Module 9).
  • Parallelism = min(partitions, consumers) for a classic or KIP-848 consumer group.
Consumer group playgroundOne topic, one consumer group. Change the group and watch which partitions move.

The sticky option is simplified: it keeps every partition it can and moves the minimum needed for balance, which is the behavior the real assignor aims for.

7.4subscribe or assign

subscribe(topics) assign(partitions)
Who picks partitions The group protocol You
Rebalancing Automatic when members change None
Committed offsets Stored per group Optional (you may still commit with a group.id)
Used by Almost every application Stream processors that manage their own state (Flink), tools, replay jobs
  • subscribe(Pattern) follows topics that match a regular expression, including new ones as they appear.
  • Do not mix subscribe and assign on one consumer.

7.5Where a group starts reading

auto.offset.reset applies only when the group has no committed offset for a partition, or its committed offset no longer exists (deleted by retention):

Value Starts at Typical use
latest (default) The end: only new records Notifications where history is irrelevant
earliest The oldest retained record Anything that must not miss data: ledgers, sinks, backfills
by_duration:PT6H (Kafka 4.0+) The first record from that long ago Start a new service with recent history
none Throws an exception You want a human to decide
Watch out

A new group with the default latest silently skips everything produced before it first connected, and so does an existing group whose offsets expired. For most backend consumers, set earliest explicitly.

7.6Fetch settings

Setting Default Effect
fetch.min.bytes 1 Broker waits for this much data before answering; raise it for throughput
fetch.max.wait.ms 500 Upper bound on that wait
max.partition.fetch.bytes 1 MB Max data per partition per fetch
fetch.max.bytes 50 MB Max data per fetch response
max.poll.records 500 Max records one poll() returns; lower it if processing is slow
max.poll.interval.ms 300,000 (5 min) Max time between polls before the member is removed

7.7Threads and ordering

  • Model A, one consumer per thread: run N consumers in the same group (in one process or many). Simple, ordering per partition is automatic, and rebalancing handles failures. Limited by the partition count.
  • Model B, a poller plus workers: one thread polls and hands records to a pool. More parallelism than partitions, but you must (1) send each key to the same worker to keep per-key order, (2) commit an offset only when every earlier record of that partition is finished, and (3) pause partitions when worker queues fill. Libraries such as Confluent's Parallel Consumer implement this pattern.
  • Share groups (Module 9) are the built-in alternative when per-key order does not matter.

7.8Lab: a consumer group in action

LabSplit partitions across consumers and watch a fourth one sit idle15 minutes

On the single broker, create a topic with 3 partitions and produce some records:

Terminal
./kafka-topics.sh --bootstrap-server localhost:9092 --create --topic orders --partitions 3 --replication-factor 1
./kafka-producer-perf-test.sh --bootstrap-server localhost:9092 --topic orders \
  --num-records 3000 --record-size 100 --throughput 100

While that runs (about 30 seconds), open three more terminals, enter the container in each (docker exec -it --workdir /opt/kafka/bin broker sh), and start one consumer per terminal in the same group:

Terminal
./kafka-console-consumer.sh --bootstrap-server localhost:9092 --topic orders --group billing \
  --formatter-property print.partition=true

In the first terminal, describe the group:

Terminal
./kafka-consumer-groups.sh --bootstrap-server localhost:9092 --describe --group billing
./kafka-consumer-groups.sh --bootstrap-server localhost:9092 --describe --group billing --members

Start a fourth consumer in a fifth terminal and describe the group again. Then stop one consumer with Ctrl-C and describe once more.

Check what you saw
  • With three consumers, --describe lists each partition with a different CONSUMER-ID. Each terminal prints lines starting with only its own Partition: number.
  • With four consumers, --members shows one member with #PARTITIONS 0: it is idle.
  • When you stop one, its partition moves to another member within seconds, and that terminal starts printing two partition numbers.
  • The LAG column shows how far each partition's committed offset is behind its end. Module 8 explains it.

7.9Common mistakes

Common mistakes

  • Sharing one KafkaConsumer across threads.
  • Running more consumers than partitions and expecting more throughput.
  • Relying on the default auto.offset.reset=latest for a consumer that must not miss data.
  • Slow work inside the poll loop that pushes the gap between polls past max.poll.interval.ms.
  • Handing records to a thread pool without keeping per-key order or tracking which offsets are safe to commit.
  • Reusing a group.id across unrelated applications, so they steal partitions from each other.

7.10Self-check

Self-checkFive more, after the lessons
  1. What does poll() do besides returning records?
    Reveal

    It sends fetch requests, runs rebalance callbacks, sends automatic commits when they are due, and keeps the member in the group. The loop must keep calling it.

  2. Why can a consumer group not use more consumers than partitions?
    Reveal

    Each partition is assigned to exactly one member of a classic or KIP-848 consumer group, so there are only as many units of work as partitions.

  3. When does auto.offset.reset apply?
    Reveal

    Only when the group has no committed offset for a partition or that offset is no longer in the log.

  4. When would you use assign() instead of subscribe()?
    Reveal

    When your application controls which partitions it reads and stores its own position, such as a stream processor with checkpointed offsets, a replay tool, or a job that reads one specific partition.

  5. Name two things you must handle if you process one partition's records in a worker pool.
    Reveal

    Per-key ordering (route a key to one worker) and safe commits (commit only offsets whose earlier records are all done); also backpressure, by pausing partitions when queues fill.

Module 8: Offsets, commits, and delivery semantics

A consumer's committed offset decides what happens after every crash, deploy, and rebalance. This module separates the four positions in a partition, compares automatic and manual commits, shows how commit order produces at-most-once or at-least-once delivery, and covers resetting offsets to replay data.

9 lessons3 figures1 lab6 mastery checks

On this page

  1. 8.1Committed offset, position, and lag
  2. 8.2Automatic commits
  3. 8.3Committing yourself
  4. 8.4Delivery semantics
  5. 8.5Making at-least-once safe
  6. 8.6Replaying and resetting offsets
  7. 8.7Lab: lag and offset reset
  8. 8.8Common mistakes
  9. 8.9Self-check
Warm-upWarm-up: one line each
  1. Your consumer processed offset 41 in a partition. Which offset should it commit?
    Reveal

    42, the next record to read. Committing 41 would reprocess offset 41 after a restart.

  2. Where are committed offsets stored?
    Reveal

    In the internal __consumer_offsets topic, keyed by group, topic, and partition.

  3. With auto-commit on, can you lose records? Can you get duplicates?
    Reveal

    Duplicates, yes: up to a commit interval's worth after a crash. Loss, only if you hand records to other threads and the commit happens before they finish.

  4. What is consumer lag?
    Reveal

    For each partition, the distance between the end of what consumers can read (the high watermark) and the group's committed offset.

  5. A group was stopped for 10 days with default broker settings. What happens to its offsets?
    Reveal

    Offsets of an empty group expire after offsets.retention.minutes (7 days). On restart the group behaves like a new one and follows auto.offset.reset.

8.1Committed offset, position, and lag

  • Committed offset: stored in Kafka for the group. It is where any member restarts reading this partition, after a crash or a rebalance.
  • Position: the next offset this consumer instance will fetch. It runs ahead of the committed offset while records are being processed.
  • High watermark: the end of the records that are replicated to all in-sync replicas. Consumers cannot read past it.
  • Log end offset: the next offset the leader will assign. Records between the high watermark and the log end are not yet fully replicated.
  • Lag = high watermark minus committed offset, per partition. Watch lag as a trend and in time ("the oldest unread record is 4 minutes old"), not only as a count.
Key idea

A committed offset always names the next record to read: last processed offset plus one.

8.2Automatic commits

  • enable.auto.commit=true is the client default. Every auto.commit.interval.ms (5 seconds), the next poll() commits the offsets of records returned by earlier polls. close() commits too.
  • Safe enough when you process each batch fully before calling poll() again: a crash replays at most a few seconds of records (at-least-once).
  • Unsafe when processing is asynchronous: if you hand records to a thread pool and keep polling, auto-commit may record them as done before the workers finish, and a crash loses them.
  • Spring for Apache Kafka turns auto-commit off by default and commits for you after your listener returns (Module 18).

8.3Committing yourself

Manual commits
props.put(ConsumerConfig.ENABLE_AUTO_COMMIT_CONFIG, false);

while (running) {
    ConsumerRecords<String, String> records = consumer.poll(Duration.ofMillis(500));
    for (ConsumerRecord<String, String> r : records) {
        process(r);
    }
    consumer.commitAsync((offsets, e) -> {          // fast path, no retries
        if (e != null) log.warn("commit failed, a later commit will cover it", e);
    });
}
// on shutdown or partition revocation: one blocking commit that retries
consumer.commitSync();
Method Blocks Retries Use
commitSync() Yes Yes, until success or a fatal error Shutdown, rebalance revocation, strict pipelines
commitAsync(callback) No No (a late retry could overwrite a newer commit) The normal loop
commitSync(Map<TopicPartition, OffsetAndMetadata>) Yes Yes Commit exact offsets, for example after each record or each sub-batch
  • To commit a specific record, commit new OffsetAndMetadata(record.offset() + 1) for its partition.
  • CommitFailedException means the group rebalanced and this member no longer owns the partition; its uncommitted records will be reprocessed by the new owner. It usually signals processing that is too slow for max.poll.interval.ms (Module 9).
  • Commit frequency trades duplicates against overhead: committing after every record minimizes replays but adds a write per record.

8.4Delivery semantics

Try it first2 minutes

Your consumer sends an SMS for each record. Should it commit before or after sending? What does each choice cost after a crash?

Reveal the answer

Committing before sending (at-most-once) can skip SMS messages that were committed but never sent. Committing after (at-least-once) can send a few SMS twice. For alerts, at-least-once plus deduplication by event ID is the usual choice: a rare duplicate is better than a missed fraud alert.

Semantics How Failure cost Use for
At-most-once Commit, then process Records can be lost Metrics where loss is fine
At-least-once Process, then commit Records can repeat The default for almost everything
Exactly-once (effect) At-least-once delivery plus idempotent processing, or transactions More design work Money, inventory, counts that must be exact

Kafka transactions give exactly-once for read-process-write pipelines that stay inside Kafka (Module 14). When the effect is in another system, make the effect idempotent.

8.5Making at-least-once safe

  • Idempotent processing: record each event's ID in a table with a unique constraint, in the same database transaction as the effect; a redelivery hits the constraint and is skipped (Module 10).
  • Natural idempotency: upserts by key (INSERT ... ON CONFLICT UPDATE), setting absolute values ("balance is 500") instead of deltas ("add 100"), or version checks that ignore older versions.
  • Store offsets with the results: write the effect and the next offset in one database transaction, and on startup seek to the stored offset. Use assign() or seek inside a rebalance listener.

8.6Replaying and resetting offsets

  • Command line (the group must have no active members):
Terminal
# preview, then apply: --dry-run is the default, --execute applies
kafka-consumer-groups.sh --bootstrap-server localhost:9092 --group billing --topic orders \
  --reset-offsets --to-earliest --dry-run
kafka-consumer-groups.sh --bootstrap-server localhost:9092 --group billing --topic orders \
  --reset-offsets --to-datetime 2026-10-17T09:00:00.000 --execute
Option Moves the committed offset to
--to-earliest, --to-latest The start or end of each partition
--to-datetime 'YYYY-MM-DDThh:mm:ss.sss' The first record at or after that time
--by-duration PT1H The first record from one hour ago
--shift-by -100 100 records back (positive moves forward)
--to-offset N Exactly N
  • In code: seek(partition, offset), seekToBeginning, seekToEnd, and offsetsForTimes to find the offset for a timestamp.
  • Expiry: committed offsets of an empty group are deleted after offsets.retention.minutes (7 days by default). A consumer that is off for longer restarts according to auto.offset.reset.
At work

Before a replay, check that consumers are idempotent and that downstream systems can take the extra load. Replaying a day of payments into a non-idempotent ledger consumer double-books every one of them.

8.7Lab: lag and offset reset

LabBuild up lag, then rewind a group15 minutes

Continue from the Module 7 lab. Stop every billing consumer, then produce more records:

Terminal
./kafka-producer-perf-test.sh --bootstrap-server localhost:9092 --topic orders \
  --num-records 1000 --record-size 100 --throughput -1
./kafka-consumer-groups.sh --bootstrap-server localhost:9092 --describe --group billing

Plan and apply a rewind of 10 records per partition, then a reset to the beginning:

Terminal
./kafka-consumer-groups.sh --bootstrap-server localhost:9092 --group billing --topic orders \
  --reset-offsets --shift-by -10 --dry-run
./kafka-consumer-groups.sh --bootstrap-server localhost:9092 --group billing --topic orders \
  --reset-offsets --shift-by -10 --execute
./kafka-consumer-groups.sh --bootstrap-server localhost:9092 --group billing --topic orders \
  --reset-offsets --to-earliest --execute
./kafka-consumer-groups.sh --bootstrap-server localhost:9092 --describe --group billing

Now try a reset while one consumer of the group is running.

Check what you saw
  • After producing, the LAG values add up to 1,000 across the three partitions (keyless records are spread batch by batch, so not exactly evenly), and the output notes the group has no active members.
  • --dry-run prints the planned NEW-OFFSET without changing anything; --execute applies it.
  • After --to-earliest, CURRENT-OFFSET is 0 and LAG equals the whole partition, so a restarted consumer re-reads everything.
  • With a member running, the reset is refused because the group is not inactive. Offsets are owned by the live members.

8.8Common mistakes

Common mistakes

  • Committing record.offset() instead of record.offset() + 1, which replays one record per partition after every restart.
  • Auto-commit with asynchronous processing, which can lose records on a crash.
  • Retrying commitAsync in its callback, which can overwrite a newer committed offset with an older one.
  • Ignoring CommitFailedException instead of fixing slow processing.
  • Replaying into non-idempotent consumers.
  • Leaving a group stopped longer than offset retention and silently skipping to latest.

8.9Self-check

Self-checkFive more, after the lessons
  1. Define committed offset, position, high watermark, and lag.
    Reveal

    Committed offset: the group's stored restart point. Position: the next offset this instance will fetch. High watermark: the end of fully replicated, readable records. Lag: high watermark minus committed offset.

  2. Why does commitAsync not retry?
    Reveal

    Commits can finish out of order. Retrying an older commit after a newer one succeeded would move the committed offset backwards and cause reprocessing.

  3. How do you get at-least-once delivery with the plain consumer?
    Reveal

    Process each record (or batch) fully, then commit; never commit offsets for records not yet processed.

  4. How do you get exactly-once effects when the consumer writes to PostgreSQL?
    Reveal

    Make the write idempotent (unique event ID or upsert in the same transaction as the effect), or store the next offset in the same database transaction as the effect and seek to it on startup.

  5. What must be true before kafka-consumer-groups.sh --reset-offsets --execute works?
    Reveal

    The group must have no active members. Stop the consumers first.

Module 9: Rebalancing, the new group protocol, and share groups

A rebalance moves partitions between the members of a group. Done badly, it stops processing and causes duplicates; done well, nobody notices. This module covers what triggers rebalances, the two liveness timers, the classic protocol with eager and cooperative assignment, static membership, rebalance listeners, the KIP-848 protocol that is GA since Kafka 4.0, and share groups for queue-style consumption.

12 lessons5 figures1 lab6 mastery checks

On this page

  1. 9.1What triggers a rebalance
  2. 9.2Two liveness timers
  3. 9.3The classic protocol
  4. 9.4Eager and cooperative rebalancing
  5. 9.5Static membership
  6. 9.6Rebalance listeners
  7. 9.7The new consumer group protocol (KIP-848)
  8. 9.8Share groups: queues for Kafka
  9. 9.9Avoiding rebalance storms
  10. 9.10Lab: watch a rebalance, then try a share group
  11. 9.11Common mistakes
  12. 9.12Self-check
Warm-upWarm-up: one line each
  1. Name three events that trigger a rebalance.
    Reveal

    A consumer joins, a consumer leaves or is declared dead (missed heartbeats or exceeded max.poll.interval.ms), or the subscription changes (new partitions, or a new topic matching a pattern).

  2. Processing one batch takes 8 minutes with default settings. What happens?
    Reveal

    The gap between polls exceeds max.poll.interval.ms (5 minutes), so the consumer leaves the group, its partitions go to others, and its later commit fails with CommitFailedException.

  3. In an eager rebalance, which partitions stop being processed?
    Reveal

    All of them. Every member revokes every partition before the new assignment.

  4. What does group.instance.id do?
    Reveal

    It makes the consumer a static member: a restart that comes back within the session timeout keeps its partitions without a rebalance.

  5. How do share groups differ from consumer groups?
    Reveal

    Members share partitions and acknowledge records one by one, so a group can have more consumers than partitions, but there is no per-key ordering.

9.1What triggers a rebalance

  • Membership changes: a consumer starts, shuts down cleanly (it sends a leave request), or crashes.
  • Liveness failures: missed heartbeats for session.timeout.ms, or no poll() call within max.poll.interval.ms.
  • Metadata changes: partitions added to a subscribed topic, or a new topic that matches a subscribed pattern.

Every rebalance has a cost: partitions pause while they move, and records processed but not yet committed are processed again by the new owner.

9.2Two liveness timers

Try it first2 minutes

A consumer's heartbeats arrive every 3 seconds, but it has been stuck in one database call for 7 minutes. Is it still in the group?

Reveal the answer

No. Heartbeats come from a background thread, so they prove only that the process is alive. The separate max.poll.interval.ms check (5 minutes) notices that the loop has not called poll(), and the consumer leaves the group so its partitions can move to a healthy member.

Setting Default Guards against Tune when
heartbeat.interval.ms 3 s n/a (how often to heartbeat) Keep at about a third of the session timeout
session.timeout.ms 45 s Dead process or lost network Lower for faster failover, higher for flaky networks
max.poll.interval.ms 5 min Stuck or slow processing Raise if a batch legitimately takes long, or lower max.poll.records

9.3The classic protocol

  • The group coordinator is the broker that leads the group's partition of __consumer_offsets.
  • Each rebalance bumps the group's generation. Commits from an older generation are rejected, which is how zombie members are kept from committing.
  • The group leader (one of the consumers) runs the assignor locally, which is why all members must agree on the assignor.
Assignor Spreads partitions Rebalance style
RangeAssignor Per topic, contiguous ranges Eager
RoundRobinAssignor Across all subscribed partitions in turn Eager
StickyAssignor Balanced, keeps existing ownership Eager
CooperativeStickyAssignor Balanced, keeps existing ownership Cooperative

The default list is [RangeAssignor, CooperativeStickyAssignor], so groups use Range. To move to cooperative rebalancing, do one rolling restart with only CooperativeStickyAssignor in the list.

9.4Eager and cooperative rebalancing

  • Eager: every member revokes everything, then receives a new assignment. Processing stops group-wide for the whole rebalance.
  • Cooperative (incremental): members keep the partitions that are not moving. A first round revokes only what must move; a second round assigns it. Most partitions never pause.
  • Cooperative rebalancing makes rolling deploys of large groups dramatically smoother.

9.5Static membership

  • Set a unique, stable group.instance.id per instance (for example the Kubernetes pod name in a StatefulSet).
  • A static member that restarts and returns within session.timeout.ms gets its partitions back without a rebalance. Raise the session timeout to cover a normal restart, for example 60 to 120 seconds.
  • Trade-off: if the instance truly dies, its partitions wait for the session timeout before moving.

9.6Rebalance listeners

Commit before giving partitions away
consumer.subscribe(List.of("payments"), new ConsumerRebalanceListener() {
    @Override
    public void onPartitionsRevoked(Collection<TopicPartition> partitions) {
        consumer.commitSync(currentOffsets(partitions));   // last chance to record progress
        flushLocalState(partitions);
    }
    @Override
    public void onPartitionsAssigned(Collection<TopicPartition> partitions) {
        loadLocalState(partitions);                         // or seek to offsets stored elsewhere
    }
    @Override
    public void onPartitionsLost(Collection<TopicPartition> partitions) {
        dropLocalState(partitions);                         // already owned by someone else: do not commit
    }
});
  • onPartitionsRevoked runs before ownership moves: commit offsets and flush buffered work.
  • onPartitionsAssigned runs after: load state, or seek() to offsets you store yourself.
  • onPartitionsLost runs when ownership was lost without a chance to hand over (for example after a session timeout); committing then would fail.

9.7The new consumer group protocol (KIP-848)

  • Generally available since Kafka 4.0 and enabled on brokers by default. Clients opt in with group.protocol=consumer; the client default is still classic, and the project plans to make consumer the default in Kafka 5.0.
  • The broker computes assignments with server-side assignors (uniform, the default, and range). There is no group leader and no JoinGroup or SyncGroup barrier.
  • Fully incremental: each member is told only what to give up and what to take; everyone else keeps working.
  • Configuration moves to the broker: with the new protocol, the client settings session.timeout.ms, heartbeat.interval.ms, and partition.assignment.strategy are not used. The broker's group.consumer.session.timeout.ms (45 s) and group.consumer.heartbeat.interval.ms (5 s) apply instead.
  • Migration: roll consumers to group.protocol=consumer one at a time; a group converts while online, as long as it uses an assignor without custom metadata. Client-side custom assignors are not supported.
Version note

Kafka Streams has its own broker-side protocol (KIP-1071), production-ready for its core features since Kafka 4.2.

9.8Share groups: queues for Kafka

  • Production-ready since Kafka 4.2 and enabled by default on new 4.2+ clusters. Use KafkaShareConsumer (or kafka-console-share-consumer.sh) with a group ID.
  • Records, not partitions, are handed out. Each fetched record is acquired with a lock (share.record.lock.duration.ms, 30 s by default). The consumer acknowledges it as ACCEPT, RELEASE (try again), REJECT (unprocessable), or RENEW (needs more time).
  • Delivery attempts are counted. After share.delivery.count.limit attempts (5 by default) a record is archived instead of redelivered.
  • Acknowledgement modes: share.acknowledgement.mode=implicit (default) accepts everything from a poll on the next poll or commit; explicit requires acknowledge() per record.
  • Use them for job queues: independent tasks where throughput matters more than order, and where you want more workers than partitions. Keep consumer groups for ordered event streams.

9.9Avoiding rebalance storms

  • Keep each poll loop iteration short: lower max.poll.records, or move slow work out of the loop safely.
  • Use cooperative rebalancing (CooperativeSticky or the new protocol).
  • Use static membership for rolling restarts.
  • Shut down cleanly: call wakeup(), commit, close() (Module 10).
  • Watch for long GC pauses and CPU throttling in containers, which look like dead consumers.
  • Monitor the rebalance rate (rebalance-rate-per-hour on the consumer, consumer-group-rebalance-rate on the coordinator).

9.10Lab: watch a rebalance, then try a share group

LabGroup protocol details and a share group20 minutes

On the single broker, start two consumers (in two terminals) in one group on the 3-partition orders topic from Module 7, both using the new protocol:

Terminal
./kafka-console-consumer.sh --bootstrap-server localhost:9092 --topic orders --group rebal \
  --command-property group.protocol=consumer

Describe the members, then stop one consumer and describe again:

Terminal
./kafka-consumer-groups.sh --bootstrap-server localhost:9092 --describe --group rebal --members --verbose
./kafka-consumer-groups.sh --bootstrap-server localhost:9092 --describe --group rebal --state

Now a share group. Run the first command in four separate terminals (four share consumers on a 3-partition topic), then produce records and describe the group:

Terminal
./kafka-console-share-consumer.sh --bootstrap-server localhost:9092 --topic orders --group jobs
./kafka-producer-perf-test.sh --bootstrap-server localhost:9092 --topic orders \
  --num-records 400 --record-size 50 --throughput 50
./kafka-share-groups.sh --bootstrap-server localhost:9092 --describe --group jobs --members
Check what you saw
  • --members --verbose lists each member's assigned partitions: one member has two, the other one. --state shows the assignment strategy (uniform, the broker-side default), the group state, and the member count.
  • After you stop one consumer, its partitions move to the other within seconds.
  • Several share consumers, often all four, print records even though there are only three partitions: records, not partitions, are handed out. Records from one partition can appear in different terminals, so their order is not preserved.
  • kafka-share-groups.sh --describe shows members and their partitions; several members can share the same partition.

9.11Common mistakes

Common mistakes

  • Slow processing inside the loop with default max.poll.records, causing the member to be kicked out again and again.
  • Not committing in onPartitionsRevoked, so the new owner reprocesses everything since the last commit.
  • Committing in onPartitionsLost, which fails because the partitions already belong to someone else.
  • Eager assignors in large groups, where every deploy stops all processing.
  • Static membership with a short session timeout, which gives no benefit, or with a very long one, which delays recovery after real failures.
  • Using share groups where per-key order matters.

9.12Self-check

Self-checkFive more, after the lessons
  1. Why are there two liveness timers?
    Reveal

    Heartbeats from a background thread detect a dead process quickly; max.poll.interval.ms detects a live process whose processing loop is stuck. Each catches a failure the other cannot.

  2. In the classic protocol, who computes the assignment?
    Reveal

    One consumer, elected group leader by the coordinator, runs the assignor and sends the result in its SyncGroup request; the coordinator hands each member its share.

  3. What makes cooperative rebalancing cheaper than eager?
    Reveal

    Members keep the partitions that are not moving and keep processing them; only partitions that change owner are revoked, over two short rounds.

  4. What changes for a client that sets group.protocol=consumer?
    Reveal

    Assignment is computed by the broker, rebalances are incremental with no group-wide barrier, and heartbeat, session timeout, and assignor settings come from the broker instead of the client.

  5. When would you choose a share group over a consumer group?
    Reveal

    For independent tasks where you need more parallel workers than partitions, per-record acknowledgement, and delivery counting, and where per-key ordering does not matter.

Phase 3: ConsumersCoreHigh priority

Module 10: Consumer failure handling, retries, and dead letters

Real consumers meet malformed records, flaky dependencies, slow databases, and redeliveries. This module turns those into design choices: blocking versus non-blocking retries, dead letter topics that someone actually watches, keeping per-key order while retrying, idempotent consumers, backpressure, and clean shutdown.

11 lessons3 figures1 lab6 mastery checks

On this page

  1. 10.1Kinds of failure
  2. 10.2Poison messages
  3. 10.3Retry strategies
  4. 10.4Dead letter topics
  5. 10.5Keeping per-key order while retrying
  6. 10.6Idempotent consumers
  7. 10.7Backpressure and slow consumers
  8. 10.8Clean shutdown
  9. 10.9Lab: build a dead letter flow
  10. 10.10Common mistakes
  11. 10.11Self-check
Warm-upWarm-up: one line each
  1. One malformed record makes your consumer throw every time. What happens to the rest of its partition?
    Reveal

    It is stuck behind that record (head-of-line blocking): the consumer never advances, and lag grows on that partition.

  2. Should a validation error and a database timeout be retried the same way?
    Reveal

    No. A timeout is transient and worth retrying with backoff. A validation error is permanent; retrying cannot fix it, so send it straight to a dead letter topic.

  3. Retry topics keep the main consumer flowing. What do they cost?
    Reveal

    Ordering. The failed record is processed later, after records that came behind it.

  4. Why must consumers be idempotent even with careful commits?
    Reveal

    Delivery is at-least-once: a crash or rebalance between processing and committing redelivers records.

  5. How do you stop a consumer cleanly from another thread?
    Reveal

    Call consumer.wakeup(). The blocked poll() throws WakeupException; catch it, commit, and close().

10.1Kinds of failure

Failure Example Retry? Typical handling
Transient Timeout, HTTP 503, deadlock, leader change Yes, with backoff Retry in place or via retry topics
Permanent (poison) Invalid amount, unknown merchant, schema mismatch No Dead letter topic, alert, fix, replay
Deserialization Bytes that are not valid JSON or Avro No Capture raw bytes to a dead letter topic, skip
Consumer crash Out of memory, pod killed Automatic Rebalance; records since the last commit are redelivered
Slow downstream Database at 100% CPU Slow down Backpressure: pause, smaller batches, circuit breaker

10.2Poison messages

  • A poison message blocks its partition if the consumer keeps retrying it. Other partitions are fine, which is a useful diagnostic: lag on one partition only.
  • Deserialization errors surface inside poll(). The Java client throws RecordDeserializationException, which carries the partition and offset: log the raw record, send it to a dead letter topic, then seek() to offset + 1. Alternatively consume byte[] and deserialize in your own code where you can catch errors per record. Spring offers ErrorHandlingDeserializer for this (Module 18).
  • Bound every retry loop. No record deserves infinite attempts.

10.3Retry strategies

Try it first3 minutes

A downstream fraud API is down for 10 minutes. Compare (a) retrying each record in place with backoff, and (b) moving failures to a retry topic with a 1-minute delay. What happens to throughput, ordering, and the API in each?

Reveal the answer

(a) The partition stalls for 10 minutes but stays in order; backoff keeps load on the API low. Lag builds and then drains. (b) The main consumer keeps flowing, but every record fails into the retry topic, then fails again; nothing succeeds until the API returns, ordering is lost, and the retry topics fill up. When the dependency itself is down, pausing (a, or a circuit breaker) beats retry topics; retry topics shine when only some records fail.

Blocking retry in place Non-blocking retry topics
How Seek back to the failed offset, back off, try again; pause the partition while waiting Publish the failed record to topic-retry-1m, topic-retry-10m; consumers there wait until due
Order Preserved Lost for the retried record
Partition progress Stops during retries Continues
Best for Ordered streams; a dependency that is fully down Occasional failures of individual records
Watch out max.poll.interval.ms: back off with pause(), not sleep() Retry storms when everything fails; topic sprawl
  • Exponential backoff with jitter for in-place retries, and a cap on attempts.
  • A circuit breaker around the dependency: after repeated failures, pause the partitions instead of failing record after record.
  • Retry topics delay by waiting: the retry consumer reads a record, and if it is not yet due, pauses the partition until it is. Kafka has no per-message delay (Case study 8).

10.4Dead letter topics

A dead letter topic (DLT) holds records that could not be processed after all attempts. It is a work queue for people, not a trash can.

  • Keep the original record: same key and value bytes, so it can be replayed as is.
  • Add headers that explain it: original topic, partition, offset, timestamp, exception class and message, attempt count, consumer group, and application version.
  • Alert on any DLT traffic, and show the reason in a dashboard.
  • Build a replay tool: after a fix, republish selected DLT records to the original topic (or a retry topic).
  • Give the DLT long retention, longer than your investigation time.
Send a failed record to the DLT, then move on
try {
    process(record);
} catch (NonRetryableException e) {
    ProducerRecord<byte[], byte[]> dead =
        new ProducerRecord<>("payments-dlt", record.key(), record.value());
    record.headers().forEach(h -> dead.headers().add(h));
    dead.headers()
        .add("dlt.original.topic", record.topic().getBytes(UTF_8))
        .add("dlt.original.partition", Integer.toString(record.partition()).getBytes(UTF_8))
        .add("dlt.original.offset", Long.toString(record.offset()).getBytes(UTF_8))
        .add("dlt.exception", e.toString().getBytes(UTF_8));
    dltProducer.send(dead).get();   // wait: it must be in the DLT before the offset is committed
}

10.5Keeping per-key order while retrying

When order per key matters (account balance events), a retried record must not be overtaken by later records of the same key:

  • Block the partition: retry in place. Simple and correct; one bad key stalls every key in that partition.
  • Park the key: keep a set of "blocked keys". When a record of a blocked key arrives, send it to a parking topic in order instead of processing it. When the head record finally succeeds (or is resolved by a person), replay that key's parked records in order. Other keys keep flowing. It is more complex but isolates one bad entity.
  • Decide per use case: notifications rarely need strict order; ledgers always do.

10.6Idempotent consumers

PostgreSQL: dedup and effect in one transaction
CREATE TABLE processed_events (
  consumer_group text        NOT NULL,
  event_id       text        NOT NULL,
  processed_at   timestamptz NOT NULL DEFAULT now(),
  PRIMARY KEY (consumer_group, event_id)
);

BEGIN;
INSERT INTO processed_events (consumer_group, event_id)
VALUES ('ledger', 'e-77')
ON CONFLICT DO NOTHING;                 -- 0 rows inserted: duplicate, skip the effect
UPDATE accounts SET balance = balance - 1250 WHERE id = 42;   -- only if 1 row was inserted
COMMIT;
  • The event ID must come from the producer (a UUID or a business key), not from Kafka offsets, which change if records are republished.
  • Keep dedup rows longer than any redelivery or replay window, then prune them.
  • Other options: upsert by business key, absolute values instead of increments, or version numbers that ignore stale updates.

10.7Backpressure and slow consumers

  • pause() and resume(): stop fetching specific partitions while still calling poll(), so the consumer stays in the group. Use it when a downstream is unhealthy or a worker queue is full.
  • Smaller max.poll.records keeps each loop iteration within max.poll.interval.ms.
  • Batch downstream writes: one database round trip for 500 records instead of 500.
  • Scale out up to the partition count. Autoscalers such as KEDA can scale consumers on lag.
  • Shed or degrade non-critical work when lag threatens retention (Module 20 has the lag drain math).

10.8Clean shutdown

wakeup() pattern
final Thread mainThread = Thread.currentThread();
Runtime.getRuntime().addShutdownHook(new Thread(() -> {
    consumer.wakeup();                       // makes the blocked poll() throw WakeupException
    try { mainThread.join(); } catch (InterruptedException ignored) { }
}));

try {
    consumer.subscribe(List.of("payments"));
    while (true) {
        ConsumerRecords<String, String> records = consumer.poll(Duration.ofSeconds(1));
        for (ConsumerRecord<String, String> r : records) process(r);
        consumer.commitAsync();
    }
} catch (WakeupException e) {
    // expected during shutdown
} finally {
    try {
        consumer.commitSync();               // final, retried commit
    } finally {
        consumer.close();                    // leaves the group promptly: fast rebalance
    }
}

10.9Lab: build a dead letter flow

LabWrite a consumer that retries transient errors and dead-letters poison records45 minutes

In your Java project (see Lab setup):

  1. Create topics payments and payments-dlt on the single broker.
  2. Write a consumer for payments that parses each value as an integer amount. Treat a non-number as a poison record; treat an amount of exactly 503 as a transient error that succeeds on the third attempt.
  3. Retry transient errors in place up to 5 times with backoff, using pause() and seek() rather than Thread.sleep() for long waits.
  4. Send poison records to payments-dlt with the headers from this module, then continue.
  5. Commit only after a record succeeded or reached the DLT.
  6. Produce 100, abc, 503, 250 with the console producer and watch the logs. Then read payments-dlt with --formatter-property print.headers=true.
Check what you saw
  • 100 and 250 succeed at once; 503 succeeds on attempt 3 while the partition waits, and 250 is processed after it (order kept).
  • abc appears in payments-dlt with the original topic, partition, offset, and exception in its headers.
  • If you kill the consumer between processing and committing, restarting it reprocesses that record: run the same input twice and check your output for duplicates. That is the reason for the next step: make process idempotent by event ID.

10.10Common mistakes

Common mistakes

  • Infinite retries that block a partition forever.
  • Retrying permanent errors such as validation failures.
  • Thread.sleep() inside the poll loop for long backoffs, which exceeds max.poll.interval.ms and triggers rebalances.
  • A DLT that nobody alerts on or replays from.
  • Retry topics for an ordered stream without a plan for order.
  • Deduplicating by Kafka offset instead of a producer-assigned event ID.
  • Killing consumers without close(), which delays the rebalance until the session times out.

10.11Self-check

Self-checkFive more, after the lessons
  1. When are retry topics a bad idea?
    Reveal

    When per-key order matters, or when a dependency is completely down (every record would cycle through the retry topics). Use in-place retries, pausing, or a circuit breaker instead.

  2. What should a DLT record contain?
    Reveal

    The original key, value, and headers, plus metadata: original topic, partition, offset, timestamp, exception details, attempt count, and the consumer that failed.

  3. How do you skip a record that cannot be deserialized?
    Reveal

    Catch RecordDeserializationException, record the raw bytes (for example to a DLT), and seek() to its offset + 1. Or consume bytes and deserialize yourself.

  4. How does a processed-events table make a consumer idempotent?
    Reveal

    Inserting the event ID with a unique constraint in the same transaction as the effect means a duplicate insert fails or inserts nothing, so the effect runs once.

  5. Why use pause() rather than stopping calls to poll()?
    Reveal

    poll() keeps the consumer alive in the group and lets other partitions continue; not polling would exceed max.poll.interval.ms and trigger a rebalance.

Phase 4: Inside the brokerCoreDeep dive

Module 11: Storage: the log on disk

Why can a Kafka broker serve hundreds of megabytes per second from ordinary disks? This module opens a partition directory: segments, sparse indexes, record batches, the page cache, zero-copy transfers, how retention deletes data, why Kafka does not fsync every write, and how tiered storage moves history to object storage.

10 lessons5 figures1 lab6 mastery checks

On this page

  1. 11.1A partition is a directory of segments
  2. 11.2Finding an offset
  3. 11.3Record batches
  4. 11.4Why Kafka is fast
  5. 11.5Retention and deletion
  6. 11.6Durability without fsync
  7. 11.7Tiered storage
  8. 11.8Lab: look inside a partition
  9. 11.9Common mistakes
  10. 11.10Self-check
Warm-upWarm-up: one line each
  1. Is one partition stored as one big file?
    Reveal

    No. It is a directory of segment files. New records go to the active segment; older segments are sealed.

  2. How does Kafka find offset 52,400 without scanning gigabytes?
    Reveal

    It picks the segment by base offset from its file name, looks up the nearest earlier entry in that segment's sparse index, and scans forward a few kilobytes.

  3. Does Kafka keep its own cache of recent records in the JVM heap?
    Reveal

    No. It relies on the operating system's page cache, so recently written data is usually served from memory.

  4. Does Kafka fsync each write to disk before acknowledging it?
    Reveal

    Not by default. Durability comes from replication to several brokers; flushing to disk is left to the operating system.

  5. Retention is 7 days. Can a record older than 7 days still be read?
    Reveal

    Yes, for a while. Retention deletes whole segments, and a segment goes only when its newest record is older than the limit.

11.1A partition is a directory of segments

  • Each partition replica is a directory named <topic>-<partition> under one of the broker's log.dirs.
  • A segment is a .log file of record batches plus a .index (offset to byte position) and a .timeindex (timestamp to offset). The file names are the segment's base offset, the first offset it contains.
  • The active segment receives appends. It rolls (is sealed and a new one starts) when it reaches segment.bytes (1 GiB by default), when it is older than segment.ms (7 days), or when its index fills up.
  • Other files you may see: .txnindex (aborted transactions, Module 14), .snapshot (producer state for idempotence), leader-epoch-checkpoint, and partition.metadata (the topic ID).

11.2Finding an offset

  • Segment lookup: brokers keep segments sorted by base offset, so finding the right one is a binary search.
  • Sparse index: one entry per log.index.interval.bytes (4 KB) of log data, mapping a relative offset to a byte position. Index files are memory-mapped and small.
  • Short scan: from that position, read forward to the exact offset. Reads are sequential and usually hit the page cache.
  • The time index works the same way for timestamps. It answers "first offset at or after 09:00", which is how offset resets by time and offsetsForTimes work.

11.3Record batches

  • Producers send, brokers store, and consumers receive record batches, not single records. A batch header holds the base offset, the leader epoch, timestamps, a CRC, compression and transaction flags, and the producer ID, epoch, and base sequence number used for idempotence.
  • Records inside a batch store small deltas (offset delta, timestamp delta) with variable-length encoding, so many small records cost little overhead.
  • With the topic's default compression.type=producer, the broker keeps batches compressed exactly as the producer sent them and serves them as is; consumers decompress.

11.4Why Kafka is fast

Try it first2 minutes

List four design choices that let one broker handle very high throughput on ordinary hardware.

Reveal the answer

Sequential appends instead of random writes; the operating system's page cache instead of an application cache; zero-copy transfer from page cache to network for consumers; batching and compression end to end; and spreading partitions over many disks and brokers.

  • Sequential I/O: appends and tail reads are sequential, which disks (even spinning ones) do very fast.
  • The page cache: Kafka writes into the operating system's page cache and reads from it. Consumers that keep up read data that is still in memory, so many caught-up clusters show almost no disk reads. Give brokers a modest JVM heap (a few GB) and leave the rest of RAM to the page cache.
  • Zero-copy: the broker sends file data straight from the page cache to the socket.
  • Batching and compression shrink request counts and bytes on the wire and on disk.
  • No per-message bookkeeping on the broker: consumers track their own offsets, so a read does not change broker state.
Watch out

TLS encryption happens in user space, so brokers cannot use sendfile for TLS connections. Expect more broker CPU and somewhat lower throughput with TLS; plan capacity with it on, since production clusters should encrypt.

11.5Retention and deletion

  • A background task runs every log.retention.check.interval.ms (5 minutes). With cleanup.policy=delete, it deletes a sealed segment when its newest record is older than retention.ms, or deletes the oldest segments while the partition is larger than retention.bytes.
  • Deleted segments are renamed with a .deleted suffix and removed after log.segment.delete.delay.ms (1 minute).
  • The log start offset moves to the first remaining offset. A consumer asking for an older offset gets "offset out of range" and resets per auto.offset.reset.
  • kafka-delete-records.sh (the deleteRecords API) moves the log start offset forward on demand, for example to purge bad data.
  • To delete data sooner, lower segment.ms as well as retention.ms, because only sealed segments can be deleted.

11.6Durability without fsync

  • By default Kafka does not force an fsync for each write: flush.messages and flush.ms are effectively unlimited, so the operating system decides when dirty pages reach disk.
  • Durability comes from replication: an acks=all write sits in the page cache of every in-sync replica, on different machines. Losing all of them at once, before any flushes, is far less likely than losing one disk.
  • After a crash, a broker recovers its unflushed segments (rebuilding indexes, truncating partial batches) and then catches up from the current leader.
  • You can force frequent flushes per topic, but it costs throughput; replication with acks=all and min.insync.replicas=2 is the standard answer.

11.7Tiered storage

  • Generally available since Kafka 3.9. Brokers copy completed segments to remote object storage and keep only recent data locally (local.retention.ms or local.retention.bytes); retention.ms still sets total retention.
  • Why: long retention (months or years) without huge broker disks; faster broker replacement and reassignment because less data lives locally.
  • Setup: enable remote.log.storage.system.enable=true on brokers, plug in a RemoteStorageManager implementation for your store (Kafka does not ship one for S3), then set remote.storage.enable=true per topic.
  • Limits: not supported for compacted topics; reads of old data are slower than local tail reads.

11.8Lab: look inside a partition

LabWatch segments roll, dump a log, and see retention delete segments20 minutes

On the single broker, create a topic with tiny 1 MB segments (the minimum allowed) and fill it:

Terminal
./kafka-topics.sh --bootstrap-server localhost:9092 --create --topic seglab --partitions 1 \
  --replication-factor 1 --config segment.bytes=1048576
./kafka-producer-perf-test.sh --bootstrap-server localhost:9092 --topic seglab \
  --num-records 5000 --record-size 1000 --throughput -1
ls -l /tmp/kraft-combined-logs/seglab-0/

Dump the first segment and its index:

Terminal
./kafka-dump-log.sh --files /tmp/kraft-combined-logs/seglab-0/00000000000000000000.log | head -8
./kafka-dump-log.sh --files /tmp/kraft-combined-logs/seglab-0/00000000000000000000.index | head -8

Now make retention very short, wait about 6 minutes, and check the files and the earliest offset:

Terminal
./kafka-configs.sh --bootstrap-server localhost:9092 --alter --entity-type topics \
  --entity-name seglab --add-config retention.ms=60000
ls -l /tmp/kraft-combined-logs/seglab-0/
./kafka-get-offsets.sh --bootstrap-server localhost:9092 --topic seglab --time earliest
Check what you saw
  • About five .log files appear, each near 1 MB, named by their base offsets, each with a .index and .timeindex.
  • The log dump prints batches with baseOffset, lastOffset, count, producerId, baseSequence, and compresscodec. The index dump shows a sparse list of offset and position pairs, not one per record.
  • After the retention check runs (every 5 minutes) all sealed segments are deleted; files briefly carry a .deleted suffix. Only the active segment remains, and the earliest offset jumps from 0 to that segment's base offset.

11.9Common mistakes

Common mistakes

  • Giving the broker JVM most of the machine's RAM, starving the page cache that Kafka actually relies on.
  • Expecting retention to delete data exactly on time: whole segments go, and only sealed ones.
  • Forcing fsync per message for "safety" instead of using replication and acks=all.
  • Running consumers far behind, so their reads miss the page cache and hit disk, slowing everyone.
  • Turning on tiered storage for compacted topics, which it does not support.
  • Forgetting TLS costs when sizing broker CPU.

11.10Self-check

Self-checkFive more, after the lessons
  1. What files make up a segment, and what does each do?
    Reveal

    The .log holds record batches; the .index maps relative offsets to byte positions; the .timeindex maps timestamps to offsets. The name is the base offset.

  2. Why is the offset index sparse?
    Reveal

    Indexing every record would make the index large. One entry per 4 KB keeps it small and memory-mapped; a short sequential scan finds the exact record.

  3. What is zero-copy, and when does Kafka lose it?
    Reveal

    Using sendfile to move data from the page cache directly to the network socket without copying through the application. It is not possible with TLS, which must encrypt in user space.

  4. When exactly does time-based retention delete a segment?
    Reveal

    When the segment is sealed and its newest record's timestamp is older than retention.ms, at the next retention check.

  5. Where does Kafka's durability come from if it does not fsync each write?
    Reveal

    From replication: an acknowledged acks=all record is in memory or on disk on every in-sync replica, on separate machines.
