Module 12: Replication and fault tolerance

Replication is how Kafka survives broker failures without losing acknowledged data. This module goes inside it: how followers fetch, what keeps a replica in the ISR, the log end offset and high watermark, leader election and epochs, truncation, the unclean election trade-off, eligible leader replicas, and rack-aware placement.

11 lessons4 figures1 lab6 mastery checks

On this page

  1. 12.1Leaders, followers, and fetching
  2. 12.2The in-sync replica set
  3. 12.3Log end offset and high watermark
  4. 12.4acks and failures together
  5. 12.5Leader election and epochs
  6. 12.6Unclean leader election
  7. 12.7Preferred leaders and balance
  8. 12.8Racks, zones, and follower fetching
  9. 12.9Lab: replication in action
  10. 12.10Common mistakes
  11. 12.11Self-check
Warm-upWarm-up: one line each
  1. Do followers receive data pushed by the leader?
    Reveal

    No. Followers send fetch requests to the leader, like consumers, and append what they receive.

  2. What gets a follower removed from the ISR?
    Reveal

    Not catching up to the leader's log end within replica.lag.time.max.ms (30 s), or losing its session with the controller (the broker is fenced).

  3. Can a consumer read a record the moment the leader writes it?
    Reveal

    No. Consumers read only below the high watermark, which advances when every in-sync replica has the record.

  4. What does unclean leader election trade?
    Reveal

    Availability for durability. It lets an out-of-sync replica become leader, so the partition comes back sooner but acknowledged records can be lost.

  5. An old leader comes back after a failover with records the new leader never got. What happens to them?
    Reveal

    The old leader truncates them, using leader epochs to find where its log diverged, and then follows the new leader.

12.1Leaders, followers, and fetching

  • Every partition has one leader and zero or more followers on other brokers. Producers write to the leader; consumers read from it by default.
  • Followers run replica fetcher threads that send fetch requests to the leader and append the returned batches, so their logs are identical copies with the same offsets.
  • Leaders are spread across brokers so that write load is balanced. The first replica in a partition's replica list is its preferred leader.

12.2The in-sync replica set

  • A replica is in sync when its broker has an active session with the controller and it has caught up to the leader's log end within the last replica.lag.time.max.ms (30 s).
  • The leader shrinks the ISR when a follower falls behind and expands it when the follower catches up; the controller records each change in the metadata log.
  • The guarantee: a committed record will not be lost as long as at least one in-sync replica survives.

12.3Log end offset and high watermark

  • Log end offset (LEO): on each replica, the offset the next record will get.
  • High watermark (HW): on the leader, the highest offset that every in-sync replica has; records below it are committed. Followers learn the HW from fetch responses.
  • Consumers see only committed records, so a consumer never reads a record that a failover could erase.
  • An acks=all produce request completes once the HW passes its records. Since Kafka 3.7 the HW also stops advancing while the ISR is smaller than min.insync.replicas.

12.4acks and failures together

Durability and availability simulatorOne partition. Click a broker to cycle it through in sync, lagging (alive but out of the ISR), and down.

Model: in-sync replicas hold every committed record; lagging replicas are missing recent ones. The high watermark rule shown here (it stops while the ISR is below min.insync.replicas) applies since Kafka 3.7.

Scenario (RF 3, min ISR 2) acks=1 acks=all
Leader dies right after acknowledging, before followers fetch The acknowledged record is lost Cannot happen: acknowledgment waited for the ISR
One follower down Writes fine Writes fine (ISR of 2 meets the minimum)
Two replicas down Writes accepted, not visible to consumers Writes rejected with NotEnoughReplicas
All in-sync replicas lost at once Data since the last replicated point is lost Partition offline until an in-sync replica returns

12.5Leader election and epochs

  • The controller notices a dead broker when its heartbeats stop for broker.session.timeout.ms (9 s) and fences it. A clean shutdown is faster: the broker asks the controller to move its leaderships first (controlled shutdown).
  • The controller picks a new leader from the ISR and increases the partition's leader epoch. Every replica and client uses the epoch to reject stale leaders and stale requests.
  • Clients get NOT_LEADER_OR_FOLLOWER or connection errors, refresh metadata, and retry against the new leader automatically.
  • Truncation: a returning replica asks the leader where the log of its last epoch ended, then truncates anything beyond it before fetching. This is how records that were never committed disappear, and why acks=1 writes can vanish.

12.6Unclean leader election

  • If every in-sync replica is gone, the partition has no safe leader.
  • unclean.leader.election.enable=false (default): stay offline until an in-sync replica returns. No acknowledged data is lost; availability suffers.
  • true: elect any live replica now. The partition is available sooner, but records only the lost replicas had are gone, and later writes reuse their offsets.
  • Choose false for anything financial or auditable. Some teams enable it on low-value topics such as metrics.
Go deeper

Eligible leader replicas (Kafka 4.x)

Kafka 4.0 introduced eligible leader replicas (ELR, KIP-966 part 1), enabled by default on new clusters since 4.1. Because the high watermark cannot advance while the ISR is below min.insync.replicas, a replica that drops out of the ISR in that state is still guaranteed to hold every committed record. The controller tracks such replicas as the ELR and may elect one of them if the ISR becomes empty, before falling back to the last known leader. The practical effect: fewer cases where the only choices are "stay offline" or "unclean election and lose data". With ELR enabled, min.insync.replicas must be set at the cluster or topic level, not per broker.

12.7Preferred leaders and balance

  • After a broker restarts, it rejoins as a follower and leads nothing, so load is skewed toward the others.
  • auto.leader.rebalance.enable=true (default) moves leadership back to preferred leaders periodically (checked every 5 minutes by default). To do it now, run kafka-leader-election.sh --election-type preferred --all-topic-partitions.
  • Spread preferred leaders evenly when you create or reassign topics; tools such as Cruise Control keep replicas and leaders balanced automatically.

12.8Racks, zones, and follower fetching

  • Set broker.rack to each broker's availability zone. Kafka then places each partition's replicas in different racks, so losing a whole zone loses one copy, not all of them.
  • Follower fetching: set replica.selector.class=org.apache.kafka.common.replica.RackAwareReplicaSelector on brokers and client.rack on consumers. Consumers then read from a replica in their own zone, cutting cross-zone network cost, which is a large share of cloud Kafka bills.
  • Writes still go to the leader, wherever it is.
In production

A common cloud layout: one region, three availability zones, replication factor 3 with one replica per zone, min.insync.replicas=2, acks=all. Any one zone can fail with no data loss and writes continuing, and follower fetching keeps consumer traffic inside each zone.

12.9Lab: replication in action

LabWatch the ISR shrink and grow, and find the high watermark15 minutes

On the three-broker cluster with the k helper, create a topic and write some data:

Terminal
k kafka-topics.sh --create --topic repl --partitions 1 --replication-factor 3 --config min.insync.replicas=2
k kafka-producer-perf-test.sh --topic repl --num-records 20000 --record-size 200 --throughput -1
k kafka-topics.sh --describe --topic repl

Note the leader. Stop a follower, produce more, then check the ISR and the end offset. (The commands assume node 3 is a follower; if it is the leader, stop and later start kafka-2 instead.)

Terminal
docker stop kafka-3
k kafka-producer-perf-test.sh --topic repl --num-records 20000 --record-size 200 --throughput -1
k kafka-topics.sh --describe --topic repl
k kafka-topics.sh --describe --under-min-isr-partitions
k kafka-get-offsets.sh --topic repl

Start it again and watch it rejoin:

Terminal
docker start kafka-3
k kafka-topics.sh --describe --topic repl
Check what you saw
  • With all three running, Isr lists three brokers.
  • After stopping a follower, Isr lists two, writes still succeed (2 meets min.insync.replicas=2), and --under-min-isr-partitions prints nothing because the partition is at, not under, the minimum.
  • kafka-get-offsets.sh returns the latest offset that consumers can read: 40000, the high watermark.
  • After the restart, the follower first truncates to the leader's history if needed, then fetches the records it missed and reappears in Isr within seconds.

12.10Common mistakes

Common mistakes

  • Believing acks=1 is "almost as safe": it loses acknowledged records whenever a leader dies before followers fetch.
  • Enabling unclean leader election on important topics to "improve availability".
  • Replicas in one availability zone, so one zone outage takes all copies.
  • Ignoring under-replicated partitions, which means running without the redundancy you planned.
  • Leaving leadership skewed after restarts, overloading some brokers.
  • Skipping follower fetching in the cloud and paying for cross-zone consumer traffic.

12.11Self-check

Self-checkFive more, after the lessons
  1. Define LEO and HW, and say which one consumers care about.
    Reveal

    LEO is the next offset a replica will write; HW is the highest offset every in-sync replica has. Consumers read only below the HW.

  2. Why does Kafka elect leaders from the ISR?
    Reveal

    In-sync replicas have every committed record, so electing one of them guarantees no committed record is lost.

  3. What is a leader epoch for?
    Reveal

    It numbers each leadership period. Replicas and clients use it to reject stale leaders and to find exactly where a returning replica's log diverged, so it can truncate safely.

  4. What happens when all in-sync replicas of a partition fail?
    Reveal

    With unclean election off, the partition is unavailable until an in-sync replica returns (or, with ELR, an eligible replica can be chosen). With it on, a lagging replica becomes leader and committed records it lacks are lost.

  5. How does follower fetching save money?
    Reveal

    Consumers read from a replica in their own availability zone instead of the leader's zone, avoiding cross-zone data transfer charges.

Module 13: Log compaction

Deletion by time keeps recent history; compaction keeps the latest value for every key, forever. That turns a topic into a durable table you can rebuild state from. This module covers what compaction guarantees, tombstones for deletes, how the log cleaner decides what to clean, the settings that control it, and where compacted topics are used.

7 lessons2 figures1 lab5 mastery checks

On this page

  1. 13.1The idea: keep the latest value per key
  2. 13.2What compaction guarantees
  3. 13.3How the log cleaner works
  4. 13.4Where compacted topics are used
  5. 13.5Lab: watch compaction happen
  6. 13.6Common mistakes
  7. 13.7Self-check
Warm-upWarm-up: one line each
  1. A compacted topic receives price updates for AAPL every second for a year. Roughly how many AAPL records remain?
    Reveal

    At least the latest one, plus whatever has not been cleaned yet (the active segment and the dirty part). Old updates are eventually removed.

  2. How do you delete a key from a compacted topic?
    Reveal

    Produce a tombstone: a record with that key and a null value. After cleaning and delete.retention.ms, the key disappears entirely.

  3. Does compaction change the offsets of the records it keeps?
    Reveal

    No. Kept records keep their offsets; the log simply has gaps.

  4. Can you produce records without a key to a compacted topic?
    Reveal

    No. The broker rejects keyless records on compacted topics, since compaction is per key.

  5. Name a compacted topic that every Kafka cluster has.
    Reveal

    __consumer_offsets: only the latest committed offset per group and partition matters.

13.1The idea: keep the latest value per key

Idea

For each key, keep at least the most recent record and remove older ones in the background. The topic becomes a snapshot of current state, plus recent changes.

Analogy

Your phone's contacts versus its call log. The call log keeps every call in order (delete by time); contacts keep only the latest number for each person (compaction).

  • Turn it on with cleanup.policy=compact. Use cleanup.policy=compact,delete to also drop records older than retention.ms.
  • Every record must have a key; the key is what compaction compares.
  • A tombstone (key with a null value) means "this key is deleted". It is kept for delete.retention.ms (1 day) after it is cleaned so consumers can see the delete, then it is removed.

13.2What compaction guarantees

  1. A consumer that keeps up sees every record. Compaction only touches the older, cleaned part of the log.
  2. Order is preserved. Compaction removes records; it never reorders them.
  3. Offsets never change.
  4. A consumer reading from the beginning sees at least the final value of every key, in write order. It also sees tombstones if it finishes reading within delete.retention.ms.

It does not promise that only one record per key exists at any moment. Until the cleaner runs, duplicates for a key are normal, so consumers must treat the topic as a sequence of upserts.

13.3How the log cleaner works

  • Cleaner threads (log.cleaner.threads, 1 by default) pick the partition whose log has the highest dirty ratio: the share of the log written since the last cleaning.
  • A partition is eligible when its dirty ratio exceeds min.cleanable.dirty.ratio (0.5), or when a record has waited longer than max.compaction.lag.ms.
  • The cleaner builds a map from key to latest offset over the dirty part, then rewrites the older segments keeping only records that are the latest for their key, and swaps the new segments in.
  • The active segment is never cleaned. On a low-traffic topic with the default segment.ms of 7 days, stale values can sit in the active segment for a week. Lower segment.ms if that matters.
Setting Default Controls
cleanup.policy delete compact, delete, or both
min.cleanable.dirty.ratio 0.5 How dirty a log must be before cleaning; lower means more cleaning work and less duplication
min.compaction.lag.ms 0 Minimum age before a record may be compacted away, so consumers can see every update
max.compaction.lag.ms unlimited Maximum time a record can wait before cleaning; use it to bound how long deleted data lingers
delete.retention.ms 1 day How long tombstones stay after cleaning
segment.ms 7 days How often the active segment rolls and becomes cleanable
At work

For "right to be forgotten" requests on a compacted topic, a tombstone alone is not enough: set max.compaction.lag.ms so cleaning is guaranteed within your deadline, and remember copies in other places (consumers' databases, backups, mirrors). For data on delete-policy topics, encrypt personal data with a per-person key and delete the key (crypto-shredding).

13.4Where compacted topics are used

Use Key Value
__consumer_offsets Group, topic, partition Committed offset
Kafka Streams changelogs and KTables (Module 17) Table key Latest aggregate or row
Change data capture of a table (Module 16) Primary key Latest row, tombstone on delete
Reference data (merchants, currency rates, feature flags) Entity ID Current record
Rebuilding a cache or search index Entity ID Current document
Latest position of each vehicle or device Device ID Latest location

A service can rebuild its whole state by reading a compacted topic from the beginning, then keep it current by continuing to consume.

Watch out

Do not add partitions to a compacted topic in place. A key's old value stays in its old partition and its new value lands in a new one, and the two are never compacted together, so a reader can end up with a stale value (Module 6). Tiered storage also does not support compacted topics.

13.5Lab: watch compaction happen

LabCompact a price topic and delete a key15 minutes

On the single broker, create a compacted topic with settings that make cleaning happen within seconds (lab values only):

Terminal
./kafka-topics.sh --bootstrap-server localhost:9092 --create --topic prices --partitions 1 \
  --replication-factor 1 --config cleanup.policy=compact --config segment.ms=5000 \
  --config min.cleanable.dirty.ratio=0.01 --config delete.retention.ms=1000
./kafka-console-producer.sh --bootstrap-server localhost:9092 --topic prices \
  --reader-property parse.key=true --reader-property key.separator=: \
  --reader-property null.marker=NULL

Type these lines, then wait 10 seconds and type one more line, TICK:1, so the segment rolls:

Text
AAPL:100
MSFT:300
AAPL:101
GOOG:150
AAPL:102
MSFT:301

Wait about 30 seconds (the cleaner checks every 15 seconds when idle), then read from the beginning:

Terminal
./kafka-console-consumer.sh --bootstrap-server localhost:9092 --topic prices --from-beginning \
  --formatter-property print.key=true --formatter-property print.offset=true

Now delete GOOG: produce GOOG:NULL, wait 10 seconds, produce TICK:2, wait a minute, and read again.

Check what you saw
  • The first read shows GOOG 150 at offset 3, AAPL 102 at offset 4, MSFT 301 at offset 5, and TICK 1 at offset 6. Offsets 0 to 2 are gone; the kept records kept their offsets.
  • After the tombstone, a read soon after cleaning may show GOOG null (the tombstone) for a short time; after delete.retention.ms and another cleaning pass, GOOG disappears entirely.
  • If you read before the cleaner ran, you would see all records. Compaction is eventual, never immediate.

13.6Common mistakes

Common mistakes

  • Assuming exactly one record per key at all times: duplicates exist until cleaning.
  • Producing keyless records to a compacted topic (they are rejected).
  • Low-traffic compacted topics with the default segment.ms, leaving stale values in the active segment for days.
  • Using compaction alone for data deletion deadlines without max.compaction.lag.ms.
  • Very low min.cleanable.dirty.ratio in production, which keeps the cleaner busy rewriting segments.
  • Growing the partition count of a compacted topic in place.

13.7Self-check

Self-checkFive more, after the lessons
  1. What four guarantees does compaction give?
    Reveal

    Caught-up consumers see every record; order is preserved; offsets never change; a consumer reading from the start sees at least the latest value of every key (and tombstones, if it finishes within delete.retention.ms).

  2. What is a tombstone, and how long does it live?
    Reveal

    A record with a key and a null value, marking that key deleted. It stays for delete.retention.ms after the cleaner processes it, then is removed.

  3. When does the cleaner clean a partition?
    Reveal

    When its dirty ratio exceeds min.cleanable.dirty.ratio, or when a record has waited longer than max.compaction.lag.ms; the active segment is always skipped.

  4. Why use compact,delete?
    Reveal

    To keep the latest value per key but also drop anything older than retention.ms, for example windowed aggregates that are useless after some time.

  5. Why is a compacted topic a good way to rebuild a cache?
    Reveal

    Reading it from the beginning yields the current value of every key without replaying the full history, then live consumption keeps the cache up to date.

Module 14: Exactly-once semantics and transactions

"Exactly-once" in Kafka has a precise meaning and a precise scope. This module builds it from parts: the idempotent producer, transactions that write to many partitions atomically and commit consumer offsets with them, read_committed consumers, zombie fencing, and then what to do when the effect lives outside Kafka, with the transactional outbox.

9 lessons4 figures1 lab6 mastery checks

On this page

  1. 14.1What exactly-once means here
  2. 14.2Transactions
  3. 14.3read_committed consumers
  4. 14.4Zombie fencing
  5. 14.5Exactly-once when a database is involved
  6. 14.6Costs and pitfalls
  7. 14.7Lab: see read_committed and the LSO
  8. 14.8Common mistakes
  9. 14.9Self-check
Warm-upWarm-up: one line each
  1. Does Kafka guarantee that a record is delivered exactly once to a consumer?
    Reveal

    No. Delivery can repeat after crashes and rebalances. Kafka offers exactly-once processing for read-process-write pipelines that stay within Kafka, using transactions.

  2. A transaction writes to three partitions. Can a read_committed consumer see one partition's records but not the others?
    Reveal

    Not for long: either all of the transaction's records become visible (commit) or none do (abort). Partitions are read independently, so visibility may arrive a moment apart, but an aborted transaction is never visible anywhere.

  3. What does transactional.id give you that plain idempotence does not?
    Reveal

    Identity across restarts: a restarted instance with the same ID fences its predecessor, and unfinished transactions are completed or aborted, so a zombie cannot write duplicates.

  4. Your consumer reads Kafka and calls a bank API. Do Kafka transactions make the API call exactly-once?
    Reveal

    No. Transactions cover Kafka writes and offset commits only. The API call needs an idempotency key on the bank's side.

  5. What is the transactional outbox for?
    Reveal

    Writing a database change and publishing an event atomically, by putting the event in an outbox table inside the same database transaction and relaying it to Kafka afterwards.

14.1What exactly-once means here

Try it first3 minutes

A Kafka Streams-like job reads payments, computes a fee, and writes fees. It crashes after writing a fee but before committing its input offset. What goes wrong without transactions, and what must be atomic to fix it?

Reveal the answer

On restart it reprocesses the payment and writes a second fee: a duplicate in fees. To fix it, "write the output" and "commit the input offset" must happen atomically: both or neither. That is exactly what a Kafka transaction does.

  • The effect happens once, even though records may be delivered more than once internally. People also call it "effectively once".
  • Scope: consume from Kafka, process, produce to Kafka, and commit offsets, all inside Kafka. Effects in other systems need idempotency (Modules 8 and 10).
  • The parts: the idempotent producer (no duplicates from retries), transactions (atomic multi-partition writes plus offsets), and read_committed consumers (never see aborted data).

14.2Transactions

  • transactional.id names the producer across restarts. The transaction coordinator for that ID is the broker leading its partition of __transaction_state.
  • initTransactions() gets a producer ID and bumps the epoch, fencing any older instance with the same ID, and finishes or aborts its open transaction.
  • Inside a transaction the producer writes to any number of partitions, and sendOffsetsToTransaction() adds the consumed offsets.
  • Commit is a two-phase protocol run by the coordinator: it records PREPARE_COMMIT, writes a commit marker (a control record that takes an offset) into every involved partition, then records COMPLETE_COMMIT. Abort is the same with abort markers.
Consume, transform, produce with exactly-once
producerProps.put(ProducerConfig.TRANSACTIONAL_ID_CONFIG, "fee-calculator-" + instanceId);
consumerProps.put(ConsumerConfig.ISOLATION_LEVEL_CONFIG, "read_committed");
consumerProps.put(ConsumerConfig.ENABLE_AUTO_COMMIT_CONFIG, false);

producer.initTransactions();
consumer.subscribe(List.of("payments"));
while (running) {
    ConsumerRecords<String, String> records = consumer.poll(Duration.ofMillis(200));
    if (records.isEmpty()) continue;
    try {
        producer.beginTransaction();
        for (ConsumerRecord<String, String> r : records) {
            producer.send(new ProducerRecord<>("fees", r.key(), computeFee(r.value())));
        }
        producer.sendOffsetsToTransaction(nextOffsets(records), consumer.groupMetadata());
        producer.commitTransaction();
    } catch (ProducerFencedException | OutOfOrderSequenceException | AuthorizationException e) {
        producer.close();          // fatal: another instance took over, or we lack permission
        throw e;
    } catch (KafkaException e) {   // includes timeouts and TransactionAbortableException
        producer.abortTransaction();
        rewindToCommitted(consumer); // seek back so the batch is processed again
    }
}
  • nextOffsets(records) returns, for each partition, the last processed offset plus one.
  • consumer.groupMetadata() lets the broker fence a zombie by consumer group generation too, so one transactional producer per application instance is enough.
  • Since Kafka 4.0, treat a TimeoutException or TransactionAbortableException during a transaction as a reason to abort and retry, never to continue.

14.3read_committed consumers

  • isolation.level=read_committed delivers committed transactional records and non-transactional records, skips aborted ones (brokers keep an aborted-transactions index per segment), and stops at the last stable offset (LSO).
  • The default, read_uncommitted, delivers everything up to the high watermark, including records from transactions that later abort.
  • An open transaction holds back the LSO for every read_committed consumer of that partition, even for records from other producers written after it. Long transactions mean visible delay.
  • transaction.timeout.ms (60 s on the producer, at most transaction.max.timeout.ms, 15 minutes, on the broker) bounds how long a transaction may stay open before the coordinator aborts it.

14.4Zombie fencing

  • Every initTransactions() call increases the epoch for that transactional.id. Writes and commits carrying an older epoch are rejected with ProducerFencedException.
  • Choose IDs that are stable per instance and unique across instances, such as the application name plus a pod ordinal. Two live instances sharing an ID keep fencing each other.
  • Kafka 4.0 strengthened the protocol (KIP-890): the epoch is bumped on every transaction and brokers verify that a partition belongs to an ongoing transaction before accepting transactional writes. This closes holes that could leave "hanging" transactions.

14.5Exactly-once when a database is involved

Try it first3 minutes

The order service must save an order in PostgreSQL and publish OrderPlaced. Why is "commit the database transaction, then call producer.send()" not safe, and why is the reverse order not safe either?

Reveal the answer

DB first: a crash after the commit but before the send loses the event forever. Send first: a crash before the DB commit publishes an event for an order that does not exist. Two separate systems cannot be updated atomically without help; this is the dual-write problem.

  • Producer side, transactional outbox: write the business row and an outbox row (event type, key, payload, ID) in one database transaction. A relay publishes outbox rows to Kafka: Debezium's outbox event router reading the write-ahead log (Module 16), or a poller using SELECT ... FOR UPDATE SKIP LOCKED. The relay is at-least-once, so every event carries an ID.
  • Consumer side, idempotent consumer: apply the effect and record the event ID in one database transaction (Module 10), or store the consumed offset in that transaction (Module 8).
  • End to end: outbox plus idempotent consumers gives exactly-once effects across services, without distributed transactions.

14.6Costs and pitfalls

  • Latency: records become visible to read_committed consumers only at commit. Commit every few hundred milliseconds or every few hundred records, not per record.
  • Throughput: markers and coordinator round trips cost a little; batching many records per transaction amortizes it.
  • Hanging transactions (a producer died mid-transaction on an older version) block the LSO until they time out. kafka-transactions.sh find-hanging and abort handle them.
  • Kafka Streams wraps all of this: set processing.guarantee=exactly_once_v2 (Module 17). Flink uses its own checkpoints plus a transactional Kafka sink.
Interview signal

"How do you guarantee each payment produces exactly one ledger entry?" A strong answer states the scope first: inside Kafka, transactions with read_committed consumers; across a database, an outbox on the producer side and idempotent writes keyed by payment ID on the consumer side; for external APIs, idempotency keys. Then names the costs: latency until commit and an LSO that open transactions hold back.

14.7Lab: see read_committed and the LSO

LabTransactional writes, two isolation levels, and the transactions tool15 minutes

On the single broker, create a topic and start a transactional load that commits every 5 seconds:

Terminal
./kafka-topics.sh --bootstrap-server localhost:9092 --create --topic txlab --partitions 1 --replication-factor 1
./kafka-producer-perf-test.sh --bootstrap-server localhost:9092 --topic txlab \
  --num-records 3000 --record-size 20 --throughput 50 \
  --transactional-id perf-tx --transaction-duration-ms 5000

While it runs, in two other terminals, start one consumer of each isolation level:

Terminal
./kafka-console-consumer.sh --bootstrap-server localhost:9092 --topic txlab \
  --isolation-level read_uncommitted --formatter-property print.offset=true
./kafka-console-consumer.sh --bootstrap-server localhost:9092 --topic txlab \
  --isolation-level read_committed --formatter-property print.offset=true

In a fourth terminal, inspect the transaction:

Terminal
./kafka-transactions.sh --bootstrap-server localhost:9092 list
./kafka-transactions.sh --bootstrap-server localhost:9092 describe --transactional-id perf-tx
Check what you saw
  • The read_uncommitted consumer prints a steady stream, about 50 records per second.
  • The read_committed consumer prints nothing for about 5 seconds, then a burst of about 250 records, then waits again: it can only read up to the last stable offset, which jumps at each commit.
  • Each commit marker takes an offset, so the offsets printed by either consumer skip a number about every 250 records.
  • list shows perf-tx with its coordinator and state; describe shows its producer ID, epoch, state (Ongoing or CompleteCommit), and the partitions in the current transaction.

14.8Common mistakes

Common mistakes

  • Promising "exactly-once delivery" to a consumer, or exactly-once effects in external systems from Kafka transactions alone.
  • Forgetting read_committed on consumers of transactional topics, so they read aborted records.
  • Sharing a transactional.id between live instances, so they fence each other.
  • Random transactional.id per start, which loses fencing of the previous instance.
  • One transaction per record, which multiplies overhead and latency.
  • Long-running transactions that hold back the LSO for every read_committed consumer.
  • Dual writes (database then Kafka, or the reverse) without an outbox.

14.9Self-check

Self-checkFive more, after the lessons
  1. Which three mechanisms combine to give exactly-once processing within Kafka?
    Reveal

    The idempotent producer, transactions (atomic writes across partitions plus consumer offsets via sendOffsetsToTransaction), and consumers with isolation.level=read_committed.

  2. What is the last stable offset?
    Reveal

    The first offset belonging to a transaction that is still open in a partition. read_committed consumers cannot read beyond it.

  3. How does Kafka fence a zombie producer?
    Reveal

    initTransactions() with the same transactional.id bumps the epoch; the broker rejects writes and commits with an older epoch, and the zombie gets ProducerFencedException.

  4. What do you do on a KafkaException during a transaction, and on a ProducerFencedException?
    Reveal

    For general errors, abort the transaction and seek back to the last committed offsets to reprocess. For fencing (and other fatal errors), close the producer and stop: another instance owns that ID.

  5. Why does the outbox pattern need idempotent consumers?
    Reveal

    The relay is at-least-once: it can publish an outbox row more than once after a crash, so consumers deduplicate by event ID.

Module 15: Schemas, serialization, and event design

Kafka moves bytes; your teams need contracts. This module covers serialization formats, how a schema registry enforces compatible evolution, the rules for changing a schema safely, how to design events and topics that age well, and what to do with payloads too large for Kafka.

10 lessons2 figures1 lab6 mastery checks

On this page

  1. 15.1Kafka stores bytes
  2. 15.2Choosing a format
  3. 15.3Schema registry
  4. 15.4Compatibility rules
  5. 15.5Designing events
  6. 15.6Designing topics
  7. 15.7Large messages
  8. 15.8Lab: design a contract
  9. 15.9Common mistakes
  10. 15.10Self-check
Warm-upWarm-up: one line each
  1. Does the Kafka broker check that a message's value is valid JSON or Avro?
    Reveal

    No. Brokers store bytes. Validation happens in producers and consumers, usually with serializers backed by a schema registry.

  2. With BACKWARD compatibility, which do you upgrade first: producers or consumers?
    Reveal

    Consumers. A backward-compatible schema can read data written with the previous schema, so new consumers can handle old and new data.

  3. Is it safe to add a field to an Avro schema?
    Reveal

    Under BACKWARD compatibility, yes if the new field has a default, so a reader on the new schema can fill it in for old records.

  4. Why should events carry their own ID?
    Reveal

    So consumers can deduplicate redeliveries and replays. Offsets are not stable identities if records are ever republished.

  5. A 50 MB document must go to five services. Send it through Kafka?
    Reveal

    Store it in object storage and publish a small event with a reference and a checksum (claim check).

15.1Kafka stores bytes

  • Producers serialize keys and values into bytes; consumers deserialize them. The broker never inspects them (except to apply compression it was told to use).
  • That makes the serializer contract the real API between teams. Without enforcement, one producer change can break every consumer silently, and old records in the log live on for the whole retention period.

15.2Choosing a format

Format Size and speed Schema Evolution Typical fit
JSON Large, slower None built in (JSON Schema optional) By convention only Prototypes, low volume, human debugging
Avro Compact binary, fast Required; field names live in the schema, not the data Excellent, with defaults and reader/writer schemas Kafka-centric data platforms, CDC
Protobuf Compact binary, fast Required; numbered fields Very good; never reuse field numbers Polyglot services already using gRPC
JSON Schema Same as JSON Validated against a schema Supported by registries Teams that want JSON plus checks

15.3Schema registry

  • A schema registry (Confluent Schema Registry is the most common; Apicurio and AWS Glue are alternatives) stores versions of each schema under a subject and assigns each schema an ID.
  • The default naming, TopicNameStrategy, uses subjects <topic>-key and <topic>-value, so a topic carries one value type. RecordNameStrategy and TopicRecordNameStrategy allow several event types in one topic.
  • Serializers prefix each message with a magic byte and the 4-byte schema ID, so the payload stays compact. Deserializers cache schemas by ID.
  • Compatibility checks run when a new version is registered. In production, register schemas through CI and turn off auto.register.schemas in producers so a code change cannot silently publish a new schema.

15.4Compatibility rules

Try it first3 minutes

Your consumers run 40 instances deployed weekly; producers deploy daily. You want to add merchant_category to PaymentAuthorized. Which compatibility mode and rollout order keep everyone working?

Reveal the answer

BACKWARD (the registry default): add merchant_category with a default value, upgrade consumers first if they need the field (new consumers read old and new data), then producers start sending it. Old consumers still work too, because Avro readers ignore fields that are not in their schema.

Mode Guarantee Upgrade first Allowed changes (Avro)
BACKWARD (default) New schema reads data written with the previous schema Consumers Delete fields; add fields with defaults
FORWARD Previous schema reads data written with the new schema Producers Add fields; delete fields that have defaults
FULL Both directions Either Add or delete only fields with defaults
*_TRANSITIVE The same, against all earlier versions, not just the last As above As above
NONE No checks Coordinate by hand Anything

Safe habits regardless of mode:

  • Add optional fields with defaults; never rename a field in place (add the new one, migrate, then remove the old).
  • Never change a field's type in an incompatible way (string to int).
  • Protobuf: never reuse or renumber field numbers; mark removed numbers and names as reserved.
  • For a breaking change, publish a new major version to a new topic (payments.v2), run both while consumers migrate, then retire the old one.

15.5Designing events

  • Name events as facts in the past tense: PaymentAuthorized, CardBlocked. Commands (AuthorizePayment) usually belong on request paths or command topics with one owner.
  • Include an envelope: event_id (UUID, for deduplication), event_type, event_time (when it happened), source, schema_version, and the entity ID that is also the key. Put tracing IDs in headers.
  • Thin or fat? A thin event (OrderPaid {order_id}) forces consumers to call back for details, coupling them to the producer's API. A fat event (event-carried state transfer, including the fields consumers need) lets consumers work alone, at the cost of larger messages and a wider contract. Most domain events should carry what their consumers need, without dumping whole database rows.
  • Domain events, not table rows: raw CDC events expose the producer's internal schema. Publish domain events through an outbox when other teams depend on them; keep raw CDC for data platforms.
  • Money and time: amounts as integer minor units or decimal types with currency, never floats; timestamps in UTC with explicit precision.

15.6Designing topics

  • One event type per topic is simplest for schemas and access control. Several event types in one topic are needed when a consumer must see them in order for the same entity (account opened, then credited, then closed); use a union schema or RecordNameStrategy.
  • Name topics consistently: <domain>.<entity>.<event>.v<major>, for example cards.authorization.approved.v1.
  • Decide per topic: key, partition count, replication factor, min.insync.replicas, retention or compaction, and who may write and read it.
  • Ownership: one owning team per topic, documented schema, and an on-call contact.

15.7Large messages

  • Defaults cap a record batch at about 1 MB (message.max.bytes on the broker, max.message.bytes per topic, max.request.size on the producer). Raising limits is possible but affects broker memory, replication, and consumer fetch sizes.
  • Claim check: put the object in object storage and send a reference with size and checksum. Consumers fetch it only when needed, and Kafka stays fast.
  • Compression helps text-heavy payloads; chunking a large message into many records is rarely worth the complexity.

15.8Lab: design a contract

LabWrite an event schema and evolve it safely20 minutes

No cluster needed. On paper or in a file:

  1. Write an Avro schema for PaymentAuthorized with an envelope (event_id, event_time as a timestamp, schema_version) and a body (card_id, amount_minor as long, currency, merchant_id).
  2. Choose the key and the topic name, and say why.
  3. Version 2 adds merchant_category and removes nothing. Write it so it is BACKWARD compatible.
  4. Version 3 renames merchant_id to merchant_ref. Explain why that is breaking and plan the migration.
Check what you saw
  • Key: card_id, so a card's authorizations stay in order. A topic name like cards.payment.authorized.v1.
  • Version 2: {"name": "merchant_category", "type": ["null", "string"], "default": null}. A union with null as the first branch and a null default is the usual Avro way to make a field optional.
  • Version 3: a rename is a delete plus an add. Old data has no merchant_ref, and a reader that requires it fails, unless it has a default, in which case old records silently lose the merchant. Instead, add merchant_ref alongside merchant_id, have producers fill both, move consumers to merchant_ref, then drop merchant_id in a later version, or publish v2 to a new topic.

15.9Common mistakes

Common mistakes

  • Free-form JSON across team boundaries with no schema or compatibility check.
  • Auto-registering schemas from application code in production.
  • Renaming or retyping fields in place.
  • Reusing Protobuf field numbers.
  • Events without IDs or event times, making deduplication and late-data handling impossible.
  • Publishing raw database rows as the public contract other teams depend on.
  • Sending large files through Kafka instead of a claim check.

15.10Self-check

Self-checkFive more, after the lessons
  1. What is in the first 5 bytes of a message written with a Confluent registry serializer?
    Reveal

    A magic byte (0) followed by the 4-byte schema ID; the encoded payload follows.

  2. Explain BACKWARD and FORWARD compatibility in one line each.
    Reveal

    BACKWARD: the new schema can read data written with the previous one (upgrade consumers first). FORWARD: the previous schema can read data written with the new one (upgrade producers first).

  3. How do you make an Avro field optional?
    Reveal

    Make its type a union with null first, ["null", "string"], and give it "default": null.

  4. When must several event types share one topic?
    Reveal

    When a consumer needs them in order for the same entity, because ordering exists only within a partition of one topic.

  5. What is the claim check pattern?
    Reveal

    Store a large payload outside Kafka (object storage) and publish an event containing a reference, size, and checksum; consumers fetch the payload when needed.

Module 16: Kafka Connect and change data capture

Most data enters and leaves Kafka through integrations you should not hand-write. This module covers Kafka Connect's workers, connectors, and tasks, converters and single message transforms, error handling with dead letter queues, and change data capture with Debezium, including the failure modes that bite in production.

9 lessons3 figures1 lab6 mastery checks

On this page

  1. 16.1Why Kafka Connect
  2. 16.2Architecture
  3. 16.3Running a connector
  4. 16.4Errors and dead letter queues
  5. 16.5Change data capture with Debezium
  6. 16.6Connect or your own code?
  7. 16.7Lab: file connectors in standalone mode
  8. 16.8Common mistakes
  9. 16.9Self-check
Warm-upWarm-up: one line each
  1. What is the difference between a connector and a task?
    Reveal

    A connector is the configured integration (for example "copy table orders to Kafka"); tasks are the units that actually copy data in parallel, up to tasks.max.

  2. Where does a distributed Connect cluster store connector configs and source offsets?
    Reveal

    In Kafka itself, in three compacted internal topics for configs, offsets, and status.

  3. What does a converter do?
    Reveal

    It translates between Connect's internal record format and the bytes in Kafka, for example JSON, Avro, Protobuf, or plain strings.

  4. Why read the database's write-ahead log for CDC instead of polling SELECT * WHERE updated_at > ?
    Reveal

    The log captures every change, including deletes and intermediate updates, in commit order, with low latency and no extra query load. Polling misses deletes and can miss updates that share a timestamp.

  5. A Debezium connector for PostgreSQL is stopped for two days. What can happen to the database?
    Reveal

    Its replication slot keeps all write-ahead log since the last confirmed position, so the database's disk can fill up.

16.1Why Kafka Connect

  • Integration without custom code: configure a connector instead of writing, deploying, and operating a producer or consumer per system.
  • Source connectors pull data into Kafka (databases via CDC or JDBC, files, message queues, SaaS APIs). Sink connectors push data out (Elasticsearch, S3, data warehouses, databases).
  • The framework handles the hard parts: offsets, scaling across workers, retries, serialization, and rebalancing tasks when workers fail.

16.2Architecture

  • Workers are JVM processes that run connectors and tasks. In distributed mode they form a cluster (like a consumer group), share work, and expose a REST API, by default on port 8083. Standalone mode runs one worker with local files, for development.
  • Tasks are the unit of parallelism. A JDBC source might use one task per table; a sink connector's tasks share topic partitions like consumers in a group named connect-<connector name>.
  • Internal topics (names you choose in the worker config) store connector configs, source offsets, and status. They must be compacted and replicated.
Piece Role Examples
Converter Bytes to and from Connect records JsonConverter, StringConverter, ByteArrayConverter, Avro or Protobuf converters with a registry
SMT Change single records in flight InsertField, ReplaceField, MaskField, Filter with predicates, RegexRouter, TimestampRouter
Connector plugin Talks to the external system Debezium, JDBC, S3 sink, Elasticsearch sink

16.3Running a connector

Create a connector through the REST API
curl -X PUT -H "Content-Type: application/json" \
  http://localhost:8083/connectors/orders-to-search/config -d '{
    "connector.class": "io.confluent.connect.elasticsearch.ElasticsearchSinkConnector",
    "topics": "shop.public.orders",
    "connection.url": "http://elasticsearch:9200",
    "tasks.max": "3",
    "key.ignore": "false",
    "errors.tolerance": "all",
    "errors.deadletterqueue.topic.name": "orders-to-search-dlq",
    "errors.deadletterqueue.context.headers.enable": "true"
  }'

curl http://localhost:8083/connectors/orders-to-search/status
  • PUT /connectors/<name>/config creates or updates a connector idempotently, which suits automation. Other endpoints pause, resume, restart failed tasks, and list connector plugins.
  • Third-party connectors come as plugins on each worker's plugin.path; check their licenses, as some popular ones are not open source.

16.4Errors and dead letter queues

  • errors.tolerance=none (default): the task fails on the first bad record and stops until someone restarts it.
  • errors.tolerance=all: skip records that fail in conversion or transformation; with errors.deadletterqueue.topic.name (sink connectors only), send them to a DLQ topic, with failure details in headers when errors.deadletterqueue.context.headers.enable=true.
  • errors.retry.timeout and errors.retry.delay.max.ms control retries of retriable operations; errors.log.enable logs failures.
  • Monitor task state: a FAILED task does nothing until restarted, while the connector may still look present.
  • Exactly-once source connectors are supported since Kafka 3.3 (exactly.once.source.support=enabled on workers), for connectors that implement it.

16.5Change data capture with Debezium

  • Debezium is a set of open-source Connect source connectors that read database change logs: PostgreSQL logical decoding (pgoutput), the MySQL binlog, SQL Server and Oracle change logs, MongoDB change streams.
  • One topic per table, named <topic.prefix>.<schema>.<table>, keyed by primary key, so all changes to a row stay in order.
  • Change events carry before, after, op (c create, u update, d delete, r snapshot read), ts_ms, and source metadata (log position, transaction ID). A delete is followed by a tombstone so compacted topics drop the key.
  • Initial snapshot: on first start the connector reads existing rows, then switches to streaming changes.
  • The outbox event router SMT turns rows from an outbox table into clean domain events on per-aggregate topics (the outbox pattern, Module 14).
Watch out

PostgreSQL replication slots retain write-ahead log until the connector confirms it. If the connector stops, fails, or falls behind, WAL accumulates and can fill the database disk. Alert on replication slot lag, set max_slot_wal_keep_size on the database as a safety limit, and enable Debezium heartbeats so slots advance on quiet databases.

  • Schema changes: Debezium tracks DDL; with a schema registry, compatible column additions flow through; destructive changes need a plan.
  • Ordering: per primary key within a table. There is no global order across tables, so consumers joining tables must handle out-of-order arrival.

16.6Connect or your own code?

Use Connect when Write a service when
A maintained connector exists for the system The logic is business-specific (validation, enrichment, decisions)
The job is moving data with light transforms You need complex error handling per record
You want restarts, scaling, and offsets for free The external API needs custom flow control or auth

16.7Lab: file connectors in standalone mode

LabMove lines from a file into Kafka and out to another file15 minutes

Open a shell in the single-broker container and prepare a worker and two connector configs:

Terminal
docker exec -it --workdir /tmp broker sh
cp /opt/kafka/config/connect-standalone.properties /tmp/worker.properties
echo "plugin.path=/opt/kafka/libs/connect-file-4.3.0.jar" >> /tmp/worker.properties
printf 'name=local-file-source\nconnector.class=FileStreamSource\ntasks.max=1\nfile=/tmp/input.txt\ntopic=connect-test\n' > /tmp/source.properties
printf 'name=local-file-sink\nconnector.class=FileStreamSink\ntasks.max=1\nfile=/tmp/output.txt\ntopics=connect-test\n' > /tmp/sink.properties
printf 'first line\nsecond line\n' > /tmp/input.txt
/opt/kafka/bin/connect-standalone.sh /tmp/worker.properties /tmp/source.properties /tmp/sink.properties

In a second terminal, append a line, then look at the output file and the topic:

Terminal
docker exec broker sh -c "echo third line >> /tmp/input.txt"
docker exec broker cat /tmp/output.txt
docker exec broker /opt/kafka/bin/kafka-console-consumer.sh --bootstrap-server localhost:9092 \
  --topic connect-test --from-beginning --max-messages 3
Check what you saw
  • output.txt contains all three lines within a few seconds: source task to Kafka to sink task.
  • The topic shows records like {"schema":{"type":"string","optional":false},"payload":"first line"} because the worker uses JsonConverter with schemas.enable=true. With value.converter.schemas.enable=false you would see just the string.
  • Stop the worker with Ctrl-C and restart it: it does not re-send the first lines, because it stored the source file position in /tmp/connect.offsets.

16.8Common mistakes

Common mistakes

  • errors.tolerance=none with no monitoring, so a task fails on one bad record and stops silently.
  • Under-replicated or non-compacted Connect internal topics.
  • Debezium without replication slot lag alerts, risking a full database disk.
  • Treating raw CDC events as a public contract for other teams.
  • Mismatched converters between the producer side and a sink connector (for example Avro data read with JsonConverter).
  • Writing custom producers for integrations a maintained connector already handles.

16.9Self-check

Self-checkFive more, after the lessons
  1. What do workers, connectors, and tasks each do?
    Reveal

    Workers are the processes; connectors are configured integrations that plan the work; tasks do the copying in parallel and are spread across workers.

  2. Which error settings make a sink connector skip bad records into a DLQ?
    Reveal

    errors.tolerance=all with errors.deadletterqueue.topic.name (and errors.deadletterqueue.context.headers.enable=true for failure details).

  3. What fields does a Debezium change event carry?
    Reveal

    before and after row images, op (c, u, d, r), ts_ms, and source metadata such as the log position and table.

  4. Why is a Debezium topic keyed by primary key?
    Reveal

    So every change to a row lands in one partition in commit order, and compaction keeps the latest row per key.

  5. What production risk is specific to PostgreSQL CDC?
    Reveal

    The replication slot retains write-ahead log while the connector is down or behind, which can fill the database disk.

Module 17: Kafka Streams, and how it compares to Flink

Stream processing turns events into running answers: totals per merchant per minute, enriched payments, fraud signals. This module teaches Kafka Streams, the Java library that ships with Kafka: streams and tables, topologies and repartitioning, state stores with changelogs, windows and late data, joins, exactly-once, and when Apache Flink is the better tool.

11 lessons4 figures1 lab6 mastery checks

On this page

  1. 17.1What Kafka Streams is
  2. 17.2Streams and tables
  3. 17.3Topologies and repartitioning
  4. 17.4State stores and fault tolerance
  5. 17.5Time, windows, and late data
  6. 17.6Joins
  7. 17.7Processing guarantees
  8. 17.8Kafka Streams, Flink, or a plain consumer
  9. 17.9Lab: run the word count demo
  10. 17.10Common mistakes
  11. 17.11Self-check
Warm-upWarm-up: one line each
  1. Does Kafka Streams need its own cluster?
    Reveal

    No. It is a Java library inside your application. You scale by running more instances, which form a consumer group.

  2. What is the difference between a KStream and a KTable?
    Reveal

    A KStream is every event (inserts). A KTable is the latest value per key (upserts), like a changelog applied to a table.

  3. Why does selectKey followed by groupByKey create an extra topic?
    Reveal

    Records must be regrouped by the new key across instances, so Streams writes them to an internal repartition topic keyed by the new key and reads them back.

  4. Where does Kafka Streams keep aggregation state, and how does it survive a crash?
    Reveal

    In local state stores (RocksDB by default), backed by compacted changelog topics in Kafka. A new owner restores the store from the changelog.

  5. What must be true of two topics before you can join them as a KStream and a KTable?
    Reveal

    They must be co-partitioned: same key, same partition count, and the same partitioning (a GlobalKTable avoids this requirement).

17.1What Kafka Streams is

Idea

A library that reads topics, transforms and aggregates records with local state, and writes results to topics, with fault tolerance built on Kafka itself.

Analogy

A spreadsheet that recalculates as rows arrive. Each new row updates totals at once, and the sheet's history is saved to Kafka so a copy can be rebuilt anywhere.

Why it matters

Stateful processing (counts, joins, windows) without operating a separate processing cluster.

  • The application.id is the consumer group ID and the prefix of all internal topics.
  • Input partitions become tasks; tasks are spread over threads (num.stream.threads) and instances. Adding instances rebalances tasks automatically.
  • Everything durable lives in Kafka: input, output, repartition topics, and changelogs.

17.2Streams and tables

Abstraction Meaning Created from
KStream Every record is an independent event builder.stream(topic)
KTable Latest value per key; a record with a null value deletes the key builder.table(topic) or an aggregation
GlobalKTable A full copy of a table on every instance builder.globalTable(topic); good for small reference data

17.3Topologies and repartitioning

MerchantTotals.java (per-merchant totals per minute)
Properties props = new Properties();
props.put(StreamsConfig.APPLICATION_ID_CONFIG, "merchant-totals");
props.put(StreamsConfig.BOOTSTRAP_SERVERS_CONFIG, "localhost:9092");
props.put(StreamsConfig.PROCESSING_GUARANTEE_CONFIG, StreamsConfig.EXACTLY_ONCE_V2);

StreamsBuilder builder = new StreamsBuilder();
KStream<String, Payment> payments =
    builder.stream("payments", Consumed.with(Serdes.String(), paymentSerde));   // keyed by card

payments
    .filter((cardId, p) -> p.status().equals("APPROVED"))
    .selectKey((cardId, p) -> p.merchantId())          // new key: forces a repartition topic
    .groupByKey(Grouped.with(Serdes.String(), paymentSerde))
    .windowedBy(TimeWindows.ofSizeAndGrace(Duration.ofMinutes(1), Duration.ofSeconds(30)))
    .aggregate(() -> 0L,
               (merchant, p, total) -> total + p.amountMinor(),
               Materialized.with(Serdes.String(), Serdes.Long()))
    .toStream()
    .map((window, total) -> KeyValue.pair(window.key(), total))
    .to("merchant-totals-1m", Produced.with(Serdes.String(), Serdes.Long()));

KafkaStreams streams = new KafkaStreams(builder.build(), props);
Runtime.getRuntime().addShutdownHook(new Thread(streams::close));
streams.start();
  • Stateless operations: filter, map, mapValues, flatMap, peek, split (branching), merge. Prefer mapValues over map when the key does not change, so no repartition is needed.
  • Stateful operations: count, reduce, aggregate, windowed versions of them, and joins. They need records grouped by key.
  • Repartitioning: any key change (selectKey, map, groupBy) before a stateful operation writes records to an internal -repartition topic so each key lands in one task. It costs a full extra write and read; design keys to avoid unnecessary ones.

17.4State stores and fault tolerance

  • Each stateful task owns a local state store, RocksDB on disk by default (in-memory stores are available), under state.dir.
  • Every update is also written to a compacted changelog topic. If an instance dies, its tasks move to another instance, which restores the store from the changelog before processing.
  • Restoration can be slow for large state. num.standby.replicas (0 by default) keeps warm copies on other instances for fast failover.
  • Interactive queries let your service read its local stores directly (for example "current total for merchant 42"), with metadata to route a query to the instance that owns the key.

17.5Time, windows, and late data

  • Event time comes from each record's timestamp by default (a custom TimestampExtractor can read it from the payload).
  • Window types: tumbling (fixed, non-overlapping), hopping (fixed size, overlapping steps), sliding (defined by the time difference between records), and session (activity separated by an inactivity gap).
  • Late records: Streams tracks stream time, the largest timestamp seen per task. A window accepts records until stream time passes its end plus the grace period; later records are dropped (and counted in metrics).
  • Final results only: windowed aggregates emit updates as records arrive. Use suppress(untilWindowCloses(...)) or the emit-final strategy when downstream needs one result per window.

17.6Joins

Join Windowed? Typical use Co-partitioning
KStream to KStream Yes, JoinWindows Match a payment with its authorization within 5 minutes Required
KStream to KTable No: each stream record looks up the table's current value Enrich payments with card or merchant data Required
KTable to KTable No Combine two changelogs; foreign-key joins supported Required (except foreign-key joins)
KStream to GlobalKTable No Enrich with small reference data keyed differently Not required

17.7Processing guarantees

  • processing.guarantee=at_least_once (default): fast; failures can duplicate output.
  • processing.guarantee=exactly_once_v2: output records, state store changelogs, and input offsets commit in one Kafka transaction (Module 14). Brokers must be 2.5 or newer.
  • commit.interval.ms defaults to 30 seconds, or 100 ms under exactly-once, which bounds end-to-end latency for downstream read_committed consumers.
  • Since Kafka 4.2, Streams can use its own broker-side rebalance protocol: group.protocol=streams.

17.8Kafka Streams, Flink, or a plain consumer

Kafka Streams Apache Flink Plain consumer
Deployment Library inside your service Separate cluster or Kubernetes operator Library
Inputs and outputs Kafka to Kafka (Connect for the rest) Many connectors: Kafka, files, databases, CDC Anything you code
State RocksDB plus Kafka changelogs RocksDB or heap plus checkpoints to durable storage Build your own
Exactly-once Kafka transactions Checkpoints plus transactional sinks Your design
Event time Stream time and grace periods Watermarks, rich windows, complex event processing Build your own
Best for Kafka-centric services with moderate state Large, multi-source pipelines and heavy event-time logic Simple per-record work
In production

Flink is common in payment platforms for status tracking and investigation pipelines: Kafka topics in, keyed state per transaction, side outputs for records that fail parsing, results to databases and alerts. Kafka Streams fits when the logic belongs inside one microservice that already owns the topics. Both rely on the same foundations: keys, partitions, state, event time, and checkpointed offsets.

17.9Lab: run the word count demo

LabWatch a stateful topology update counts15 minutes

On the single broker, create the topics and start the demo that ships with Kafka:

Terminal
./kafka-topics.sh --bootstrap-server localhost:9092 --create --topic streams-plaintext-input \
  --partitions 1 --replication-factor 1
./kafka-topics.sh --bootstrap-server localhost:9092 --create --topic streams-wordcount-output \
  --partitions 1 --replication-factor 1 --config cleanup.policy=compact
./kafka-run-class.sh org.apache.kafka.streams.examples.wordcount.WordCountDemo

In a second terminal, read the output with the right deserializers; in a third, type some lines:

Terminal
./kafka-console-consumer.sh --bootstrap-server localhost:9092 --topic streams-wordcount-output \
  --from-beginning --formatter-property print.key=true \
  --formatter-property key.deserializer=org.apache.kafka.common.serialization.StringDeserializer \
  --formatter-property value.deserializer=org.apache.kafka.common.serialization.LongDeserializer
./kafka-console-producer.sh --bootstrap-server localhost:9092 --topic streams-plaintext-input

Type kafka streams rock, then kafka is a log. Finally list the internal topics:

Terminal
./kafka-topics.sh --bootstrap-server localhost:9092 --list | grep streams-wordcount
Check what you saw
  • After the first line the consumer shows kafka 1, streams 1, rock 1; after the second, kafka 2, is 1, a 1, log 1. Each output record is an update to a table.
  • The internal topics include a -repartition topic (the demo re-keys records by word) and a -changelog topic for the counts store.
  • Stop the demo and start it again: counts continue from where they were, because state was rebuilt from the changelog and the input offsets were committed.

17.10Common mistakes

Common mistakes

  • Unnecessary repartitions from using map or selectKey when only the value changes.
  • Joining topics that are not co-partitioned.
  • Huge state with no standbys, so every failover waits for a long restore.
  • No grace period thinking: either dropping legitimate late records or holding windows open far too long.
  • Expecting one final result per window without suppress or emit-final.
  • Changing an application.id casually: it resets offsets and state, because it names the group and internal topics.

17.11Self-check

Self-checkFive more, after the lessons
  1. How does Kafka Streams scale out?
    Reveal

    Each input partition becomes a task; tasks spread over threads and instances, which share one consumer group (the application.id). Adding instances moves tasks to them.

  2. What makes state in Kafka Streams fault tolerant?
    Reveal

    Every state store update is written to a compacted changelog topic; a task's new owner restores the store from it, optionally from a standby replica that is already warm.

  3. What is the grace period?
    Reveal

    How long after a window's end, measured in stream time, the window still accepts late records before it closes.

  4. When can you join a stream with a table without co-partitioning?
    Reveal

    When the table is a GlobalKTable, which is fully replicated to every instance.

  5. When would you pick Flink over Kafka Streams?
    Reveal

    For large or multi-source pipelines, heavy event-time logic with watermarks, sources and sinks beyond Kafka, or when a dedicated processing cluster is acceptable.

Module 18: Spring for Apache Kafka in practice

Most Java services use Kafka through Spring. This module maps everything you learned onto Spring for Apache Kafka: KafkaTemplate, @KafkaListener and listener containers, how Spring commits offsets, the DefaultErrorHandler and dead letter publishing, non-blocking retries with @RetryableTopic, transactions, testing, and a production configuration you can copy.

12 lessons2 figures1 lab6 mastery checks

On this page

  1. 18.1The pieces
  2. 18.2Producing with KafkaTemplate
  3. 18.3Consuming with @KafkaListener
  4. 18.4How Spring commits offsets
  5. 18.5Error handling: DefaultErrorHandler and dead letters
  6. 18.6Non-blocking retries with @RetryableTopic
  7. 18.7Transactions in Spring
  8. 18.8A production configuration
  9. 18.9Testing
  10. 18.10Lab: a Spring Boot consumer with a DLT
  11. 18.11Common mistakes
  12. 18.12Self-check
Warm-upWarm-up: one line each
  1. Does Spring's listener container use Kafka's auto-commit by default?
    Reveal

    No. Unless you set enable.auto.commit yourself, Spring turns it off and commits offsets itself after your listener returns, by default once per batch of records from a poll.

  2. Your @KafkaListener throws an exception. What does Spring do by default?
    Reveal

    The DefaultErrorHandler retries the record up to 10 attempts in total with no delay, then logs it and moves on.

  3. What does concurrency = "3" on a listener mean?
    Reveal

    Three consumer threads, each with its own KafkaConsumer, in the same group. More than the partition count just leaves threads idle.

  4. Where does DeadLetterPublishingRecoverer send a failed record by default?
    Reveal

    To <topic>-dlt, same partition number (Spring Kafka 3.3 and later; older versions used <topic>.DLT).

  5. What does @RetryableTopic give you that the default error handler does not?
    Reveal

    Non-blocking retries: failures move to delayed retry topics so the main partition keeps flowing, at the cost of ordering.

18.1The pieces

Spring piece Kafka concept Notes
ProducerFactory, KafkaTemplate KafkaProducer One shared producer, thread-safe
ConsumerFactory KafkaConsumer settings Usually from spring.kafka.consumer.*
ConcurrentKafkaListenerContainerFactory Container settings Concurrency, ack mode, error handler, batch mode
@KafkaListener A poll loop that calls your method Runs on the container's consumer thread
DefaultErrorHandler Retry, seek, recover Blocking retries with backoff, then a recoverer
KafkaTransactionManager Transactions Wraps listener processing and sends in one Kafka transaction

Spring Boot auto-configures all of this from spring.kafka.* properties. Define your own beans only when you need to change behavior.

18.2Producing with KafkaTemplate

PaymentEvents.java
@Service
public class PaymentEvents {
    private final KafkaTemplate<String, PaymentAuthorized> template;

    public PaymentEvents(KafkaTemplate<String, PaymentAuthorized> template) {
        this.template = template;
    }

    public CompletableFuture<SendResult<String, PaymentAuthorized>> publish(PaymentAuthorized e) {
        return template.send("cards.payment.authorized.v1", e.cardId(), e)
            .whenComplete((result, ex) -> {
                if (ex != null) {
                    log.error("publish failed for {}", e.eventId(), ex);   // decide: retry, outbox, fail
                }
            });
    }
}
  • send() returns a CompletableFuture (Spring Kafka 3.0 and later). The same rules as the plain producer apply: handle failures, do not block on every send in a hot path.
  • For atomic "database row plus event", use the outbox pattern (Module 14) rather than calling send() inside a database transaction.

18.3Consuming with @KafkaListener

LedgerListener.java
@Component
public class LedgerListener {

    @KafkaListener(topics = "cards.payment.authorized.v1", groupId = "ledger", concurrency = "3")
    public void onPayment(PaymentAuthorized event,
                          @Header(KafkaHeaders.RECEIVED_PARTITION) int partition,
                          @Header(KafkaHeaders.OFFSET) long offset) {
        ledger.applyOnce(event);   // idempotent by event.eventId()
    }
}
  • Method parameters can be the converted payload, the whole ConsumerRecord, headers, an Acknowledgment (manual ack modes), or a List of records for batch listeners.
  • concurrency creates that many consumer threads; keep it at or below the topic's partition count.
  • Your method runs on the consumer thread. If it takes longer than max.poll.interval.ms for a whole poll's worth of records, the consumer is kicked out of the group (Module 9). Lower max.poll.records for slow listeners.

18.4How Spring commits offsets

AckMode Commits Use
BATCH (default) After all records returned by one poll are processed Good throughput; a failure replays the uncommitted part of the batch
RECORD After each record Fewer replays, more commit traffic
TIME, COUNT, COUNT_TIME After an interval or a number of records Tuning
MANUAL When you call acknowledgment.acknowledge(); queued and committed at the end of the poll batch You control what counts as done
MANUAL_IMMEDIATE Immediately when you acknowledge Strict control, more commit traffic

Spring sets enable.auto.commit=false unless you configure it, so the container's commits are the only ones. Combined with an idempotent listener, this gives at-least-once processing with exactly-once effects.

18.5Error handling: DefaultErrorHandler and dead letters

KafkaErrorConfig.java
@Configuration
public class KafkaErrorConfig {
    @Bean
    public DefaultErrorHandler errorHandler(KafkaTemplate<Object, Object> template) {
        var recoverer = new DeadLetterPublishingRecoverer(template);       // -> <topic>-dlt
        var backOff = new ExponentialBackOffWithMaxRetries(4);             // 4 retries
        backOff.setInitialInterval(500);
        backOff.setMultiplier(2.0);
        backOff.setMaxInterval(5_000);
        var handler = new DefaultErrorHandler(recoverer, backOff);
        handler.addNotRetryableExceptions(ValidationException.class);      // straight to the DLT
        return handler;
    }
}
  • Default behavior: 10 delivery attempts with no backoff (FixedBackOff(0, 9)), then the record is logged and skipped. Always configure a recoverer for anything important.
  • Retries are blocking: the handler seeks back so the same record is redelivered, and the partition waits. Order is preserved. Keep the total backoff for one record well under max.poll.interval.ms.
  • Not retryable by default: deserialization, message conversion, and method argument resolution failures go straight to the recoverer.
  • Dead letter records keep the original key and value and gain headers such as kafka_dlt-original-topic, kafka_dlt-original-partition, kafka_dlt-original-offset, and kafka_dlt-exception-message.
  • The DLT needs at least as many partitions as the source topic, because the default resolver keeps the same partition number. Or supply your own destination resolver.
  • Poison bytes: wrap your deserializer in ErrorHandlingDeserializer, so a record that cannot be deserialized reaches the error handler (and the DLT) instead of failing inside poll() forever.
  • Spring Boot wires a CommonErrorHandler bean like the one above into its auto-configured container factory.

18.6Non-blocking retries with @RetryableTopic

OrderListener.java (Spring Kafka 4.x)
@RetryableTopic(attempts = "4", backOff = @BackOff(delay = 1000, multiplier = 2.0),
                exclude = ValidationException.class)
@KafkaListener(topics = "orders", groupId = "fulfilment")
public void onOrder(OrderPlaced order) {
    fulfilment.handle(order);
}

@DltHandler
public void onDeadLetter(OrderPlaced order, @Header(KafkaHeaders.RECEIVED_TOPIC) String topic) {
    alerts.raise("order moved to DLT", order.orderId(), topic);
}
  • Spring creates the retry topics and the DLT (by default with 1 partition each; set numPartitions) and listeners for them. Delays work by pausing a retry topic's partition until the record is due.
  • In Spring Kafka 3.x the attribute is backoff = @Backoff(...) from Spring Retry; 4.x uses its own @BackOff.
  • Ordering is lost for retried records. Use blocking retries (the error handler) for ordered streams.

18.7Transactions in Spring

  • Set spring.kafka.producer.transaction-id-prefix; Spring Boot then creates a KafkaTransactionManager, and the listener container runs each poll's processing and its offset commit in a Kafka transaction (consume-transform-produce, Module 14).
  • KafkaTemplate.executeInTransaction(...) runs a block of sends in one transaction outside a listener.
  • Consumers of transactional topics need isolation.level: read_committed.
  • Database work is not part of a Kafka transaction; use the outbox and idempotent consumers for database effects.

18.8A production configuration

application.yml (Spring Boot 4, Spring Kafka 4.x)
spring:
  kafka:
    bootstrap-servers: kafka-1:9092,kafka-2:9092,kafka-3:9092
    producer:
      acks: all
      key-serializer: org.apache.kafka.common.serialization.StringSerializer
      value-serializer: org.springframework.kafka.support.serializer.JacksonJsonSerializer
      properties:
        enable.idempotence: true
        linger.ms: 10
        compression.type: lz4
    consumer:
      group-id: ledger
      auto-offset-reset: earliest
      max-poll-records: 200
      key-deserializer: org.apache.kafka.common.serialization.StringDeserializer
      value-deserializer: org.springframework.kafka.support.serializer.ErrorHandlingDeserializer
      properties:
        spring.deserializer.value.delegate.class: org.springframework.kafka.support.serializer.JacksonJsonDeserializer
        spring.json.trusted.packages: "com.example.events"
        isolation.level: read_committed
    listener:
      ack-mode: record
      concurrency: 3
      observation-enabled: true
  • On Spring Kafka 3.x (Spring Boot 3), use JsonSerializer and JsonDeserializer; 4.x deprecates them in favor of the Jackson 3 based JacksonJsonSerializer and JacksonJsonDeserializer.
  • observation-enabled turns on Micrometer observations (tracing context across Kafka hops); Micrometer also exposes the Kafka client metrics.
  • Add the DefaultErrorHandler bean from above, and consider group.instance.id per pod for static membership (Module 9).

18.9Testing

  • Unit tests: call listener methods directly with built objects; mock KafkaTemplate.
  • Embedded broker: spring-kafka-test provides @EmbeddedKafka, an in-process KRaft broker, for fast integration tests.
  • Real broker: Testcontainers' Kafka module runs the official apache/kafka image, and Spring Boot's @ServiceConnection wires its address into spring.kafka.bootstrap-servers. Closer to production, slower to start.
  • Test the unhappy paths: a poison record reaches the DLT, a duplicate event is applied once, and a rebalance mid-batch does not double-apply effects.

18.10Lab: a Spring Boot consumer with a DLT

LabBuild a listener with retries and dead letters45 minutes

Using Spring Boot with spring-kafka against the single broker:

  1. Configure the application.yml above (single bootstrap server localhost:9092) and create topics payments (3 partitions) and payments-dlt (3 partitions).
  2. Write a @KafkaListener that parses a JSON payment and throws ValidationException when amount is negative, and a TransientException on a flag field the first two times it sees an event ID.
  3. Add the DefaultErrorHandler bean with DeadLetterPublishingRecoverer, exponential backoff, and ValidationException as not retryable.
  4. Publish a valid payment, a negative one, a transient one, and a line of invalid JSON with the console producer.
  5. Read payments-dlt with --formatter-property print.headers=true.
Check what you saw
  • The valid payment is processed once. The transient one is retried with growing delays and then succeeds, and payments behind it on the same partition wait (blocking retries keep order).
  • The negative payment and the invalid JSON go straight to payments-dlt: the first because it is not retryable, the second because ErrorHandlingDeserializer turned the parse failure into a DeserializationException.
  • The DLT records carry kafka_dlt-* headers with the original topic, partition, offset, and exception message.
  • If you delete payments-dlt and leave topic auto-creation off, publishing to the DLT fails; with too few DLT partitions, records from higher partitions fail to publish. Create DLTs deliberately.

18.11Common mistakes

Common mistakes

  • Keeping the default error handler for important data, so failures are logged and skipped after 10 instant attempts.
  • A DLT with fewer partitions than the source topic.
  • concurrency above the partition count, expecting more throughput.
  • Slow listeners with the default max-poll-records, causing rebalance loops.
  • @RetryableTopic on an ordered stream.
  • Calling KafkaTemplate.send() inside a database transaction and assuming both commit together.
  • Missing ErrorHandlingDeserializer, so one bad payload stalls a partition.

18.12Self-check

Self-checkFive more, after the lessons
  1. In the default BATCH ack mode, when are offsets committed?
    Reveal

    After the listener has processed every record returned by one poll; a failure means the uncommitted remainder of that batch is redelivered.

  2. How do you make validation errors skip retries and go straight to the DLT?
    Reveal

    Register them with addNotRetryableExceptions on the DefaultErrorHandler (or exclude them in @RetryableTopic).

  3. Why must the DLT have at least as many partitions as the source topic by default?
    Reveal

    DeadLetterPublishingRecoverer sends each failed record to the same partition number in the DLT.

  4. Blocking retries or @RetryableTopic for account balance events?
    Reveal

    Blocking retries through the DefaultErrorHandler: they keep per-partition order. @RetryableTopic would let later events overtake a failed one.

  5. What does ErrorHandlingDeserializer solve?
    Reveal

    It catches deserialization failures and hands them to the error handler as a DeserializationException, so a poison payload goes to the DLT instead of blocking poll().
