Module 19: Performance, tuning, and capacity planning

Tuning Kafka means choosing where to sit between throughput, latency, durability, and cost, then measuring. This module gives you the knobs that matter on producers, consumers, brokers, and topics, explains where end-to-end latency goes, and shows how to size disks and network for a cluster.

10 lessons2 figures1 lab6 mastery checks

On this page

  1. 19.1Think in trade-offs
  2. 19.2Producer knobs
  3. 19.3Consumer knobs
  4. 19.4End-to-end latency
  5. 19.5Broker and topic levers
  6. 19.6Sizing a cluster
  7. 19.7Benchmarking
  8. 19.8Lab: acks and consumer throughput
  9. 19.9Common mistakes
  10. 19.10Self-check
Warm-upWarm-up: one line each
  1. Does acks=all cut producer throughput in half?
    Reveal

    No. With batching and several requests in flight, acks=all mostly adds latency per request; throughput stays high. It matters most for a producer that sends one record at a time synchronously.

  2. Your producer sends small batches at low traffic. Which one setting most improves efficiency?
    Reveal

    linger.ms: waiting a few milliseconds lets batches fill, which also improves compression.

  3. A consumer group cannot keep up. Name the first two things to check.
    Reveal

    Whether processing (not Kafka) is the bottleneck, for example a slow database call per record, and whether the group has as many consumers as partitions.

  4. With acks=1, can a consumer read a record as soon as the leader writes it?
    Reveal

    No. Consumers read only below the high watermark, so replication to all in-sync replicas is on the consumer's path even when the producer did not wait for it.

  5. Ingress is 100 MB/s with replication factor 3. How much data do brokers write to disk in total?
    Reveal

    About 300 MB/s across the cluster, before compression: every byte is stored three times.

19.1Think in trade-offs

  • Measure first: know your target (records per second, p99 latency, durability requirement) and today's numbers.
  • Change one thing at a time, with realistic payloads, at steady state, for long enough to include GC and segment rolls.
  • The usual bottleneck is not the broker: it is per-record processing in consumers, network between zones, or a downstream database.

19.2Producer knobs

Setting Default For throughput For latency Notes
batch.size 16 KB 64 KB to 256 KB Default Per partition; memory comes from buffer.memory
linger.ms 5 ms 10 to 50 ms 0 to 5 ms Low traffic benefits most
compression.type none lz4 or zstd lz4 or none Cuts network and disk; costs some CPU
buffer.memory 32 MB Raise with many partitions or bursts Default Full buffer blocks send()
acks all all (keep it) 1 only if loss is acceptable Durability first
max.in.flight.requests.per.connection 5 5 5 Above 5 breaks idempotence

19.3Consumer knobs

Setting Default For throughput For latency
fetch.min.bytes 1 64 KB to 1 MB 1
fetch.max.wait.ms 500 500 100 or less
max.partition.fetch.bytes 1 MB Raise for large records or high-volume partitions Default
max.poll.records 500 Higher if processing is fast Lower if processing is slow
  • Processing dominates: batch database writes (one statement for 500 records), cache lookups, and avoid a network call per record.
  • Parallelism: consumers up to the partition count; beyond that, the worker-pool pattern (Module 7) or share groups (Module 9).

19.4End-to-end latency

  • Producer side: linger.ms and batch filling, then one network hop.
  • Broker side: append, then replication until the high watermark moves. Replication lag directly delays consumers.
  • Consumer side: fetch.max.wait.ms when there is little data, then your processing.
  • Exactly-once adds the transaction commit interval for read_committed consumers (Module 14).
  • Low-latency setups use linger.ms 0 to 5, small fetch.max.wait.ms, fast disks, brokers and clients in the same zone, and lean processing. Kafka commonly reaches end-to-end latencies in the low tens of milliseconds at p99 when tuned for it.

19.5Broker and topic levers

  • Partitions spread load over brokers and disks (Module 6). Keep leaders balanced.
  • Threads: num.network.threads (3) accept and answer requests; num.io.threads (8) do the disk work; num.replica.fetchers (1) parallelize follower replication. Raise them when idle percentages (NetworkProcessorAvgIdlePercent, RequestHandlerAvgIdlePercent) stay low.
  • Memory: a modest JVM heap (about 6 GB is a common starting point) and the rest of RAM for page cache. Consumers that fall far behind read from disk and slow everyone.
  • Disks: several data directories (log.dirs) or RAID 10; separate them from the OS disk; watch fill level, since a full disk takes the broker's partitions offline.
  • Network: replication multiplies ingress by RF - 1, and every consumer group multiplies egress. Network is often the first limit, especially across zones.
  • Compression at the producer, with topic compression.type=producer, so brokers never recompress.

Host settings that matter. Kafka needs little OS tuning, but these come up on every production checklist:

Setting Starting point Why
JVM heap -Xmx6g -Xms6g with G1 (the Kafka docs' example) Kafka keeps data in the page cache, not the heap; a huge heap starves the cache and lengthens GC pauses
File descriptors at least 100,000 Every segment file and client connection holds one
vm.max_map_count above the Linux default (about 65,530) for many partitions Each segment's offset and time index is memory-mapped: about 2 map areas per segment
Filesystem XFS or ext4, mounted with noatime Kafka never reads access times, so updating them on every read is wasted writes
vm.swappiness low, often 1 (common practice) A swapped-out broker pauses long enough to be fenced and trigger leader elections
Data disks dedicated to Kafka, not shared with OS logs Keeps append latency steady

19.6Sizing a cluster

Disk and network sizingBack-of-the-envelope cluster storage for a topic set. Use average rates for storage and peak rates for network.
  • Storage = ingress per day x retention days x replication factor x compressed ratio, plus headroom (30 to 50 percent free for growth, reassignments, and failures).
  • Network in per broker = (ingress x RF) / brokers. Network out = consumer groups x ingress + replication.
  • Failure headroom: the cluster must carry full load with one broker (or one zone) down, so size for N - 1.
  • Partitions per broker in the low thousands are normal; much higher counts need testing.

19.7Benchmarking

Load tests with the bundled tools
# producer: 1 KB records as fast as possible with batching and compression
kafka-producer-perf-test.sh --bootstrap-server localhost:9092 --topic perf \
  --num-records 2000000 --record-size 1024 --throughput -1 \
  --command-property acks=all --command-property linger.ms=20 \
  --command-property batch.size=131072 --command-property compression.type=lz4

# consumer: read the same records back
kafka-consumer-perf-test.sh --bootstrap-server localhost:9092 --topic perf \
  --num-records 2000000 --group perf-reader
  • Use payloads that look like production (real JSON compresses; random bytes do not).
  • Report records/s, MB/s, and p99 latency, and watch broker CPU, disk, and network at the same time.
  • Run long enough to fill the page cache and roll segments; first-minute numbers flatter.

19.8Lab: acks and consumer throughput

LabCompare acks settings on three brokers, then measure consumer speed20 minutes

On the three-broker cluster with the k helper:

Terminal
k kafka-topics.sh --create --topic bench --partitions 6 --replication-factor 3 --config min.insync.replicas=2
k kafka-producer-perf-test.sh --topic bench --num-records 500000 --record-size 512 --throughput -1 \
  --command-property acks=1 --command-property linger.ms=10
k kafka-producer-perf-test.sh --topic bench --num-records 500000 --record-size 512 --throughput -1 \
  --command-property acks=all --command-property linger.ms=10
k kafka-consumer-perf-test.sh --topic bench --num-records 1000000 --group bench-reader
Check what you saw
  • acks=all usually shows a higher average and p99 latency than acks=1, while records per second stay in the same range, because batching hides most of the extra round trip.
  • On a single laptop all three brokers share one disk and CPU, so differences are smaller and noisier than on real hardware.
  • The consumer test usually reports much higher throughput than the producer: consumers read sequentially from the page cache with no replication on their path.

19.9Common mistakes

Common mistakes

  • Tuning without a target or without measuring before and after.
  • Lowering durability (acks=1) for throughput that batching would have delivered safely.
  • Giving brokers huge heaps, starving the page cache.
  • Forgetting replication and consumer fan-out when sizing network.
  • Sizing for average load instead of peak, and for all brokers up instead of one down.
  • Benchmarking with random bytes and expecting compression gains.

19.10Self-check

Self-checkFive more, after the lessons
  1. Name three producer settings you would change for higher throughput.
    Reveal

    Larger batch.size, higher linger.ms, and compression.type of lz4 or zstd (and enough buffer.memory).

  2. Why does replication delay consumers even with acks=1?
    Reveal

    Consumers read only below the high watermark, which advances only when all in-sync replicas have the records.

  3. How do you compute total disk for a topic?
    Reveal

    Ingress per day times retention days times replication factor times the compressed size ratio, plus 30 to 50 percent headroom.

  4. Broker RequestHandlerAvgIdlePercent is near 0. What does it mean?
    Reveal

    The I/O request threads are saturated; requests queue. Look for disk pressure, too many small requests, or raise num.io.threads.

  5. Why size for N - 1 brokers?
    Reveal

    When a broker fails, its partitions' load moves to the others; the cluster must handle full traffic without it.

Module 20: Operating Kafka: monitoring, changes, security, and disaster recovery

Running Kafka well is mostly watching the right numbers and changing the cluster carefully. This module covers the metrics that matter, consumer lag done properly, everyday changes, partition reassignment, rolling upgrades, encryption, authentication, ACLs, quotas, and cross-region replication with MirrorMaker 2.

11 lessons4 figures1 lab6 mastery checks

On this page

  1. 20.1What to monitor
  2. 20.2Consumer lag done right
  3. 20.3Everyday changes
  4. 20.4Partition reassignment and adding brokers
  5. 20.5Rolling restarts and upgrades
  6. 20.6Security
  7. 20.7Multi-cluster and disaster recovery
  8. 20.8Managed Kafka
  9. 20.9Lab: change replication with a reassignment
  10. 20.10Common mistakes
  11. 20.11Self-check
Warm-upWarm-up: one line each
  1. Which broker metric best tells you the cluster has lost redundancy?
    Reveal

    UnderReplicatedPartitions above zero (and UnderMinIsrPartitionCount above zero is worse: acks=all writes to those partitions are failing).

  2. Across all controllers, what should ActiveControllerCount add up to?
    Reveal

    Exactly 1. Zero means no active controller; more than one indicates a serious problem.

  3. You add a fourth broker. Does Kafka move partitions to it automatically?
    Reveal

    No. New topics may use it, but existing partitions stay put until you run a reassignment (or a tool like Cruise Control does).

  4. Name the three layers of Kafka security.
    Reveal

    Encryption in transit (TLS), authentication (mTLS or SASL), and authorization (ACLs checked per request).

  5. MirrorMaker 2 copies topic orders from cluster east to west. What is the topic called in west by default?
    Reveal

    east.orders: the default replication policy prefixes the source cluster alias.

20.1What to monitor

Metric Healthy Alert when Usually means
UnderReplicatedPartitions 0 Above 0 for minutes A broker is down, slow, or its disk or network is saturated
UnderMinIsrPartitionCount 0 Above 0 acks=all writes to those partitions are failing
OfflinePartitionsCount (controller) 0 Above 0 Partitions with no leader: unavailable
ActiveControllerCount (sum) 1 Not 1 Controller quorum problem
RequestHandlerAvgIdlePercent Well above 0.3 Below 0.2 I/O threads saturated
NetworkProcessorAvgIdlePercent Well above 0.3 Below 0.2 Network threads saturated
IsrShrinksPerSec, IsrExpandsPerSec Near 0 Flapping Followers struggling to keep up
TotalTimeMs (Produce, Fetch) p99 Stable Rising Overload, slow disks, GC
Producer record-error-rate 0 Above 0 Sends failing after retries
Consumer lag Small, stable Growing, or high in time Consumers too slow or stuck

Also watch disk usage (alert well before full), network throughput against capacity, CPU, GC pauses, and open file descriptors.

20.2Consumer lag done right

  • Measure from outside the consumer: an exporter (for example kafka-lag-exporter or Burrow) or the Admin API compares each group's committed offsets with partition end offsets. A dead consumer reports no metrics of its own.
  • Alert on lag in time ("oldest unprocessed record is 6 minutes old") and on growth trend, not on a fixed message count that means different things for different topics.
  • Per partition: one stuck partition hides inside a healthy total (poison message, hot key).
  • Compare with retention: lag in time approaching retention means imminent data loss.
Lag drain calculatorHow long until a backlog clears, or until unread data starts expiring.

20.3Everyday changes

Common admin commands
# change a topic config at runtime (no restart)
kafka-configs.sh --bootstrap-server localhost:9092 --alter --entity-type topics \
  --entity-name payments --add-config retention.ms=1209600000
kafka-configs.sh --bootstrap-server localhost:9092 --describe --entity-type topics --entity-name payments

# add partitions (keyed topics: read Module 6 first)
kafka-topics.sh --bootstrap-server localhost:9092 --alter --topic payments --partitions 24

# purge records before an offset in partition 0 (moves the log start offset)
echo '{"partitions":[{"topic":"payments","partition":0,"offset":1000}],"version":1}' > purge.json
kafka-delete-records.sh --bootstrap-server localhost:9092 --offset-json-file purge.json
  • Many broker configs are dynamic: change them with kafka-configs.sh --entity-type brokers without restarting.
  • Keep topic configuration in code (Terraform, a GitOps repo, or an operator such as Strimzi) so changes are reviewed and repeatable.

20.4Partition reassignment and adding brokers

Move partitions with a throttle
# 1. let Kafka propose a plan for these topics across brokers 1-4
kafka-reassign-partitions.sh --bootstrap-server localhost:9092 \
  --topics-to-move-json-file topics.json --broker-list 1,2,3,4 --generate
# 2. save the proposed plan as plan.json, then execute it with a replication throttle (bytes/s)
kafka-reassign-partitions.sh --bootstrap-server localhost:9092 \
  --reassignment-json-file plan.json --execute --throttle 50000000
# 3. check progress; once complete, verify also removes the throttle
kafka-reassign-partitions.sh --bootstrap-server localhost:9092 \
  --reassignment-json-file plan.json --verify
  • Always throttle large moves so replication traffic does not starve producers and consumers.
  • Save the current assignment (printed by --generate) as a rollback plan.
  • Tools such as Cruise Control automate balancing by disk, network, and leader counts.
  • Removing a broker: reassign its replicas away first, then shut it down.

20.5Rolling restarts and upgrades

  • One broker at a time: stop it cleanly (controlled shutdown moves leadership away), restart, and wait until UnderReplicatedPartitions returns to 0 before the next.
  • Upgrades in KRaft: roll every node onto the new software, verify behavior, then finalize with kafka-features.sh --bootstrap-server ... upgrade --release-version 4.3. Some metadata versions cannot be downgraded after finalizing, so test first.
  • Clients: Kafka keeps clients and brokers compatible across versions in both directions, with a floor: 4.x clients and brokers need the other side to be at least 2.1.
  • Controllers in a dedicated quorum are rolled one at a time too, keeping a majority up.

20.6Security

Layer Options Notes
Encryption TLS (SSL or SASL_SSL listeners) Encrypts client and inter-broker traffic; disables zero-copy
Authentication mTLS client certificates; SASL/SCRAM-SHA-512; SASL/OAUTHBEARER (OIDC); SASL/GSSAPI (Kerberos); SASL/PLAIN (only over TLS) Produces a principal such as User:ledger-service
Authorization ACLs with the KRaft StandardAuthorizer Allow or deny an operation on a topic, group, cluster, or transactional ID
Quotas producer_byte_rate, consumer_byte_rate, request_percentage Per user or client ID; protect the cluster from noisy tenants. A client over its quota is not failed: the broker answers with a throttle time and mutes that connection for that long, so the client slows down
Least-privilege ACLs for a consumer and a producer
kafka-acls.sh --bootstrap-server localhost:9092 --command-config admin.properties --add \
  --allow-principal User:ledger-service --operation Read --topic payments --group ledger
kafka-acls.sh --bootstrap-server localhost:9092 --command-config admin.properties --add \
  --allow-principal User:payments-api --producer --topic payments
kafka-configs.sh --bootstrap-server localhost:9092 --command-config admin.properties --alter \
  --entity-type users --entity-name payments-api --add-config producer_byte_rate=10485760
  • --producer and --consumer are shortcuts that grant the operations a producer or consumer needs (Write, Describe, and Create for producers; Read and Describe on the topic plus Read on the group for consumers).
  • Use prefixed resource patterns (--resource-pattern-type prefixed) to grant a team all topics starting with payments..
  • Rotate credentials, never share one principal across services, and audit who can create or delete topics.

20.7Multi-cluster and disaster recovery

  • Within a region, a cluster stretched across three availability zones (Module 12) survives a zone loss with no data loss. Most teams stop here.
  • Across regions, latency makes synchronous replication impractical, so a second cluster receives an asynchronous copy:
    • MirrorMaker 2, built on Kafka Connect, replicates topics, configs, and ACLs, and emits checkpoints that translate consumer group offsets between clusters.
    • Active-passive: producers write to one region; on failover, consumers start in the backup region from translated offsets. Expect some duplicates and a small loss window equal to replication lag (RPO).
    • Active-active: each region writes locally; topics are mirrored both ways under prefixed names so loops are impossible. Consumers read local and remote topics; designs must tolerate the same entity being updated in two regions.
  • Offsets differ between clusters, which is why translation is needed; never copy raw offset numbers across. MirrorMaker 2 emits checkpoints every 60 seconds by default; with sync.group.offsets.enabled=true (off by default) it also writes the translated offsets into the target cluster's __consumer_offsets for groups that are not running there, so standby consumers can simply start.
  • Commercial alternatives (for example Confluent Cluster Linking) preserve offsets byte for byte.
Topology Write latency Data loss if a region dies (RPO) Offsets Use when
One cluster across 3 zones About 1 to 2 ms None for a zone loss; a region loss takes the cluster down One space The default for most systems
Stretch cluster across 3 regions Adds cross-region round trips to every acks=all write (tens of ms) None, with replicas and controllers in 3 regions One space Rare: zero loss across regions is worth the latency
Two clusters, active-passive (MM2) Local Seconds of replication lag Translated Regional disaster recovery
Two clusters, active-active (MM2) Local in each region Seconds for the other region's data Translated, prefixed topics Users write in their own region
  • A stretch cluster needs three locations, not two. The KRaft controllers need a majority. With voters in only two regions, one region must hold the majority, and losing that region stops the quorum. A third region (or a small witness site holding a controller) removes that single point of failure.
Go deeper

Failing over and failing back with MirrorMaker 2

Failover (primary region lost):

  1. Stop or fence producers in the failed region if they are still partly up, so two regions do not accept writes for the same data.
  2. Point producers at the backup cluster (DNS or config). In active-passive with the default replication policy, they now write to local topics such as orders, while the mirrored history sits in east.orders; consumers subscribe to both (or a pattern) until the old topic drains. For one-way replication, IdentityReplicationPolicy keeps topic names identical instead, which simplifies clients but cannot be used for active-active.
  3. Start consumers in the backup region from translated offsets (synced group offsets, or RemoteClusterUtils.translateOffsets). Translation can land slightly early, so expect some duplicates; idempotent consumers absorb them.
  4. Accept that records still in flight when the region died (the replication lag) may be missing until the old region returns; reconcile critical data afterwards.

Failback (primary region back):

  1. Do not switch producers back yet: the backup has writes the primary never saw.
  2. Run MirrorMaker 2 in the reverse direction, wait until lag reaches zero and checkpoints are current.
  3. Switch producers back in a quiet window, then consumers using translated offsets, then restore the original replication direction.
  4. Rehearse both directions regularly; an untested runbook is the most common failure.

20.8Managed Kafka

Managed services (Confluent Cloud, Amazon MSK, Aiven, and others) run brokers, upgrades, and disks for you. You still own topic design, keys and partitions, client configuration, schemas, security policies, consumer lag, and cost (especially cross-zone traffic).

20.9Lab: change replication with a reassignment

LabRaise a topic from replication factor 2 to 3 without downtime15 minutes

On the three-broker cluster:

Terminal
k kafka-topics.sh --create --topic grow --partitions 3 --replication-factor 2
k kafka-topics.sh --describe --topic grow
printf '%s' '{"version":1,"partitions":[{"topic":"grow","partition":0,"replicas":[1,2,3]},{"topic":"grow","partition":1,"replicas":[2,3,1]},{"topic":"grow","partition":2,"replicas":[3,1,2]}]}' \
  | docker exec -i kafka-1 sh -c 'cat > /tmp/plan.json'
k kafka-reassign-partitions.sh --reassignment-json-file /tmp/plan.json --execute --throttle 10000000
k kafka-reassign-partitions.sh --reassignment-json-file /tmp/plan.json --verify
k kafka-topics.sh --describe --topic grow

Then change a config at runtime and read it back:

Terminal
k kafka-configs.sh --alter --entity-type topics --entity-name grow --add-config retention.ms=86400000
k kafka-configs.sh --describe --entity-type topics --entity-name grow
Check what you saw
  • Before: each partition lists two replicas. --execute prints the current assignment (save it as a rollback plan) and starts the move.
  • --verify reports each partition's reassignment as complete and clears the throttle; describe now shows three replicas and three ISR members per partition, with the first replica as preferred leader.
  • The topic stayed readable and writable throughout: replicas were added, caught up, then joined the ISR.
  • --describe on configs shows retention.ms=86400000 as a dynamic topic config.

20.10Common mistakes

Common mistakes

  • Alerting on lag in messages only, or measuring lag from inside the consumer that is stuck.
  • Unthrottled reassignments that saturate the network in business hours.
  • Restarting the next broker before under-replicated partitions return to zero.
  • PLAINTEXT listeners in production, or SASL/PLAIN without TLS.
  • One shared principal for many services, which makes ACLs and audits meaningless.
  • Copying consumer offsets as numbers between clusters instead of translating them.
  • No tested failover runbook for the second region.

20.11Self-check

Self-checkFive more, after the lessons
  1. What is the difference between UnderReplicatedPartitions and UnderMinIsrPartitionCount?
    Reveal

    Under-replicated means some replicas are out of the ISR (less redundancy); under min ISR means the ISR is below min.insync.replicas, so acks=all writes to those partitions fail.

  2. Why measure consumer lag externally?
    Reveal

    A crashed or hung consumer stops reporting its own metrics; an external checker compares committed offsets with end offsets regardless.

  3. What are the three steps of a partition reassignment?
    Reveal

    Generate (or write) a plan, execute it with a throttle, and verify until complete (which also removes the throttle).

  4. What does finalizing an upgrade with kafka-features.sh do?
    Reveal

    It raises the cluster's metadata version so new features take effect, after all nodes run the new software; some versions cannot be downgraded after this.

  5. Why can't a stretch cluster across two regions survive the loss of either region on its own?
    Reveal

    The KRaft controller quorum needs a majority. With voters in two regions, one region holds the majority, and losing it stops the quorum; a third location (a witness) fixes that.

  6. Why does MirrorMaker 2 need offset checkpoints?
    Reveal

    The same record has different offsets in the source and target clusters, so consumer positions must be translated to resume correctly after failover.

Module 21: Troubleshooting playbook

When Kafka misbehaves at 2 AM you need a method, not a search engine. This module is a playbook: a general approach, then symptom by symptom (lag, rebalance loops, duplicates, missing data, producer errors, broker trouble, ordering, connectivity) with checks, causes, and fixes, and a set of incident drills to practice on.

12 lessons1 figures6 mastery checks

On this page

  1. 21.1A method for any incident
  2. 21.2Consumer lag keeps growing
  3. 21.3Rebalance loops and CommitFailedException
  4. 21.4Duplicates downstream
  5. 21.5Missing or lost messages
  6. 21.6Producer errors
  7. 21.7Broker and cluster problems
  8. 21.8Ordering surprises
  9. 21.9Connectivity and configuration
  10. 21.10Incident drills
  11. 21.11Common mistakes
  12. 21.12Self-check
Warm-upWarm-up: one line each
  1. Lag grows on one partition only. What are the two most likely causes?
    Reveal

    A poison record that the consumer keeps failing on, or a hot key sending far more traffic to that partition.

  2. Consumers log CommitFailedException and the group keeps rebalancing. What is usually wrong?
    Reveal

    Processing a batch takes longer than max.poll.interval.ms, so members are removed mid-batch and their commits are rejected.

  3. A new consumer group "lost" all historical messages. What is the usual reason?
    Reveal

    It started with the default auto.offset.reset=latest and so began at the end of each partition.

  4. Producers report NotEnoughReplicasException. What does that tell you?
    Reveal

    The partition's ISR is smaller than min.insync.replicas, usually because brokers are down or followers are lagging.

  5. Clients connect for bootstrap and then time out connecting to kafka-2:9092. Where do you look?
    Reveal

    At advertised.listeners on the brokers: the advertised address is not reachable from the clients.

21.1A method for any incident

  1. Scope it: which topics, partitions, consumer groups, clients, brokers? All or some? Since when?
  2. What changed? Deploys, config changes, traffic spikes, broker restarts, certificate expiry, a new consumer group.
  3. Read metrics by layer: producer errors and latency; broker URP, under-min-ISR, offline partitions, idle ratios; consumer lag per partition and rebalance rate.
  4. Read logs near the start time: client exceptions, broker server.log and state-change.log, controller logs.
  5. Form one hypothesis, test it, fix, and watch the metric recover.
  6. Prevent it: an alert, a config change, a runbook entry.

21.2Consumer lag keeps growing

Check Command or signal If yes
Lag on one or a few partitions only? kafka-consumer-groups.sh --describe --group G Poison record (same offset for minutes) or hot key (high bytes in on that partition)
Fewer active consumers than partitions? --describe --members Scale out, or find crashed instances
Rebalancing often? Consumer logs, rebalance-rate-per-hour Fix poll interval, static membership, cooperative assignor
Produce rate jumped? Broker MessagesInPerSec per topic Scale consumers (up to partitions); add partitions for the future
Processing slower? Consumer processing time, downstream latency Fix the downstream, batch writes, add caching
Consumers healthy but fetches slow? Broker TotalTimeMs for FetchConsumer Broker overload, cold reads from disk, network

21.3Rebalance loops and CommitFailedException

  • Symptom: logs show members leaving and rejoining, CommitFailedException, and the same records processed repeatedly.
  • Causes: processing per poll longer than max.poll.interval.ms; long GC pauses or CPU throttling (containers with low CPU limits) causing missed heartbeats; pods restarted repeatedly by failing health checks; frequent deploys with an eager assignor.
  • Fixes: lower max.poll.records, speed up or move slow work, raise max.poll.interval.ms if a batch legitimately takes long; give consumers enough CPU; use static membership and cooperative rebalancing (or group.protocol=consumer); make liveness probes independent of Kafka processing.

21.4Duplicates downstream

  • Expected sources (at-least-once): crash or rebalance between processing and commit; producer retries without idempotence; application-level resends; replays and offset resets; outbox relays.
  • Checks: do duplicates share an event ID (redelivery) or have different IDs (the producer created two events)? Did a rebalance or deploy happen at that time?
  • Fixes: idempotent consumers keyed by event ID (Module 10); idempotent producer on (default); commit after processing; transactions for Kafka-to-Kafka pipelines (Module 14).

21.5Missing or lost messages

Go through this list in order; most "lost" messages were never lost.

Cause How to confirm Fix
New group started at latest Group's first committed offsets equal end offsets at start time auto.offset.reset=earliest, or reset offsets by time
Committed offsets expired (group idle more than 7 days) Group had no members for a long time Longer offsets.retention.minutes, or reset deliberately
Records expired by retention before being read Lag in time exceeded retention.ms Longer retention, faster consumers, lag alerts in time
Consumer is read_committed and transactions aborted or are open Producer uses transactions Expected behavior; check the producer's transaction errors
Producer send failed and the error was ignored Producer record-error-rate, logs Handle callback errors; outbox
acks=1 (or 0) and a leader failed Broker failover at that time acks=all, min.insync.replicas=2
Unclean leader election UncleanLeaderElectionsPerSec above 0 Disable unclean election on important topics
Auto-commit with asynchronous processing Offsets committed before workers finished Commit only completed work
Consumer filtered or mis-deserialized records Application logs, DLT Fix logic; route failures to a DLT

21.6Producer errors

Error Meaning Fix
TimeoutException: Expiring N record(s) Records waited longer than delivery.timeout.ms Brokers unreachable or slow; check leaders, network, broker load
TimeoutException on metadata after max.block.ms Cannot fetch metadata or topic missing Wrong bootstrap address, topic does not exist and auto-create is off, ACLs
NotEnoughReplicasException ISR below min.insync.replicas Restore brokers or followers; check disks and network
RecordTooLargeException Record bigger than max.request.size or the topic's max.message.bytes Shrink payloads (claim check) or raise limits consistently
TopicAuthorizationException Principal lacks Write or Describe on the topic Add ACLs
ProducerFencedException Another instance with the same transactional.id started Expected after a failover; make IDs unique per live instance
BufferExhaustedException buffer.memory full for max.block.ms Producer faster than the cluster accepts: fix broker side, raise buffer, or slow down

21.7Broker and cluster problems

  • Under-replicated partitions: find which brokers host the lagging replicas. Usual causes: a broker down or restarting, disk or network saturation, a slow disk, or too few num.replica.fetchers. Check kafka-topics.sh --describe --under-replicated-partitions.
  • Offline partitions: no in-sync replica is available. Bring back the brokers that hold them; consider unclean election only for data you can afford to lose.
  • Disk full: the broker marks the affected log directory offline (a broker with a single log directory shuts down). Free space by lowering retention, deleting unneeded topics, or adding disks, and alert at 70 to 80 percent next time.
  • Controller trouble: ActiveControllerCount not summing to 1, or metadata changes stalling. Check controller quorum health with kafka-metadata-quorum.sh describe --status and keep a majority of controllers up.
  • Hot broker: uneven leaders or partitions. Run a preferred leader election, then rebalance replicas with a reassignment or Cruise Control.

21.8Ordering surprises

  • Different partitions: the producer used no key, a different key, or a different partitioner (Java versus librdkafka defaults).
  • Partition count changed: keys remapped (Module 6).
  • Retries reordering: idempotence turned off with more than one request in flight (Module 5).
  • Consumer-side parallelism: a worker pool without per-key routing, or retry topics overtaking later records.

21.9Connectivity and configuration

Symptom Likely cause
Bootstrap works, then "unknown host" or timeouts to specific brokers advertised.listeners not reachable from the client network
SSL handshake failed Wrong truststore, expired certificate, hostname mismatch
SaslAuthenticationException Wrong credentials or mechanism mismatch between client and listener
UnsupportedVersionException Client or broker too old for a feature; 4.x needs the other side at 2.1 or newer
Works locally, fails in Kubernetes Clients cannot reach individual broker addresses; only bootstrap is exposed

21.10Incident drills

Guided designSix incidents to practiceAnswer each before revealing
  1. 1
    Black Friday lag

    Checkout events lag reaches 40 minutes on every partition of a 12-partition topic. The group has 12 consumers, CPU is low, and the downstream payments database shows high latency.

    Write your answer, then reveal

    Consumers are waiting on the database, so scaling consumers (already at the partition count) will not help and would add load. Batch writes per poll, add a connection pool or caching, shed non-critical work, and if the database is the hard limit, slow producers or accept lag. Long term: more partitions plus a faster sink, and lag-in-time alerts against retention.

  2. 2
    The partition that never moves

    Lag grows only on partition 7 of orders; the committed offset there has been 88213 for an hour. Other partitions are fine.

    Write your answer, then reveal

    Classic poison record at offset 88213. Read it with kafka-console-consumer.sh --partition 7 --offset 88213 --max-messages 1, check consumer logs for the exception, then route it to a DLT (or skip by resetting that partition's offset to 88214 with the group stopped). Add bounded retries and a DLT so it cannot recur.

  3. 3
    Rebalance storm after a deploy

    After a release that added a slow fraud check, the group rebalances every few minutes and processes the same records again and again.

    Write your answer, then reveal

    Each poll's batch now takes longer than max.poll.interval.ms, so members are removed mid-batch. Lower max.poll.records, make the fraud check faster or asynchronous with proper offset tracking, and raise max.poll.interval.ms only if needed. Cooperative rebalancing and static membership reduce the blast radius.

  4. 4
    The new service saw nothing

    A new analytics service deployed yesterday shows no data before yesterday, though the topic keeps 30 days.

    Write your answer, then reveal

    Its consumer group started with the default auto.offset.reset=latest. Stop the group and reset offsets: --reset-offsets --to-earliest (or --to-datetime) with --execute, then restart. Make sure processing is idempotent before replaying 30 days.

  5. 5
    NotEnoughReplicas at 3 AM

    Producers to ledger fail with NotEnoughReplicasException; one broker is down for disk replacement and another just restarted.

    Write your answer, then reveal

    With RF 3 and min.insync.replicas=2, one broker down is fine, but the restarted broker has not rejoined the ISR yet, leaving one in-sync replica. Writes correctly refuse. Wait for the restarted broker to catch up (watch URP fall), and in future never take a second broker down until URP is zero. Do not lower min.insync.replicas in a panic.

  6. 6
    Duplicate emails

    Customers receive some payment emails twice. The duplicates have identical event_id values and occurred during a deploy.

    Write your answer, then reveal

    Same event ID means redelivery, not double publishing: the deploy caused a rebalance, and records processed but not yet committed were processed again by the new owner. Make the email consumer idempotent by event ID (a processed-events table, or the email provider's idempotency key), commit in onPartitionsRevoked, and use cooperative rebalancing to shrink the window.

21.11Common mistakes

Common mistakes

  • Scaling consumers beyond the partition count to fix lag.
  • Lowering min.insync.replicas or enabling unclean election during an incident and forgetting to revert it.
  • Resetting offsets without checking idempotency of downstream effects.
  • Restarting brokers one after another without waiting for under-replicated partitions to clear.
  • Treating every "missing message" report as data loss before checking offsets, retention, and isolation level.
  • No runbook: rediscovering the same fix in every incident.

21.12Self-check

Self-checkFive more, after the lessons
  1. What is the first question to ask about growing lag?
    Reveal

    Is it on all partitions or only some? Some points to a poison record or hot key; all points to more input, slower processing, too few consumers, or rebalances.

  2. How do you tell a redelivery from a double publish?
    Reveal

    Compare event IDs: identical IDs mean the same event was delivered twice; different IDs mean the producer created two events.

  3. List three causes of "missing" messages that are not data loss.
    Reveal

    A new group starting at latest, expired committed offsets, and a read_committed consumer hiding aborted or open transactions. (Also consumer-side filtering or deserialization failures.)

  4. What does UnsupportedVersionException usually mean?
    Reveal

    A client and broker version combination lacks a needed API version, for example a client too old for a 4.x broker (which needs 2.1 or newer).

  5. During an incident, why not just enable unclean leader election to bring partitions back?
    Reveal

    It can elect a replica that is missing committed records, permanently losing acknowledged data. Use it only for data you can afford to lose, and document the decision.

Mastery checklist

Tick an item only when it is true with your notes closed.

Case study 1Starter40 min

Case study 1: Order events with the outbox pattern

An e-commerce order service must tell payments, inventory, shipping, notifications, and analytics about every order change, reliably and in order per order, without distributed transactions and without slowing down checkout.

Uses: M14 outbox, M16 Debezium, M10 idempotent consumers
Your status

On this page

  1. C1.1Requirements
  2. C1.2Estimates
  3. C1.3Topics and events
  4. C1.4High-level design
  5. C1.5Deep dives
  6. C1.6Failures and bottlenecks
  7. C1.7What a strong answer shows
  8. C1.8Follow-up questions
Try it first40 minutes, on paper, before reading

Design how the order service publishes order events to the rest of the company. Cover: how the database write and the event stay consistent, topic and key choice, ordering, consumers that must not double-charge or double-ship, adding a new consumer next quarter, and schema changes.

Reveal the answer

A strong answer covers: the dual-write problem and the transactional outbox (or CDC); Debezium or a poller as the relay; one topic of order events keyed by order_id for per-order order; a consumer group per downstream service; idempotent consumers keyed by event_id; a schema registry with BACKWARD compatibility; retention long enough for a new consumer to backfill or a snapshot topic; DLTs per consumer; monitoring of outbox lag and replication slot growth.

C1.1Requirements

Functional

  • Publish an event for each order state change: created, paid, packed, shipped, delivered, cancelled.
  • Five consumers today (payments, inventory, shipping, notifications, warehouse); new ones must subscribe without changes to the order service.
  • Consumers see an order's events in the order they happened.

Non-functional

  • No event lost and no event for an order that does not exist.
  • Checkout latency unaffected by consumers.
  • 5 million orders per day, peak 10x average during sales.

C1.2Estimates

Quantity Calculation Result
Events per day 5M orders x 6 events 30M
Average rate 30M / 86,400 about 350 events/s
Peak rate 10x average about 3,500 events/s
Event size JSON or Avro with envelope about 1 KB
Peak throughput 3,500 x 1 KB about 3.5 MB/s
Storage for 30 days 30 GB/day x 30 x RF 3 about 2.7 TB before compression

C1.3Topics and events

Topic Key Partitions Retention Notes
orders.events.v1 order_id 24 30 days All order event types, so per-order order holds
<consumer>.orders.dlt order_id 24 90 days One DLT per consuming service
  • One topic for all order event types: consumers need OrderCreated before OrderPaid for the same order, and order exists only within one partition of one topic.
  • Partitions: 3,500 events/s at peak; if the slowest consumer handles about 500 events/s per instance, it needs at least 7. 24 leaves room to grow without remapping keys.
  • Envelope: event_id, event_type, event_time, order_id, schema_version, plus a body with what consumers need (items, amounts, address for shipping).

C1.4High-level design

  1. The order service writes the orders row and an outbox row (event ID, type, key, payload) in one database transaction, then returns to the client.
  2. Debezium reads the write-ahead log and, with its outbox event router, publishes each outbox row to orders.events.v1 with key order_id.
  3. Each downstream service consumes with its own consumer group, applies events idempotently, and commits after processing.

C1.5Deep dives

Guided designDeep divesAnswer each before revealing
  1. 1
    The dual-write problem

    Why not write the order and then call producer.send()?

    Write your answer, then reveal

    A crash between the two leaves an order with no event (or, in the reverse order, an event with no order). Two systems cannot be updated atomically without help. The outbox makes the event part of the same database transaction; the relay then delivers it at least once.

  2. 2
    Relay choice

    CDC with Debezium or a polling publisher?

    Write your answer, then reveal

    CDC reads the write-ahead log: low latency, no extra query load, strict commit order. A poller (SELECT ... WHERE published = false ORDER BY id LIMIT 500 FOR UPDATE SKIP LOCKED, publish, mark published) is simpler to run without Connect but adds load and latency, and ordering across concurrent transactions needs care. Either way, delivery is at-least-once.

  3. 3
    Ordering per order

    Can a consumer see OrderShipped before OrderPaid?

    Write your answer, then reveal

    Not if both are keyed by order_id in one topic: they land in the same partition in commit order, and a consumer processes a partition in order. Ordering can still break on the consumer side (retry topics, worker pools); use blocking retries for ordered processing.

  4. 4
    Idempotent consumers

    The relay or a rebalance delivers OrderPaid twice. How does shipping avoid two shipments?

    Write your answer, then reveal

    Shipping records processed event_ids in its database, in the same transaction as creating the shipment, with a unique constraint. A duplicate is skipped. Business keys help too: "one shipment per order" as a unique constraint.

  5. 5
    A new consumer next quarter

    A loyalty service needs all orders from the last year. Retention is 30 days.

    Write your answer, then reveal

    Options: keep a compacted snapshot topic (orders.state.v1, latest state per order) that the new service reads from the beginning; backfill from the warehouse; or use longer retention with tiered storage. The event stream gives changes; a snapshot gives current state cheaply.

  6. 6
    Schema changes

    Shipping needs delivery_window. Inventory does not care.

    Write your answer, then reveal

    Add delivery_window as an optional field with a default (BACKWARD compatible), register the schema through CI, deploy consumers that use it, then producers. Old consumers keep working. A breaking change goes to orders.events.v2 with a migration period.

  7. 7
    Outbox housekeeping

    The outbox table grows by 30M rows a day.

    Write your answer, then reveal

    Delete published rows (Debezium only needs the insert in the log, so the router pattern can even delete the row in the same transaction), or partition the table by day and drop old partitions. Monitor replication slot lag so a stopped connector does not fill the database disk.

C1.6Failures and bottlenecks

Failure Effect Mitigation
Debezium connector down Events delayed; WAL accumulates in the database Alert on slot lag; max_slot_wal_keep_size; restart quickly
Consumer bug Bad side effects or DLT growth DLT per consumer, alerts, replay tool after the fix
Hot key (one huge order) Unlikely; orders are small Not a concern with order_id keys
Broker failure Brief leader failover RF 3, min.insync.replicas=2, acks=all on the relay
Schema break Consumers fail to deserialize Registry compatibility checks in CI

C1.7What a strong answer shows

Interview signal

SDE-2: names the dual-write problem and solves it with an outbox; keys by order_id for per-order order; idempotent consumers; separate consumer groups; schema registry. Senior adds: relay trade-offs (CDC vs polling), slot and outbox housekeeping, a compacted state topic for new consumers, consumer-side ordering pitfalls, and how choreography differs from an orchestrated saga for payment and inventory.

C1.8Follow-up questions

PracticeAnswer out loud, then reveal
  1. Why not use a distributed transaction (two-phase commit) between the database and Kafka?
    Reveal

    Kafka does not take part in XA transactions with your database, and 2PC couples availability and adds latency. The outbox gives the same atomicity with one local transaction.

  2. How does the payments service tell the order service that payment succeeded?
    Reveal

    It publishes PaymentSucceeded (through its own outbox) keyed by order_id; the order service consumes it and moves the order to Paid. That is a choreographed saga; an orchestrator service is the alternative when steps grow.

  3. How do you replay one day of events into a fixed consumer?
    Reveal

    Stop that consumer group, reset offsets with --to-datetime, restart. Idempotent processing makes the replay safe.

  4. What if the order service must also publish to two topics atomically?
    Reveal

    Two outbox rows in the same database transaction; the relay routes each to its topic. Or Kafka transactions, if the producer is a Kafka-to-Kafka processor.

Case study 2Stretch45 min

Case study 2: Card transaction pipeline

A card issuer must turn every authorization into ledger postings, fraud signals, customer notifications, and an audit archive, then match the network's clearing records days later. Money moves on these events, so nothing may be lost or applied twice, and card data must stay protected.

Uses: M5 idempotence, M14 transactions, M17 windows, M12 durability
Your status

On this page

  1. C2.1Requirements
  2. C2.2Estimates
  3. C2.3Topics and events
  4. C2.4High-level design
  5. C2.5Deep dives
  6. C2.6Failures and bottlenecks
  7. C2.7What a strong answer shows
  8. C2.8Follow-up questions
Try it first45 minutes, on paper, before reading

Design the event pipeline behind card authorizations for an issuer processing 20 million transactions a day. Decide what stays synchronous, how events are published, topic and key design, how the ledger avoids double posting, how fraud features are computed in time windows, how clearing records are matched, how card data is protected, and how long data is kept.

Reveal the answer

A strong answer keeps the authorization decision synchronous and publishes its outcome through an outbox; keys everything by card token so a card's events stay ordered; uses acks=all, RF 3, min.insync.replicas=2; posts to the ledger idempotently by authorization ID; computes fraud features with event-time windows in Flink or Kafka Streams with exactly-once; matches clearing to authorization with a stateful join and an exception queue; never puts full card numbers in Kafka; archives to object storage for years; and plans replay and reconciliation.

C2.1Requirements

Functional

  • For every authorization (approved or declined): post holds to the ledger, update fraud features, notify the customer, archive the event.
  • Later, match clearing (settlement) records from the card network to authorizations, convert holds to postings, and raise exceptions for unmatched items.
  • Support reversals and partial clearings.

Non-functional

  • Authorization decisions within the network's deadline (tens to low hundreds of milliseconds); Kafka is not on that path.
  • No lost and no duplicated ledger effects.
  • Keep Kafka out of PCI DSS card data scope: no full card number (PAN) in events or logs.
  • Audit retention for years.

C2.2Estimates

Quantity Calculation Result
Authorizations 20M per day about 230/s average
Peak about 8x average (lunch, sales) about 2,000/s
Events per authorization decision, then posting and notification downstream about 3 events across topics
Peak event rate 2,000 x 3 about 6,000/s
Event size Avro with envelope about 1.5 KB
Peak throughput 6,000 x 1.5 KB about 9 MB/s
Daily volume 20M x 3 x 1.5 KB about 90 GB/day
Hot retention 90 GB x 7 days x RF 3 about 1.9 TB before compression
Archive 7 years in object storage Sink connector, Parquet

C2.3Topics and events

Topic Key Partitions Retention Notes
card.auth.events.v1 card token 48 7 days AuthorizationApproved, AuthorizationDeclined, AuthorizationReversed
card.clearing.events.v1 card token 48 30 days Parsed from network clearing files
ledger.postings.v1 account ID 24 30 days Output of the ledger service
fraud.features.v1 card token 48 3 days Windowed features for scoring
  • Key by card token: a card's authorizations, reversals, and clearings stay in order on one partition, and the matcher can join auth and clearing streams because both are co-partitioned (same key, same partition count).
  • Card token, not PAN: the tokenization service maps PAN to token; events carry the token and the last four digits only.

C2.4High-level design

  1. The card network sends an authorization request; the auth service decides synchronously (balance, limits, rules, risk score) and writes the decision and an outbox row in its database.
  2. CDC publishes the outbox row to card.auth.events.v1.
  3. Consumers: the ledger service posts holds idempotently by auth_id; a Flink job maintains fraud features; notifications send push or SMS; a sink connector archives to object storage.
  4. Clearing files are parsed into card.clearing.events.v1; a matcher joins them with authorizations by card token and authorization code within a time window, emits matched results, and routes breaks to an operations queue.

C2.5Deep dives

Guided designDeep divesAnswer each before revealing
  1. 1
    What stays synchronous

    Why not put Kafka in the authorization path?

    Write your answer, then reveal

    The network expects an answer within a strict deadline, and the decision needs current balance and limits. Adding an asynchronous hop adds latency and failure modes. The decision is synchronous against the source of truth; Kafka distributes the outcome to everything that can happen afterwards.

  2. 2
    Never lose, never double-post

    Walk through what makes a ledger posting happen exactly once.

    Write your answer, then reveal

    Producer side: outbox in the same transaction as the decision, so every decision yields an event; relay with acks=all and idempotence. Broker side: RF 3, min.insync.replicas=2, unclean election off. Consumer side: the ledger applies a posting and records auth_id (plus event type) in the same database transaction with a unique constraint, then commits the offset. Redeliveries hit the constraint and change nothing.

  3. 3
    Ordering and reversals

    A reversal arrives for an authorization the ledger has not seen yet. How?

    Write your answer, then reveal

    It should not happen within one partition, since both are keyed by card token and published in commit order. It can happen if the reversal comes from another system or a replay mixes sources. Make handlers robust: park a reversal for an unknown authorization briefly and retry, or record it and apply it when the authorization arrives (state machine per authorization).

  4. 4
    Fraud features in windows

    Compute "number of transactions and total amount per card in the last 5 minutes" for scoring.

    Write your answer, then reveal

    A Flink or Kafka Streams job keyed by card token keeps windowed aggregates in event time (hopping or sliding windows), with a grace period for late events, and writes features to fraud.features.v1 and a low-latency store the risk engine reads. Exactly-once processing keeps counts correct across failures. The synchronous risk check reads the latest features; it does not wait for the stream.

  5. 5
    Matching clearing to authorization

    Clearing arrives 1 to 3 days later, sometimes for a different amount, sometimes never.

    Write your answer, then reveal

    A stateful job keyed by card token stores open authorizations (state store or database) and matches clearing records by authorization code, amount tolerance, and time window. Matches convert holds to postings; unmatched clearings and expired authorizations (holds released after N days) go to a reconciliation queue for operations. This is a stream-table style join with long-lived state, not a short windowed stream-stream join.

  6. 6
    Card data and access

    How do you keep this PCI-friendly?

    Write your answer, then reveal

    No PAN in Kafka: tokens and last four digits only. TLS on all listeners, SASL or mTLS authentication, ACLs so only the ledger can read postings and only the auth service can write auth events, encryption at rest for brokers and archives, and audit of topic access. Keep cardholder data environments separate from analytics topics.

  7. 7
    Replay and audit

    An auditor asks for all events of one card from 3 years ago; a bug requires reprocessing last Tuesday.

    Write your answer, then reveal

    Audit: the object storage archive (partitioned by date, queryable with a lake engine, with write-once retention such as S3 Object Lock so records cannot be altered), not Kafka. Never use a compacted topic as an audit trail: compaction removes the intermediate events an auditor needs. Reprocessing: retention of 7 days lets you reset the ledger consumer's offsets to Tuesday, and idempotency makes it safe; for anything older, replay from the archive into a dedicated topic.

C2.6Failures and bottlenecks

Failure Effect Mitigation
Ledger database slow Lag on postings; customers see stale balances Batch writes per poll, alert on lag in time, scale to partition count
Broker loss Short failover RF 3 across zones, min.insync.replicas=2
Relay down Events delayed, not lost Outbox persists; alert on outbox age
Late or missing clearing Holds outstanding Expiry rules, reconciliation queue
Hot card (merchant test card) One partition busy Rate limits upstream; per-card limits

C2.7What a strong answer shows

Interview signal

SDE-2: synchronous decision plus asynchronous distribution; outbox; key by card token; acks=all with idempotence; idempotent ledger postings; windowed fraud features; no PAN in events. Senior adds: matching with long-lived state and reconciliation, exactly-once in the stream processor versus idempotency at the ledger, co-partitioning requirements, retention tiers (hot Kafka, archive), multi-region failover and its duplicate window.

C2.8Follow-up questions

PracticeAnswer out loud, then reveal
  1. Could the ledger use Kafka transactions instead of a processed-IDs table?
    Reveal

    Only if its output were Kafka records. The ledger writes to a database, so Kafka transactions do not cover the effect; idempotency in the database transaction does.

  2. Why 48 partitions for card.auth.events at about 2,000 events/s peak?
    Reveal

    If one ledger instance posts about 100 events/s (one database transaction each), peak needs 20 instances; 48 leaves growth headroom, divides evenly by 2, 3, 4, 6, 8, 12, 16, and 24, and the clearing topic uses the same count so the two are co-partitioned.

  3. How would you notify customers without spamming duplicates during rebalances?
    Reveal

    Idempotency key per notification (auth_id + channel) stored before sending, and providers' idempotency features; accept that rare duplicates are possible after ambiguous timeouts.

  4. What changes for multi-region?
    Reveal

    Run active-passive per region with MirrorMaker 2 or keep regional clusters with per-region ownership of cards. Ledger idempotency absorbs duplicates during failover; reconciliation catches gaps.

Case study 3Core40 min

Case study 3: Notification fan-out with priorities

Many services need to reach users by SMS, email, and push. One-time passwords must arrive in seconds even while a marketing campaign sends 20 million messages, providers enforce rate limits, and nobody should get the same message twice.

Uses: M9 share groups, M10 retries, M10 dead letters, M10 idempotency
Your status

On this page

  1. C3.1Requirements
  2. C3.2Estimates
  3. C3.3Topics and events
  4. C3.4High-level design
  5. C3.5Deep dives
  6. C3.6Failures and bottlenecks
  7. C3.7What a strong answer shows
  8. C3.8Follow-up questions
Try it first40 minutes, on paper, before reading

Design a notification platform used by every team. Cover the request API, how preferences and templates are applied, topic layout, keeping urgent messages fast during a bulk campaign, provider rate limits, retries and failures, duplicates, and how you would measure delivery.

Reveal the answer

A strong answer separates traffic by channel and priority into different topics with their own workers, so bulk sends cannot delay urgent ones; uses a router to apply preferences, quiet hours, and templates; scales bulk workers with share groups (or consumer groups with enough partitions); enforces provider and per-user rate limits with token buckets; uses retry topics and a DLT for failures; deduplicates by notification_id before calling providers; and tracks delivery status from provider callbacks.

C3.1Requirements

Functional

  • Any service sends a notification request: user, template, data, priority, and an idempotency key.
  • Respect user preferences (opt-outs per channel and category), quiet hours, and frequency caps.
  • Channels: SMS, email, push. Track status (sent, delivered, failed) for each message.

Non-functional

  • Urgent messages (one-time passwords, fraud alerts) delivered to the provider within 5 seconds, p99, even during campaigns.
  • 100 million notifications per day; a campaign can add 20 million in 30 minutes.
  • No duplicates in normal operation; never exceed provider rate limits.

C3.2Estimates

Quantity Calculation Result
Average rate 100M / 86,400 about 1,200/s
Campaign burst 20M / 1,800 s about 11,000/s
SMS provider limit contract for example 1,000/s
Message size request plus rendered content about 2 KB
Peak throughput 12,000 x 2 KB about 24 MB/s
Backlog at SMS limit 20M SMS at 1,000/s about 5.5 hours (so campaigns must be paced or spread across providers)

The last line is the important one: Kafka can absorb the burst, but the provider decides how fast it drains. Plan for backlog and make sure it never sits in front of urgent traffic.

C3.3Topics and events

Topic Key Partitions Consumers
notify.requests.v1 user_id 24 Router (consumer group)
notify.sms.high, notify.email.high, notify.push user_id 12 each Channel workers (consumer group)
notify.sms.bulk, notify.email.bulk user_id 12 each Bulk workers (share group)
notify.<channel>.retry-<delay> user_id 6 each Retry consumers
notify.dlt user_id 6 Alerting and replay tool
notify.status.v1 notification_id 12 Status service, analytics
  • Priority by topic: Kafka has no message priority. Separate topics with separate workers give urgent traffic its own lane.
  • Key by user_id: one user's messages stay in order on the router and high-priority lanes, and per-user frequency caps can be checked locally.

C3.4High-level design

  1. Services produce requests to notify.requests.v1 (or call a thin API that does). Each request carries notification_id as an idempotency key.
  2. The router loads preferences and templates (cached), drops opted-out or capped messages, renders content, and produces to the right channel and priority topic.
  3. Channel workers take a rate-limit token, check the dedup store, call the provider, record the result, and publish status events.
  4. Failures that may succeed later go to retry topics; permanent failures and exhausted retries go to notify.dlt.
  5. Provider callbacks (delivered, bounced) update status through notify.status.v1.

C3.5Deep dives

Guided designDeep divesAnswer each before revealing
  1. 1
    Keeping urgent messages fast

    A 20 million message campaign starts. Why do one-time passwords still arrive in seconds?

    Write your answer, then reveal

    They never share a queue with the campaign. notify.sms.high has its own workers and its own share of the provider's rate (for example, reserve 20% of the SMS limit for high priority). The campaign backlog sits in notify.sms.bulk and drains at the remaining rate. Watch lag in time per topic, and alert on the high lane only if it exceeds a few seconds.

  2. 2
    Share groups for bulk workers

    Why use a share group for bulk channels?

    Write your answer, then reveal

    Bulk messages are independent and their order does not matter. A share group (production-ready since Kafka 4.2) hands out records, not partitions, so you can run more workers than partitions, acknowledge each record, and let Kafka count delivery attempts (RELEASE to retry, REJECT for permanent failure). On an older cluster, use a consumer group with enough partitions, which works but ties parallelism to the partition count.

  3. 3
    Rate limits

    The SMS provider allows 1,000 requests per second across all workers.

    Write your answer, then reveal

    Use a shared token bucket (for example in Redis) per provider and lane; a worker takes a token before each call. When tokens run out the worker waits, but must keep its loop healthy: a consumer group worker must still call poll() within max.poll.interval.ms, and a share group worker must finish or renew records within the lock duration (30 s by default), so fetch small batches. Per-user caps ("at most 3 marketing SMS a day") are checked in the router.

  4. 4
    Retries and failures

    The provider returns a timeout, a 429, or "invalid phone number".

    Write your answer, then reveal

    Classify. Invalid number is permanent: send to the DLT (or mark failed) immediately. Timeouts and 5xx are transient: retry with backoff through notify.sms.retry-30s and notify.sms.retry-5m, then the DLT. A 429 means slow down: back off the whole worker, not just one message. For OTPs, a retry after a minute may be useless; give them a short time to live and drop expired ones.

  5. 5
    Duplicates

    A worker sends an SMS and crashes before its offset is committed. The record is delivered again.

    Write your answer, then reveal

    Before calling the provider, insert notification_id into a dedup store with a unique constraint (or SET NX with a TTL in Redis); skip if present. Pass the same ID as the provider's idempotency key when supported. The remaining gap (crash after the provider accepted but before recording the result) cannot be closed fully; this is at-least-once with idempotency, and that is acceptable for notifications.

  6. 6
    Measuring delivery

    How do you know the system works?

    Write your answer, then reveal

    Per lane: request rate, lag in seconds, provider latency and error rate, token bucket saturation, DLT rate. Per message: status events from send through provider callback, so support can answer "did the user get it?". End-to-end: time from request to provider accepted, p50 and p99, for the high lanes.

C3.6Failures and bottlenecks

Failure Effect Mitigation
Provider outage Retries pile up; lane lag grows Circuit breaker, failover to a second provider, pause bulk lanes
Router slow (preference store) All channels delayed Cache preferences, scale router to 24 partitions
Campaign floods SMS Bulk backlog for hours Separate lanes, reserved rate for urgent, pacing at campaign creation
Poison request (bad template data) Repeated failures Validate in router, send to DLT with the error
Duplicate sends Annoyed users, extra cost Dedup by notification_id, provider idempotency keys

C3.7What a strong answer shows

Interview signal

SDE-2: priority through separate topics and workers, a router for preferences and templates, rate limiting, retry topics and a DLT, dedup by an idempotency key. Senior adds: rate reservation between lanes, why backlog is set by provider limits not Kafka, share groups versus partitions for parallelism, TTLs for time-sensitive messages, provider failover, and a status pipeline for support and analytics.

C3.8Follow-up questions

PracticeAnswer out loud, then reveal
  1. Why not one topic with a priority field?
    Reveal

    A consumer reads a partition in order, so an urgent record waits behind every bulk record before it. Priority needs separate lanes.

  2. Should the router call providers directly?
    Reveal

    No. Splitting routing from sending lets each channel scale, fail, and rate-limit independently, and keeps a slow provider from blocking other channels.

  3. How would you schedule a notification for 9 AM in each user's time zone?
    Reveal

    Store scheduled notifications by due time and publish them when due (a scheduler, see the delayed jobs case study), rather than holding them in Kafka.

  4. Retry topics break ordering. Does that matter here?
    Reveal

    Rarely for notifications. Where it does (for example "card blocked" then "card unblocked"), keep those in the high lane with blocking retries, or include a version and drop stale messages.

Case study 4Stretch45 min

Case study 4: Real-time ad click aggregation

Advertisers pay per click and watch dashboards in near real time. Count clicks per ad per minute from a billion daily events, correctly, despite duplicates, late arrivals, bots, and a few viral ads that get most of the traffic.

Uses: M17 windows, M17 exactly-once, M6 hot partitions, M13 compaction
Your status

On this page

  1. C4.1Requirements
  2. C4.2Estimates
  3. C4.3Topics and events
  4. C4.4High-level design
  5. C4.5Deep dives
  6. C4.6Failures and bottlenecks
  7. C4.7What a strong answer shows
  8. C4.8Follow-up questions
Try it first45 minutes, on paper, before reading

Design a system that counts ad clicks per ad per minute for dashboards (fresh within a minute) and billing (must be exact). Cover ingestion, partitioning, duplicates, event time and late data, hot ads, exactly-once, storage for queries, and how you would recompute after a bug.

Reveal the answer

A strong answer ingests clicks into Kafka keyed by click_id for even spread; deduplicates by click_id with a TTL store; filters bots; aggregates in event time with 1-minute tumbling windows and a grace period; handles hot ads with salted two-stage aggregation; runs the stream job with exactly-once; writes results keyed by (ad, window) to a compacted topic and an OLAP store with upserts; archives raw clicks; and reconciles billing from raw data, recomputing with a fresh application ID or batch job after bugs.

C4.1Requirements

Functional

  • Count clicks per ad per minute; query by ad and time range; top ads in the last N minutes.
  • Billing totals per advertiser per day must be exact.

Non-functional

  • 1 billion clicks per day, peaks 5x average.
  • Dashboards fresh within about a minute.
  • Count each click once, even when clients retry and the pipeline restarts.

C4.2Estimates

Quantity Calculation Result
Average rate 1B / 86,400 about 11,600/s
Peak 5x about 60,000/s
Click event size IDs, timestamps, user agent, IP about 300 bytes
Peak ingest 60,000 x 300 B about 18 MB/s
Dedup state 1 h of IDs at average rate: 42M x about 50 B about 2 GB across instances (5x at peak)
Output active ads x 1 row per minute small, for example 500k rows/min

C4.3Topics and events

Topic Key Partitions Retention Notes
ad.clicks.v1 click_id 48 3 days Raw clicks; also archived to object storage
internal repartition topics ad_id + salt, then ad_id 48 Managed by Streams Created by groupBy
ad.counts.1m.v1 ad_id + window start 24 compacted Latest count per ad per minute
  • Key raw clicks by click_id: spreads load evenly and puts every duplicate of a click on the same partition, so deduplication is local.
  • Output keyed by (ad, window): writing a corrected count simply overwrites the old one, in the compacted topic and in the OLAP store.

C4.4High-level design

  1. Edge collectors receive clicks, attach a server timestamp and click_id, and produce to ad.clicks.v1 (acks=all, idempotent, lz4).
  2. A Kafka Streams or Flink job, with exactly-once processing:
    1. Filters bots (IP and device rate rules, deny lists).
    2. Deduplicates by click_id using a state store of IDs seen in the last hour.
    3. Re-keys by ad_id plus a salt (0 to 9) and pre-aggregates per 1-minute window.
    4. Re-keys by ad_id and sums the partial counts per window.
  3. Results go to ad.counts.1m.v1, which an OLAP store (Pinot, Druid, or ClickHouse) ingests with upsert by key.
  4. A sink archives raw clicks to object storage for billing reconciliation and recomputation.

C4.5Deep dives

Guided designDeep divesAnswer each before revealing
  1. 1
    Event time and late clicks

    A mobile client buffers clicks offline and sends them 90 seconds late. Which minute do they count in?

    Write your answer, then reveal

    The minute they happened: aggregate by event time (the click's timestamp, validated against the server time), not arrival time. A grace period of 2 minutes keeps each window open for late records, then closes it. Clicks later than the grace period are dropped by the window (and counted in a dropped-records metric); billing picks them up in the daily reconciliation from raw data.

  2. 2
    Deduplication

    Clients retry, so the same click arrives twice. How is it counted once?

    Write your answer, then reveal

    Every click gets a unique click_id at the source. Because raw clicks are keyed by click_id, duplicates land on the same partition and task, which keeps a store of IDs seen in the last hour and drops repeats. The store is backed by a changelog topic, so it survives restarts. Duplicates arriving more than an hour apart are rare and handled by reconciliation.

  3. 3
    Hot ads

    One viral ad gets 30% of all clicks. What happens if you key by ad_id?

    Write your answer, then reveal

    One partition and one task would take 30% of the load, and adding partitions would not help. Salt the key: ad_id plus a random or hashed salt from 0 to 9 spreads the ad over ten partitions for the first aggregation. The second stage, keyed by ad_id alone, only sums ten partial counts per window, which is cheap.

  4. 4
    Exactly-once

    The job crashes after updating state but before writing output. Do counts double?

    Write your answer, then reveal

    Not with exactly-once processing (processing.guarantee=exactly_once_v2 in Kafka Streams, or Flink checkpoints with a transactional Kafka sink). Input offsets, state changelog writes, and output records commit atomically, so a restart resumes from the last committed point. The OLAP store sits outside that transaction, which is why output is keyed by (ad, window) and loaded with upserts: a replayed result overwrites rather than adds.

  5. 5
    Freshness versus final counts

    Dashboards want updates every few seconds; billing wants the final number once.

    Write your answer, then reveal

    Dashboards can take intermediate updates as the window fills (with record caching to reduce churn). Billing needs final values: suppress output until the window closes (suppress(untilWindowCloses) or emitStrategy(onWindowClose) in Kafka Streams), or compute billing from the closed windows plus daily reconciliation against raw clicks.

  6. 6
    Recomputing after a bug

    A filter bug overcounted for two days.

    Write your answer, then reveal

    Fix the code, then reprocess from Kafka (3 days retention) with a new application ID writing to a new output version, or run a batch job over the archived raw clicks. Because output keys are (ad, window), loading corrected rows overwrites the bad ones. Compare totals with the old output before switching readers.

C4.6Failures and bottlenecks

Failure Effect Mitigation
Hot ad One task overloaded Salted two-stage aggregation
Stream task restart Pause while state restores Standby replicas, compacted changelogs
Clock skew on devices Clicks in wrong minute or rejected Use server receive time when device time is implausible
Bot traffic Inflated counts Filter before counting; reconcile billing
OLAP ingestion down Dashboards stale, data safe Kafka retains output; OLAP catches up

C4.7What a strong answer shows

Interview signal

SDE-2: event time with tumbling windows and grace, dedup by click ID, exactly-once processing, hot key salting, keyed upserts into a query store. Senior adds: the boundary of exactly-once (Kafka to Kafka) and idempotent loading beyond it, final versus intermediate results, reconciliation for billing, reprocessing strategy, and state size and restore time.

C4.8Follow-up questions

PracticeAnswer out loud, then reveal
  1. Why not key raw clicks by ad_id from the start?
    Reveal

    Hot ads would overload single partitions, and deduplication by click_id would still need all copies of a click together. Keying by click_id gives even load and local dedup; re-keying later is a cheap repartition.

  2. Could the OLAP store do all of this itself?
    Reveal

    Real-time OLAP stores can ingest raw clicks from Kafka and aggregate at query time or with rollups. That removes the stream job but makes deduplication, bot filtering, and exact billing harder. Many systems do both: OLAP on raw data for exploration, a stream job for trusted counts.

  3. How big should the grace period be?
    Reveal

    Look at the distribution of lateness (arrival time minus event time). A grace covering p99.9 keeps dropped clicks rare; longer grace delays final results and keeps more windows in state.

  4. What if the business wants hourly and daily counts too?
    Reveal

    Roll up from the minute counts (in the stream job or the OLAP store) rather than recounting raw clicks.
