Case study 5Starter35 min

Case study 5: Centralized log pipeline

Thousands of pods write logs. Engineers need to search the last week in seconds, compliance needs a year of history, and a logging spike from one buggy service must not take down search for everyone else.

Uses: M4 compression, M6 keyless records, M16 Connect, M20 quotas
Your status

On this page

  1. C5.1Requirements
  2. C5.2Estimates
  3. C5.3Topics and events
  4. C5.4High-level design
  5. C5.5Deep dives
  6. C5.6Failures and bottlenecks
  7. C5.7What a strong answer shows
  8. C5.8Follow-up questions
Try it first35 minutes, on paper, before reading

Design a pipeline that collects logs from 5,000 pods and makes them searchable within seconds, keeps a year of history cheaply, and alerts on error spikes. Cover collection, topic layout, keys, compression, retention, sinks, protecting the cluster from noisy services, sensitive data, and what happens when search is slow.

Reveal the answer

A strong answer uses node agents with disk buffers that produce to Kafka with no key, lz4 or zstd compression, and large batches; splits topics by team or tier for retention, ACLs, and quotas; keeps a few days in Kafka as a buffer; uses Connect sinks to a search cluster (short retention) and object storage (long retention) with idempotent writes; adds a small stream job for error-rate alerts; scrubs secrets and personal data at the agent; and relies on Kafka to absorb spikes and sink outages.

C5.1Requirements

Functional

  • Collect application logs from all pods; search the last 7 days by service, time, level, and text.
  • Keep all logs for 1 year at low cost; alert when a service's error rate spikes.

Non-functional

  • Searchable within about 30 seconds of being written.
  • Survive a search cluster outage of several hours without losing logs.
  • Losing a few log lines in rare failures is acceptable; losing hours is not.

C5.2Estimates

Quantity Calculation Result
Lines per second 5,000 pods x 40 lines/s 200,000/s
Raw volume 200,000 x 400 B about 80 MB/s, about 7 TB/day
On the wire with lz4 text compresses about 4x about 20 MB/s
Kafka storage 7 TB / 4 x 3 days x RF 3 about 16 TB
Search (7 days hot) 7 TB x 7, plus index overhead about 50 TB or more
Archive (1 year) Parquet compresses about 10x about 250 TB in object storage

C5.3Topics and events

Topic Key Partitions Retention Notes
logs.<team> none 6 to 24, by volume 3 days One per team: own quota, ACLs, retention
logs.audit none 12 7 days acks=all, min.insync.replicas=2; stricter handling
logs.alerts service name 6 1 day Output of the alerting job
  • No key: log lines need no per-key order (search sorts by timestamp), so keyless records with the sticky partitioner build full batches and spread load evenly.
  • Per-team topics: one noisy team cannot change another team's retention, and quotas and ACLs map cleanly to teams.

C5.4High-level design

  1. An agent on each node (Fluent Bit or Vector) tails container logs, parses them to JSON, removes secrets and personal data, and produces to the team's topic with large batches (linger.ms 50 to 100, batch.size 256 KB or more) and lz4 compression. It buffers on local disk if Kafka is unreachable.
  2. Kafka keeps 3 days, so a sink can be down for a long weekend without losing data.
  3. Connect sinks write to OpenSearch (7 days) and to object storage as Parquet partitioned by date and team (1 year).
  4. A small stream job counts errors per service per minute and publishes alerts.
  5. Broker quotas cap each team's produce rate.

C5.5Deep dives

Guided designDeep divesAnswer each before revealing
  1. 1
    Why put Kafka in the middle?

    Agents could write straight to the search cluster. Why not?

    Write your answer, then reveal

    Search clusters ingest slowly under spikes and go down for upgrades. Kafka absorbs bursts, keeps days of buffer, and lets several consumers (search, archive, alerting, security tools) read the same data independently. Without it, every agent needs retry logic for every destination, and a slow destination backs up into the pods.

  2. 2
    Throughput settings

    What makes the producers efficient at 200,000 lines per second?

    Write your answer, then reveal

    Big batches and compression: linger.ms around 50 to 100 and a large batch.size let each request carry hundreds of KB, and lz4 (or zstd for better ratio) compresses whole batches about 4x. Keyless records use the sticky partitioner, which fills one batch at a time. acks=all with idempotence costs little at this batch size; for debug logs, acks=1 is an acceptable trade if you want lower latency.

  3. 3
    Noisy neighbors

    A buggy service logs 50 times its normal volume.

    Write your answer, then reveal

    Per-team produce quotas (producer_byte_rate per user or client ID) make the broker throttle that team instead of filling disks and slowing everyone. The agent's disk buffer absorbs the throttling, and an alert tells the team. Per-team topics also confine the extra retention cost.

  4. 4
    Sink outage

    OpenSearch is down for 6 hours.

    Write your answer, then reveal

    The sink connector's lag grows; Kafka still has the data (3 days). When search returns, the connector catches up, faster if you add tasks up to the partition count. Writes are idempotent if the document ID comes from topic, partition, and offset, so retries after the outage overwrite instead of duplicating.

  5. 5
    Sensitive data

    A service logs full request bodies with card numbers and tokens.

    Write your answer, then reveal

    Scrub at the agent, before data leaves the node: drop known secret fields and mask patterns such as card numbers and emails. Doing it later means the data already sits in Kafka, backups, and every consumer. Add ACLs so only the sinks and the security team read raw logs, and keep logs.audit separate.

  6. 6
    Alerting on error spikes

    How do you page on a service whose error rate jumps?

    Write your answer, then reveal

    A Kafka Streams or Flink job filters level=ERROR, counts per service in 1-minute windows, compares with a baseline, and publishes to logs.alerts, which an alert manager consumes. Small state and simple logic; it does not need exactly-once, since an occasional double count does not change an alert.

C5.6Failures and bottlenecks

Failure Effect Mitigation
Search cluster slow or down Search lag grows Kafka buffer (3 days), catch up with more tasks
Log storm from one service Broker load, disk use Quotas, per-team topics, agent sampling of debug logs
Broker failure Brief failover RF 3; keyless records route around unavailable partitions
Agent cannot reach Kafka Logs pile up on nodes Disk buffer with a size cap; drop oldest debug logs first
Malformed lines Indexing errors Connect errors.tolerance=all with a DLQ topic

C5.7What a strong answer shows

Interview signal

Starter level: Kafka as a buffer between many producers and slow sinks, keyless records with batching and compression, retention as a safety margin, Connect sinks for search and archive. SDE-2 adds: quotas and per-team topics, idempotent sink writes, scrubbing at the source, separate handling for audit logs, and capacity numbers for each layer.

C5.8Follow-up questions

PracticeAnswer out loud, then reveal
  1. Would you use the same pipeline for metrics?
    Reveal

    Usually not. Metrics are small, numeric, and queried by time series databases; Prometheus-style scraping or remote write is simpler. Kafka helps for metrics only at very large scale or when many consumers need the raw stream.

  2. Why only 3 days in Kafka if search keeps 7?
    Reveal

    Kafka is the buffer, not the store. 3 days covers sink outages and replays; search and object storage hold the long-term copies more cheaply.

  3. How would you reduce cost?
    Reveal

    Drop or sample debug logs at the agent, shorten hot search retention, use zstd, and query older logs from object storage with a lake engine instead of keeping them in search.

  4. Should you key by pod to keep each pod's lines in order?
    Reveal

    Usually no. Timestamps order lines at query time, and pod keys make busy pods hot partitions. Key by pod only if a consumer truly needs per-pod sequence.

Case study 6Core40 min

Case study 6: Change data capture to search and cache

A product catalog lives in PostgreSQL. Search, the cache, and a product view API must reflect every change within seconds, without the application writing to four systems, and the search index must be rebuildable at any time.

Uses: M16 Debezium, M13 compaction, M17 tables, M17 joins
Your status

On this page

  1. C6.1Requirements
  2. C6.2Estimates
  3. C6.3Topics and events
  4. C6.4High-level design
  5. C6.5Deep dives
  6. C6.6Failures and bottlenecks
  7. C6.7What a strong answer shows
  8. C6.8Follow-up questions
Try it first40 minutes, on paper, before reading

Keep a search index, a Redis cache, and a denormalized product view in sync with a PostgreSQL catalog. Cover how changes are captured, topic configuration, deletes, ordering and stale writes, rebuilding the index from scratch, joining two tables, schema changes, and operating the database side.

Reveal the answer

A strong answer uses Debezium to stream row changes into compacted topics keyed by primary key; has independent consumers for search (upsert, delete on delete events) and cache (evict or versioned set); uses source versions (LSN) to reject stale writes; rebuilds search by replaying the compacted topic into a new index and swapping an alias; joins products and stock with a table-table join; handles schema evolution through the registry; and watches replication slot lag. It also notes that raw CDC couples consumers to the table schema, and uses an outbox for events meant for other teams.

C6.1Requirements

Functional

  • Search reflects product changes (name, price, description, availability) within seconds.
  • The cache never serves data older than a few seconds after a change.
  • A product view combining product and stock is available to APIs.
  • Rebuild the search index from scratch without downtime.

Non-functional

  • 50 million products; 2,000 changes per second on average, 5,000 at peak (mostly stock).
  • No dual writes in application code.

C6.2Estimates

Quantity Calculation Result
Change rate stock and price updates 2,000/s average, 5,000/s peak
Change event size Debezium envelope with before and after about 2 KB
Peak throughput 5,000 x 2 KB about 10 MB/s
Compacted products topic 50M x about 2 KB about 100 GB per replica
Full reindex 50M documents at 20,000/s about 45 minutes

C6.3Topics and events

Topic Key Partitions Cleanup Notes
shop.public.products id 24 compact Debezium names topics <prefix>.<schema>.<table>
shop.public.stock product_id 24 compact Same partition count as products, for the join
product_view.v1 product_id 24 compact Output of the join, read by APIs
  • Compacted: the topic always holds the latest change for every row, so a new consumer can rebuild full state by reading from the beginning. Deletes become tombstones that compaction eventually removes.
  • Keyed by primary key: all changes to one row are in one partition, in commit order.

C6.4High-level design

  1. Debezium (on Kafka Connect) takes an initial snapshot of the tables, then reads the write-ahead log through a replication slot and publishes each committed row change.
  2. The search indexer consumes products, upserts documents by id, and deletes documents on delete events.
  3. The cache updater evicts (or sets) Redis keys per change.
  4. A Kafka Streams job joins products and stock as tables and writes product_view.v1, which APIs read or which feeds another store.

C6.5Deep dives

Guided designDeep divesAnswer each before revealing
  1. 1
    Why CDC instead of application writes?

    The service could update the database, then Elasticsearch, then Redis.

    Write your answer, then reveal

    That is the dual-write problem three times: a crash or failure between writes leaves systems inconsistent, and every service that writes products must remember all of it. CDC reads the database's own log, so every committed change is captured once, in commit order, and nothing in the application changes when you add a consumer.

  2. 2
    Deletes

    A product is deleted. How does it leave search and the cache?

    Write your answer, then reveal

    Debezium emits a delete event (with the old row in before) and, by default, a tombstone (same key, null value). Consumers treat either as "remove this key": delete the search document, evict the cache key. In the compacted topic the tombstone stays for delete.retention.ms (1 day by default) so consumers have time to see it, then disappears.

  3. 3
    Stale writes

    During a replay or a retry, an older version of a product reaches the index after a newer one.

    Write your answer, then reveal

    Within a partition, order is preserved, but replays and parallel workers can still apply old data late. Use the change's source position (the PostgreSQL LSN, or an updated_at version column) as an external version: the index rejects writes with a lower version than it holds (OpenSearch and Elasticsearch support version_type=external). For Redis, evicting instead of setting avoids the problem entirely; reads repopulate from the database.

  4. 4
    Rebuilding search

    A new analyzer requires a full reindex, with no downtime.

    Write your answer, then reveal

    Create products_v2, start a new consumer group on shop.public.products from the earliest offset, and index everything. Because the topic is compacted, this is the full current catalog plus recent changes, not years of history. When the new group's lag reaches near zero, point the products alias at products_v2, then stop the old indexer and drop the old index.

  5. 5
    Joining products and stock

    APIs want price and availability in one document.

    Write your answer, then reveal

    In Kafka Streams, read both topics as KTables and join on the product ID; both topics have the same key and partition count, so the join is local per partition. Each change to either side emits an updated view. If the key differed (stock keyed by warehouse and SKU), you would re-key first or use a foreign-key table join.

  6. 6
    Schema changes

    A developer adds a column, another renames one.

    Write your answer, then reveal

    Debezium registers the new value schema; with Avro and a registry, adding a nullable column is backward compatible and consumers carry on. A rename is a drop plus an add, which breaks consumers expecting the old field. Raw CDC exposes the table design to every consumer, so keep it for internal read models and publish curated events through an outbox for other teams.

  7. 7
    The database side

    The connector stops for a weekend.

    Write your answer, then reveal

    The replication slot keeps WAL until Debezium confirms it, so the database disk fills. Alert on slot lag, set max_slot_wal_keep_size as a safety limit (accepting a re-snapshot if exceeded), and configure heartbeats (heartbeat.interval.ms) so the slot advances even when the captured tables are quiet.

C6.6Failures and bottlenecks

Failure Effect Mitigation
Connector down Search and cache go stale; WAL grows Slot lag alerts, quick restart, WAL size cap
Search cluster slow Indexer lag; search is stale Bulk requests, more partitions and tasks, lag alerts in seconds
Stale write after replay Older data in index External versioning by LSN
Bulk update of 10M rows Burst of changes Kafka buffers it; indexer catches up; schedule big updates off-peak
Breaking schema change Consumers fail Registry compatibility checks; outbox for public events

C6.7What a strong answer shows

Interview signal

SDE-2: CDC instead of dual writes, compacted topics keyed by primary key, handling deletes and tombstones, idempotent upserts, rebuilding from the compacted topic with an alias swap. Senior adds: version-based rejection of stale writes, eviction versus setting for caches, co-partitioning for joins, slot and WAL operations, and when to prefer an outbox over raw CDC.

C6.8Follow-up questions

PracticeAnswer out loud, then reveal
  1. Why is reading a compacted topic from the beginning enough to rebuild the index?
    Reveal

    Compaction keeps at least the latest record for every key, so the topic contains the current state of every row (plus recent history), and deleted rows have been removed or appear as tombstones.

  2. Can the cache ever serve stale data?
    Reveal

    Briefly: between the database commit and the eviction (CDC lag, usually under a second), and when a read repopulates the cache just before an eviction arrives. Short TTLs bound the worst case.

  3. How do you add a new consumer that needs only the last week of changes?
    Reveal

    Start its group with auto.offset.reset set to by_duration:P7D, or reset offsets with --to-datetime. On a compacted topic, older updates may already have been compacted away.

  4. Why not query the database directly instead of keeping a read model?
    Reveal

    For simple reads, do. Read models help when queries need denormalized data, full-text search, or load the primary database cannot take.

Case study 7: Design a distributed log (Kafka itself)

The interviewer says "design Kafka". This tests whether you understand why Kafka works the way it does: partitioned append-only logs, sequential disk I/O, pull-based consumers, leader-follower replication with an in-sync set, and a separate metadata quorum.

Uses: M11 segments, M12 high watermark, M12 epochs, M3 KRaft
Your status

On this page

  1. C7.1Requirements
  2. C7.2Estimates
  3. C7.3High-level design
  4. C7.4Deep dives
  5. C7.5Failures and bottlenecks
  6. C7.6What a strong answer shows
  7. C7.7Follow-up questions
Try it first50 minutes, on paper, before reading

Design a durable, horizontally scalable, replayable message log. Cover the data model, the storage format on disk, how writes are replicated and acknowledged, failure handling and leader election, where metadata lives, the producer and consumer protocols, and how the system scales.

Reveal the answer

A strong answer partitions topics and orders only within a partition; stores each partition as segment files with sparse offset and time indexes; relies on sequential writes, the page cache, batching, and zero-copy reads; replicates by followers pulling from a leader, tracking an in-sync replica set and a high watermark; uses leader epochs to truncate divergent logs after failover; keeps metadata in a small Raft quorum; makes producers idempotent with producer IDs and sequence numbers; lets consumers pull and store their offsets in an internal compacted log; and scales by adding partitions and brokers, with tiered storage for long retention.

C7.1Requirements

Functional

  • Producers append records to named topics; consumers read from any position and replay.
  • Ordering per key; many independent consumer groups; records kept by time or size.

Non-functional

  • 1 GB/s writes, 3 GB/s reads; 3 days retention.
  • No acknowledged write lost when one machine fails; failover within seconds.
  • Horizontal scale by adding machines.

C7.2Estimates

Quantity Calculation Result
Disk writes with RF 3 1 GB/s x 3 3 GB/s across the cluster
Network in producers 1 GB/s + replication 2 GB/s 3 GB/s
Network out consumers 3 GB/s + replication 2 GB/s 5 GB/s
Storage 1 GB/s x 86,400 x 3 days x RF 3 about 780 TB
Brokers for storage 780 TB / 12 TB usable each about 65
Brokers for throughput about 300 MB/s in and 500 MB/s out each about 10 to 15

Storage, not throughput, sets the broker count here. Tiered storage (old segments in object storage) would let 15 to 20 brokers do the job.

C7.3High-level design

  • Topics and partitions: a topic is split into partitions; each partition is an ordered, append-only log on one leader broker with followers on other brokers. Keys hash to partitions.
  • Brokers: store partitions, serve produce and fetch requests, replicate from leaders.
  • Controller quorum: 3 or 5 nodes running Raft; holds the metadata log (topics, partitions, leaders, ISRs, configs) and elects partition leaders.
  • Clients: producers batch by partition and send to leaders; consumers pull from leaders (or nearby followers) and commit offsets.

C7.4Deep dives

Guided designDeep divesAnswer each before revealing
  1. 1
    Storage on disk

    How is a partition stored so that writes and reads are fast?

    Write your answer, then reveal

    A directory of segment files. Writes append to the active segment, which is sequential I/O that disks and the page cache handle very well. Each segment has a sparse offset index (an entry every 4 KB of data) and a time index, so finding an offset is a binary search plus a short scan. Retention deletes whole old segments, which is cheap. Records are stored in the same batch format producers send, so brokers do not re-encode them, and reads use sendfile to copy from page cache to socket without passing through the application (zero-copy, when TLS is not used).

  2. 2
    Replication and acknowledgement

    When is a write safe to acknowledge?

    Write your answer, then reveal

    Followers fetch from the leader like consumers. The leader tracks which replicas are caught up (the in-sync replica set, ISR; a replica falls out after replica.lag.time.max.ms). The high watermark is the highest offset every ISR member has; consumers only see records below it. With acks=all, the leader answers once all current ISR members have the record, and refuses writes if the ISR is smaller than min.insync.replicas. With RF 3 and min ISR 2, any single failure loses no acknowledged write.

  3. 3
    Why an ISR and not a majority quorum per write?

    Raft would need a majority. What is the trade-off?

    Write your answer, then reveal

    To survive f failures, a majority quorum needs 2f + 1 replicas; an ISR needs f + 1 (every acknowledged write is on every in-sync replica, so any of them can lead). The cost: a write waits for the slowest in-sync replica until it is removed from the ISR, while a majority quorum ignores the slowest. Kafka uses ISR for data and Raft for metadata; some Kafka-compatible systems use Raft per partition instead.

  4. 4
    Failover and divergent logs

    The leader dies after appending records that followers had not copied.

    Write your answer, then reveal

    The controller notices missed heartbeats (broker.session.timeout.ms, 9 s by default) and picks a new leader from the ISR, bumping the leader epoch. The old leader's unreplicated tail was never below the high watermark, so it was never acknowledged with acks=all. When it returns, it asks the new leader where its epoch ended and truncates everything after that point before following. Electing a replica outside the ISR (unclean election) would lose acknowledged data, so it is off by default.

  5. 5
    Metadata

    Where do topic definitions, leaders, and ISRs live?

    Write your answer, then reveal

    In a replicated metadata log managed by a Raft quorum of controllers (KRaft). The active controller makes decisions and appends them; brokers replicate the log and keep metadata in memory, so any broker can tell clients who leads each partition. Keeping metadata separate and small makes failover fast even with hundreds of thousands of partitions.

  6. 6
    Producers

    How do producers achieve high throughput without duplicates on retry?

    Write your answer, then reveal

    They batch records per partition (batch.size, linger.ms), compress whole batches, and pipeline several requests per connection. For exactly-once appends, each producer gets a producer ID and numbers its batches per partition; the leader remembers the last sequence numbers and drops duplicates from retries, while still allowing up to 5 requests in flight with ordering preserved.

  7. 7
    Consumers

    Why pull instead of push, and where do offsets live?

    Write your answer, then reveal

    Pull lets each consumer go at its own pace, batch naturally, and rewind to replay; the broker stays simple and does not track per-message state. Long polling (fetch.min.bytes, fetch.max.wait.ms) avoids busy loops. A group coordinator assigns partitions to group members, and committed offsets are records in an internal compacted topic keyed by (group, topic, partition), so the latest commit per partition survives.

  8. 8
    Scaling and operations

    Traffic doubles. What do you do?

    Write your answer, then reveal

    Add brokers, then reassign some partition replicas onto them (throttled copying); add partitions to topics that need more parallelism, knowing that keys will map differently. Spread replicas across racks or zones. For long retention, move old segments to object storage so local disks hold only recent data.

C7.5Failures and bottlenecks

Failure Effect Mitigation
Broker crash Leaders on it move to ISR followers RF 3, min ISR 2, rack-aware placement
Slow follower Writes wait until it leaves the ISR replica.lag.time.max.ms, monitoring
Controller failure A standby controller takes over 3 or 5 controller quorum
Disk full Partitions go offline on that broker Retention by size and time, alerts, tiered storage
Too many partitions Slower failover, more memory Size partitions by throughput, not by habit

C7.6What a strong answer shows

Interview signal

SDE-2: partitioned append-only logs, segments and indexes, page cache and sequential I/O, leader-follower replication with ISR and high watermark, acks and min ISR, consumer offsets as data. Senior adds: ISR versus majority quorum, leader epochs and truncation, separate metadata quorum, idempotent producer sequence numbers, zero-copy and its limits with TLS, and storage-driven sizing with tiered storage.

C7.7Follow-up questions

PracticeAnswer out loud, then reveal
  1. Why does Kafka not fsync every write?
    Reveal

    Durability comes from replication: a write acknowledged with acks=all is in memory on several machines, which is unlikely to fail together. Flushing is left to the operating system for throughput; forcing fsync is possible but rarely worth it.

  2. How would you add exactly-once processing across partitions?
    Reveal

    Transactions: a coordinator writes transaction state to an internal log, and markers written to every involved partition commit or abort the records together; consumers with read_committed skip aborted ones.

  3. How would you support millions of topics?
    Reveal

    Partitions carry fixed costs (files, memory, metadata), so millions of tiny topics strain the design. Group them into fewer topics with a tenant field, or use a system built around many lightweight topics.

  4. Why is ordering only per partition?
    Reveal

    Total order would need one writer path for the whole topic, which caps throughput at one machine. Per-partition order scales, and keys give order where it matters.

Case study 8Core40 min

Case study 8: Delayed and scheduled jobs

Kafka delivers records as soon as they are written; it has no per-message delay. Yet teams need "retry in 10 minutes", "send a reminder in 3 days", and "charge the subscription on the 1st". This case shows the two patterns that work and why a single delay topic does not.

Uses: M10 retry topics, M10 pause and resume, M9 share groups, M14 outbox
Your status

On this page

  1. C8.1Requirements
  2. C8.2Estimates
  3. C8.3Topics and events
  4. C8.4High-level design
  5. C8.5Deep dives
  6. C8.6Failures and bottlenecks
  7. C8.7What a strong answer shows
  8. C8.8Follow-up questions
Try it first40 minutes, on paper, before reading

Design a service that runs jobs at a requested time, from seconds to months ahead: reminders, subscription renewals, retries. 10 million jobs are scheduled per day, jobs can be cancelled or rescheduled, and each must run once, within a few seconds of its due time. Where does Kafka fit, and where does it not?

Reveal the answer

A strong answer explains head-of-line blocking (one topic cannot hold arbitrary delays); uses delay tier topics for a few fixed delays, where each tier is ordered by due time and a consumer pauses until the head is due; uses a store indexed by due time plus pollers (FOR UPDATE SKIP LOCKED or time buckets) for arbitrary times; publishes due jobs to an execution topic consumed by idempotent workers (a share group fits); handles cancellation with a status check at run time; and plans for spikes at popular times such as midnight or the top of the hour.

C8.1Requirements

Functional

  • Schedule a job (type, payload, due time), cancel it, or reschedule it.
  • Recurring jobs (every month on the 1st).
  • Query job status.

Non-functional

  • 10 million new jobs per day; up to 100 million pending.
  • Run within about 5 seconds of the due time.
  • Each job runs at least once and has effect once (idempotent handlers).

C8.2Estimates

Quantity Calculation Result
New jobs 10M / 86,400 about 115/s
Pending jobs up to 100M x about 1 KB about 100 GB in the store
Due-time spike 1M renewals due at 00:00 on the 1st 1M jobs to dispatch at once
Dispatch rate needed 1M in about 2 minutes about 8,000/s

The spike matters more than the average: popular times cluster. Either the business accepts spreading (jitter within a window), or dispatch and workers must handle the burst.

C8.3Topics and events

Topic Key Partitions Notes
delay.1m, delay.10m, delay.1h original key 6 to 12 each Pattern A: fixed delay tiers
jobs.execute job_id 24 Due jobs to run, from either pattern
jobs.results job_id 12 Outcomes for status and auditing

C8.4High-level design

Why not one delay topic? A consumer reads a partition in order. If a record due next month sits ahead of one due in a minute, the second waits a month. This is head-of-line blocking, and it rules out arbitrary delays in a single topic.

Pattern A, delay tiers: every record in delay.10m has the same delay, so records are already ordered by due time (write time plus 10 minutes). The tier consumer looks at the head record: if it is due, it forwards it to jobs.execute (or back to the original topic); if not, it pauses the partition until it is due, still calling poll(). This is how retry topics work (Spring Kafka's @RetryableTopic does the same).

Pattern B, scheduler with a store: the API writes jobs to a database indexed by due_at. Pollers repeatedly claim due jobs and publish them to jobs.execute. Workers run them and report results.

C8.5Deep dives

Guided designDeep divesAnswer each before revealing
  1. 1
    When to use which

    Retries after 1, 10, and 60 minutes versus reminders at arbitrary times.

    Write your answer, then reveal

    A few fixed delays: tiers. Simple, all in Kafka, no database, ordered and cheap. Arbitrary times, long delays, cancellation, and queries: a store. Holding a job in Kafka for weeks means long retention and no way to cancel or query it. Many systems use both: tiers for retries, a scheduler for business schedules.

  2. 2
    Claiming due jobs safely

    Several poller instances run for availability. How do they avoid sending the same job twice?

    Write your answer, then reveal

    Each poller runs SELECT ... WHERE due_at <= now() AND status = 'scheduled' ORDER BY due_at LIMIT 500 FOR UPDATE SKIP LOCKED, publishes the batch, marks the rows enqueued, and commits. SKIP LOCKED lets pollers share work without blocking each other. A crash after publishing but before commit sends those jobs again later, so workers must be idempotent by job_id. To remove the gap, mark the rows and insert outbox rows in one transaction and let CDC publish (the outbox pattern).

  3. 3
    Scaling the store

    100 million pending jobs and 8,000 dispatches per second at midnight.

    Write your answer, then reveal

    Partition the jobs table by due time (for example by day), so the pollers touch only the current partition, and old partitions are dropped. Shard further by hash(job_id) with one poller per shard if one database is not enough. A key-value store keyed by (minute bucket, shard) works the same way: a poller reads the current bucket for its shard.

  4. 4
    Execution

    Who runs the job, and what if it fails?

    Write your answer, then reveal

    Workers consume jobs.execute. Jobs are independent, so a share group fits well: more workers than partitions, per-record acknowledgement, and a delivery attempt limit. A consumer group also works. Workers check that the job is still active, run it idempotently, and publish to jobs.results. Failures retry with delay tiers, then go to a DLT.

  5. 5
    Cancel and reschedule

    A user cancels a reminder 1 second before it is due.

    Write your answer, then reveal

    Mark the row cancelled (or update due_at to reschedule, with a version number). If the job was already published, the worker re-reads its status before running and skips it if cancelled or if the version does not match. Some jobs will be too late to cancel; the API reports that honestly.

  6. 6
    Recurring jobs

    Charge every subscription on the 1st of each month.

    Write your answer, then reveal

    Store the schedule rule; when a run is dispatched (or completes), compute the next due time and insert the next job in the same transaction. Each run gets its own job_id (for example subscription_id plus period), which also serves as the idempotency key for the charge.

  7. 7
    Precision and time

    How close to the due time does a job run?

    Write your answer, then reveal

    Poll interval (about a second) plus publish and consume latency, usually under a few seconds. Use database time (or a single trusted clock) for now(), not each poller's local clock. Monitor dispatch delay (now minus due_at at publish) and worker lag in seconds.

C8.6Failures and bottlenecks

Failure Effect Mitigation
Midnight spike Dispatch and workers saturated Jitter where allowed, pre-scaled workers, batch claims
Poller crash Jobs claimed but not committed are retried Transaction rollback; idempotent workers
Worker crash mid-job Job redelivered Idempotency by job_id; share group delivery limit
Database slow Dispatch delay grows Index on (status, due_at), partitioning, sharding
Long-delayed records in a tier Tier lag looks huge Measure lag as time behind due, not record count

C8.7What a strong answer shows

Interview signal

SDE-2: knows Kafka has no per-message delay and why one delay topic fails, delay tiers with pause until due, a store plus pollers with SKIP LOCKED, idempotent workers, cancellation through a status check. Senior adds: spikes at popular times, partitioning and sharding the store, outbox to close the publish gap, recurring jobs with per-run IDs, clock discipline, and meaningful lag metrics for delayed topics.

C8.8Follow-up questions

PracticeAnswer out loud, then reveal
  1. Could Kafka Streams act as the scheduler?
    Reveal

    Yes for some cases: keep pending jobs in a state store keyed by due time and use a wall-clock punctuator to emit due ones every second. It avoids a database, but cancellation, queries, and very long delays are harder than with a store.

  2. Why does the tier consumer pause instead of sleeping?
    Reveal

    Sleeping stops poll(), and after max.poll.interval.ms the consumer is removed from the group. Pausing keeps polling (and the group membership) while fetching nothing from that partition.

  3. How do you handle a job that must run exactly at 09:00:00?
    Reveal

    You cannot guarantee exact timing in a distributed system. Dispatch slightly early and let the worker wait until the exact time, and design the business process to tolerate seconds of delay.

  4. Can share groups delay redelivery?
    Reveal

    Not in Kafka 4.3: a released or timed-out record is offered again without a configurable delay (up to the delivery count limit), so share groups do not replace delay tiers or a scheduler.

Case study 9Stretch45 min

Case study 9: Multi-region disaster recovery

A payments platform runs in one region across three zones. The business now wants it to keep working if the whole region goes down, with at most a minute of lost events and back in service within 15 minutes. Design the Kafka side and the runbook.

Uses: M20 MirrorMaker 2, M12 zones, M10 idempotency, M14 outbox
Your status

On this page

  1. C9.1Requirements
  2. C9.2Estimates
  3. C9.3Topology
  4. C9.4High-level design
  5. C9.5Deep dives
  6. C9.6Failures and bottlenecks
  7. C9.7What a strong answer shows
  8. C9.8Follow-up questions
Try it first45 minutes, on paper, before reading

Extend an existing single-region Kafka platform (order and payment events, about 20,000 events/s) so it survives a full region outage. Cover the topology choice, how data and consumer positions reach the second region, what producers and consumers do during failover, duplicates and gaps, the databases behind the services, failing back, and how you prove it works.

Reveal the answer

A strong answer first separates zone failures (already handled by RF 3 across zones) from region failures; picks active-passive with MirrorMaker 2 running in the backup region, explaining why a stretch cluster costs too much latency; replicates topics, configs, ACLs, schemas, and consumer offsets; states the RPO as replication lag and keeps it visible; makes consumers idempotent because translated offsets cause duplicates; treats databases as the systems of record with their own replication and reconciliation; writes failover and failback runbooks with fencing; and rehearses them on a schedule.

C9.1Requirements

Functional

  • Keep accepting and processing order and payment events if the primary region is lost.
  • Resume consumers in the backup region close to where they stopped.
  • Return to the primary region after recovery without losing the writes made during the outage.

Non-functional

  • RPO (data loss on region loss): at most 60 seconds of events.
  • RTO (time to recover): 15 minutes.
  • Normal write latency unchanged (local, a few milliseconds).
  • No double charges after failover.

C9.2Estimates

Quantity Calculation Result
Event rate given about 20,000/s peak
Event size Avro about 2 KB
Cross-region replication 20,000 x 2 KB, compressed about 3x about 13 MB/s, about 1.1 TB/day of transfer
Replication lag budget RPO target well under 60 s; alert at 10 s
Checkpoint interval MirrorMaker 2 default 60 s (shorter for critical groups)
Inter-region round trip typical 20 to 60 ms

The round-trip time rules out synchronous replication for every write: a stretch cluster would add it to each acks=all produce.

C9.3Topology

Option RPO Write latency Verdict
Single cluster across zones (today) Region loss: everything Local Keep for zone failures
Stretch cluster across 3 regions 0 Plus a cross-region round trip per write Too slow and costly for 20,000/s; needs a third region for the controller majority
Active-passive with MirrorMaker 2 Replication lag (seconds) Local Chosen
Active-active with MirrorMaker 2 Seconds for the remote region's data Local Only if users must write in both regions; complicates every consumer

C9.4High-level design

  1. Producers and consumers run in the primary region against the primary cluster (RF 3 across zones, as today).
  2. MirrorMaker 2 runs in the backup region ("consume from remote, produce to local"), copying topics into prefixed remote topics (primary.orders) and syncing topic configs and ACLs.
  3. Checkpoints translate consumer group offsets; with sync.group.offsets.enabled the translated offsets are written into the backup cluster's __consumer_offsets for groups not running there.
  4. The schema registry and the service databases replicate to the backup region by their own mechanisms.
  5. Standby consumers and producers are deployed in the backup region but idle (or scaled to zero) until failover.

C9.5Deep dives

Guided designDeep divesAnswer each before revealing
  1. 1
    Why not a stretch cluster?

    Zero data loss sounds better. Why not one cluster across three regions?

    Write your answer, then reveal

    Every acks=all write would wait for in-sync replicas in other regions, adding tens of milliseconds to every produce, and every replica copy would cross a region boundary, which is the most expensive network path. It also needs a third region for the KRaft controller majority. It fits a small, critical stream where zero loss beats latency; for the whole platform, asynchronous replication with a seconds-long RPO is the usual trade.

  2. 2
    What exactly is replicated?

    List everything the backup region needs before a failover can work.

    Write your answer, then reveal

    Topic data (MirrorMaker 2 source connector), topic configs and ACLs (MirrorMaker 2 sync options), consumer group offsets (checkpoints and group offset sync), schemas with the same IDs (the registry must be replicated too, or deserialization fails), connector configs, client credentials and certificates, and the databases the services own. Missing any one of these is the classic surprise during a real failover.

  3. 3
    Running the failover

    The primary region is unreachable. Walk through the first 15 minutes.

    Write your answer, then reveal

    Declare the incident and fence the old region (stop its producers and relays if any part is still alive, so two regions never accept writes for the same data). Switch producers to the backup cluster through DNS or configuration; they write to local topics such as orders. Start consumers subscribed to both orders and primary.orders, from translated offsets. Watch lag, error rates, and DLTs. Communicate the RPO: events produced in the last seconds before the outage may be missing until the primary returns.

  4. 4
    Duplicates and gaps

    What do consumers see right after failover?

    Write your answer, then reveal

    Duplicates: translated offsets can be a little behind, so recent records are processed again. Idempotency by event ID (and unique constraints on effects like charges) makes that safe. Gaps: records not yet mirrored when the region died. They are not lost forever if the primary's disks survive; after recovery, reconcile by comparing event IDs or replaying the missing range from the old cluster.

  5. 5
    The databases behind the services

    The order service's outbox lives in PostgreSQL in the primary region. What happens to it?

    Write your answer, then reveal

    Kafka is not the system of record; the databases are. Replicate them to the backup region (asynchronous replicas, promoted on failover). After promotion, the outbox relay (Debezium) starts against the new primary database. Some outbox rows may be published twice (already mirrored, then relayed again), which idempotent consumers absorb. Daily reconciliation between the ledger and downstream projections catches anything else.

  6. 6
    Failing back

    The primary region is healthy again. Can you switch everything back now?

    Write your answer, then reveal

    No. The backup cluster holds writes the primary never saw. Start MirrorMaker 2 in the reverse direction, wait until lag is zero and checkpoints are current, then move producers back in a quiet window, then consumers from translated offsets, and finally restore the original replication direction. Fail back as deliberately as you failed over.

  7. 7
    Proving it works

    How do you know the runbook works before a real outage?

    Write your answer, then reveal

    Scheduled game days: fail over a non-critical service first, then the whole platform, measuring actual RPO (missing events) and RTO (time to healthy). Alert continuously on replication lag, checkpoint age, and MirrorMaker 2 task health, because a DR copy that silently stopped a week ago is worse than none.

C9.6Failures and bottlenecks

Failure Effect Mitigation
MirrorMaker 2 stalls RPO grows silently Alert on replication lag and checkpoint latency
Schemas not in backup Consumers cannot deserialize Replicate the registry with the same IDs; test it
Split brain (both regions writing) Conflicting updates Fence the old region before switching producers
Duplicate effects after failover Double charges Idempotency keys and unique constraints at the effect
Hot standby never exercised Failover fails on the day Game days, automated runbooks

C9.7What a strong answer shows

Interview signal

SDE-2: separates zone and region failures, chooses active-passive with MirrorMaker 2, explains offset translation and duplicates, and makes consumers idempotent. Senior adds: the stretch cluster trade-off and the third-region requirement, everything that must be replicated besides data, database promotion and outbox replay, fencing against split brain, failback through reverse replication, and game days with measured RPO and RTO.

C9.8Follow-up questions

PracticeAnswer out loud, then reveal
  1. Why run MirrorMaker 2 in the backup region rather than the primary?
    Reveal

    Consuming across the region boundary and producing locally keeps the writes, which need acknowledgements, on the low-latency side, and if the primary region dies the replication tooling is not lost with it.

  2. How would active-active change the consumers?
    Reveal

    Each region writes local topics and mirrors the other's under a prefix, so consumers read both (orders and other.orders) and must handle the same entity being updated in two regions, usually by giving each entity a home region or by merging with versions.

  3. Can you guarantee zero duplicates after failover?
    Reveal

    Not with asynchronous replication and translated offsets. Design for duplicates with idempotent consumers and unique constraints, and measure how many occur in game days.

  4. What would you monitor for the DR setup itself?
    Reveal

    Replication lag per topic, checkpoint latency, MirrorMaker 2 task failures, standby consumer readiness, schema registry replication, and the age of the last successful failover test.

Case study 10: Order saga with inventory reservation

Placing an order touches three services: reserve stock, authorize the payment, confirm the order, and undo the earlier steps if a later one fails. There is no distributed transaction, messages can be late or duplicated, and a payment can time out without saying whether it succeeded.

Uses: M14 outbox, M10 idempotency, M6 keys, C8 scheduled jobs
Your status

On this page

  1. C10.1Requirements
  2. C10.2Estimates
  3. C10.3Topics and events
  4. C10.4High-level design
  5. C10.5Deep dives
  6. C10.6Failures and bottlenecks
  7. C10.7What a strong answer shows
  8. C10.8Follow-up questions
Try it first40 minutes, on paper, before reading

Design checkout across an order service, an inventory service, and a payment service using Kafka. Cover choreography versus orchestration, the topics and keys, how each step is published reliably, compensations, timeouts and the "did the payment go through?" problem, late or duplicate messages, overselling during a flash sale, and how support finds a stuck order.

Reveal the answer

A strong answer uses an orchestrated saga: the order service keeps a state machine per order and sends commands through an outbox; participants reply on a replies topic; everything is keyed by order_id; every command and compensation is idempotent; timeouts come from a scheduler and resolve ambiguity by querying the payment provider with the same idempotency key before compensating; a compensation that arrives before its forward action leaves a marker so the late action becomes a no-op; inventory prevents overselling with conditional updates in its own database; and a saga table plus a stuck-saga alert make every order traceable.

C10.1Requirements

Functional

  • Checkout: create order (PENDING), reserve stock, authorize payment, confirm order (CONFIRMED).
  • If stock is unavailable: reject the order. If payment fails: release stock, cancel the order.
  • Users and support can see where an order is.

Non-functional

  • Never oversell; never charge for a cancelled order; no reservation stuck forever.
  • 2,000 orders per second during flash sales.
  • A slow payment provider must not block other orders.

C10.2Estimates

Quantity Calculation Result
Orders at peak given 2,000/s
Messages per order 2 commands, 2 replies, sometimes compensations about 5
Message rate 2,000 x 5 about 10,000/s
Message size small JSON or Avro about 1 KB
Open sagas 2,000/s x about 5 s average duration about 10,000 at once
Reservation expiry business rule 10 minutes

C10.3Topics and events

Topic Key Producer Consumer
inventory.commands.v1 order_id Order service (outbox) Inventory service
payment.commands.v1 order_id Order service (outbox) Payment service
order.saga.replies.v1 order_id Inventory and payment (outboxes) Order service
orders.events.v1 order_id Order service (outbox) Notifications, analytics
  • Commands (ReserveStock, ReleaseStock, AuthorizePayment, VoidPayment) have one owner each; replies (StockReserved, OutOfStock, PaymentAuthorized, PaymentDeclined) go back to the orchestrator; events announce outcomes to everyone else.
  • Key by order_id everywhere: a reserve and its release for the same order are in one partition, in order, and the orchestrator processes one order's replies in sequence.

C10.4High-level design

  1. The order service inserts the order (PENDING), a saga row (step = RESERVING), and a ReserveStock outbox row in one database transaction.
  2. Inventory reserves stock in its own database (with a conditional update) and replies through its outbox: StockReserved or OutOfStock.
  3. On StockReserved, the orchestrator moves to AUTHORIZING and sends AuthorizePayment; on OutOfStock, it cancels the order.
  4. On PaymentAuthorized, it confirms the order and publishes OrderConfirmed. On PaymentDeclined, it sends ReleaseStock and cancels.
  5. A scheduler fires a timeout if a step gets no reply in time.

C10.5Deep dives

Guided designDeep divesAnswer each before revealing
  1. 1
    Orchestration or choreography?

    Why not let each service react to the previous service's event?

    Write your answer, then reveal

    Choreography (inventory listens for OrderCreated, payment listens for StockReserved, inventory listens for PaymentDeclined) is fine for two steps. With more steps the workflow exists only as a web of subscriptions: nobody owns timeouts, and nobody can answer "why is this order stuck?". An orchestrator keeps the state machine in one place, makes compensations explicit, and gives support one table to look at.

  2. 2
    Publishing each step reliably

    The orchestrator updates the saga row and must send the next command. How do you avoid the dual-write problem?

    Write your answer, then reveal

    The saga state change and the outgoing command are written in the same database transaction, the command as an outbox row that CDC or a poller publishes. Participants do the same with their replies. Every hop is then at-least-once, so every handler must be idempotent.

  3. 3
    Idempotent steps

    ReserveStock for order 42 is delivered twice. What happens?

    Write your answer, then reveal

    Inventory records reservations keyed by order_id with a unique constraint: the second command finds the existing reservation and re-sends the same reply. The orchestrator also ignores replies that do not match the current step (a duplicate StockReserved while already AUTHORIZING changes nothing). Payment uses order_id as the provider's idempotency key, so a retried authorization cannot charge twice.

  4. 4
    The ambiguous timeout

    AuthorizePayment was sent 30 seconds ago and nothing came back. Release the stock and cancel?

    Write your answer, then reveal

    Not blindly: the payment may have succeeded, and cancelling would leave a charge on a cancelled order. On timeout, the orchestrator asks the payment service for the status of that order_id (which asks the provider using the same idempotency key). Authorized: continue. Declined or never received: compensate. Still unknown: retry the query with backoff, then void the authorization if it appears later. Timeouts come from a scheduler (a store of due times), not from sleeping threads.

  5. 5
    Late and reordered messages

    A timeout triggered ReleaseStock, and then the original ReserveStock arrives late (for example after a retry from the outbox relay). What protects you?

    Write your answer, then reveal

    Both are keyed by order_id, so within the topic they arrive in the order they were published. If a release still overtakes a reserve (for example after a replay), inventory records a CANCELLED marker for that order when it releases something it never reserved, so the late reserve sees the marker and does nothing. Compensations must be safe to run before, after, or twice relative to their forward action.

  6. 6
    Overselling in a flash sale

    10,000 orders for 500 units of one SKU arrive in a minute. How does inventory avoid overselling, and is that SKU a hot key?

    Write your answer, then reveal

    Kafka is keyed by order_id, so load spreads across partitions; correctness lives in the inventory database: UPDATE stock SET reserved = reserved + :q WHERE sku = :sku AND total - reserved >= :q, and zero updated rows means out of stock. The single SKU row becomes a contention point, so very hot items can split stock into several buckets (rows) or use an atomic counter in a fast store, reconciled with the database. Reservations carry an expiry so abandoned ones return to stock.

  7. 7
    Finding a stuck order

    A customer says their order has shown "Processing" for an hour.

    Write your answer, then reveal

    The saga table holds the current step, last update time, and history per order. A job alerts on sagas older than their step's timeout, and an admin action can retry the step or compensate. Trace IDs in message headers connect the order's messages across services in tracing tools.

C10.6Failures and bottlenecks

Failure Effect Mitigation
Payment provider slow Sagas wait; reservations held Timeouts with status queries; reservation expiry
Duplicate commands or replies Double reservation or charge Idempotency keys, unique constraints, state checks
Release before reserve Stock leaked CANCELLED marker makes the late reserve a no-op
Hot SKU Row contention in inventory Stock buckets or atomic counters with reconciliation
Orchestrator down Sagas pause Stateless instances over the saga table; resume from state on restart

C10.7What a strong answer shows

Interview signal

SDE-2: orchestrated saga with an explicit state machine, outbox for every step, keys by order_id, idempotent commands and compensations, and no distributed transaction. Senior adds: ambiguous timeouts resolved by status queries with idempotency keys, compensations that commute with late forward actions, reservation expiry and hot-SKU contention, and operability through a saga table and stuck-saga alerts.

C10.8Follow-up questions

PracticeAnswer out loud, then reveal
  1. Why not use Kafka transactions across the three services?
    Reveal

    Each service changes its own database; Kafka transactions only make Kafka writes and offsets atomic. Local transactions plus outboxes and idempotent handlers are what make each step reliable.

  2. Should commands go through Kafka at all, or be direct calls?
    Reveal

    Either works. Kafka commands decouple the orchestrator from participant availability and give buffering and replay; direct calls give immediate answers but need their own retries. Many systems call payment synchronously and use Kafka for everything else.

  3. How do you show the user a result quickly if the saga is asynchronous?
    Reveal

    Return the order as PENDING immediately and push or poll the final status; most sagas finish in seconds, and the UI shows "Processing" with a clear final state.

  4. How would you add a new step, such as a fraud check, without breaking orders in flight?
    Reveal

    Version the saga definition: orders started on the old version finish on it, new orders use the new state machine, and the orchestrator handles both until old sagas drain.

Producer settings

Setting Default Change it when
acks all Rarely. 1 only for data you can afford to lose
enable.idempotence true Keep on. It is silently turned off if you set acks other than all or retries=0 without setting it explicitly
retries Integer.MAX_VALUE Leave it; bound retrying with delivery.timeout.ms
delivery.timeout.ms 120000 (2 min) Total time for a send, including retries. Must be at least linger.ms + request.timeout.ms
request.timeout.ms 30000 Rarely
max.in.flight.requests.per.connection 5 Keep at most 5 with idempotence (larger values are rejected unless idempotence is disabled)
batch.size 16384 (16 KB) Raise to 64 to 256 KB for throughput
linger.ms 5 (since 4.0; 0 before) 10 to 100 for throughput; 0 for lowest latency
compression.type none lz4 or zstd for most workloads
buffer.memory 33554432 (32 MB) Raise for many partitions or large bursts
max.block.ms 60000 How long send() may block on a full buffer or missing metadata
max.request.size 1048576 (1 MB) Large records (raise the topic's max.message.bytes too)
retry.backoff.ms / retry.backoff.max.ms 100 / 1000 Rarely
partitioner.ignore.keys false Only if you do not need per-key order
transactional.id none Set for transactions; must be stable per producer instance
transaction.timeout.ms 60000 Long transactions (broker cap: transaction.max.timeout.ms, 15 min)

Consumer settings

Setting Default Change it when
group.id none Required for subscribe and commits
group.protocol classic consumer to use the new protocol (KIP-848, Kafka 4.0+ brokers)
enable.auto.commit true Set false and commit after processing (Spring does this for you)
auto.commit.interval.ms 5000 Rarely
auto.offset.reset latest earliest for pipelines that must see all data; by_duration:PT1H style since 4.0; none to fail loudly
max.poll.records 500 Lower if processing a batch can exceed max.poll.interval.ms
max.poll.interval.ms 300000 (5 min) Max time between poll() calls before the member is removed
session.timeout.ms 45000 Classic protocol only; with the new protocol the broker's group.consumer.session.timeout.ms (45 s) applies
heartbeat.interval.ms 3000 Classic protocol only; new protocol uses the broker's group.consumer.heartbeat.interval.ms (5 s)
fetch.min.bytes / fetch.max.wait.ms 1 / 500 Raise fetch.min.bytes for throughput
max.partition.fetch.bytes 1048576 (1 MB) Large records
fetch.max.bytes 52428800 (50 MB) Rarely
isolation.level read_uncommitted read_committed when reading transactional output
partition.assignment.strategy [RangeAssignor, CooperativeStickyAssignor] Classic protocol: CooperativeStickyAssignor alone for incremental rebalances
group.instance.id none Static membership: avoid rebalances on restarts
client.rack none Fetch from the closest replica (with a broker replica selector)

Broker and topic settings

Setting (topic-level name) Default Notes
log.retention.hours (retention.ms) 168 h (7 days) -1 means forever
log.retention.bytes (retention.bytes) -1 Per partition
log.segment.bytes (segment.bytes) 1 GiB Retention deletes whole segments
log.roll.hours (segment.ms) 168 h Lower it for faster retention or compaction on quiet topics
log.cleanup.policy (cleanup.policy) delete compact or compact,delete
min.insync.replicas 1 Set 2 with RF 3 for important topics
default.replication.factor 1 Set 3 in production
num.partitions 1 Default for auto-created topics
auto.create.topics.enable true Turn off in production
unclean.leader.election.enable false Keep off unless availability beats data
replica.lag.time.max.ms 30000 When a follower leaves the ISR
message.max.bytes (max.message.bytes) 1048588 Largest record batch accepted
compression.type producer Keep the producer's codec
delete.retention.ms 86400000 (1 day) How long tombstones stay in compacted topics
min.cleanable.dirty.ratio 0.5 Compaction trigger
message.timestamp.after.max.ms 3600000 (1 h, since 4.0) Rejects records timestamped too far in the future
offsets.retention.minutes 10080 (7 days) Committed offsets of empty groups expire after this
group.initial.rebalance.delay.ms 3000 Waits for more members before the first classic rebalance
broker.session.timeout.ms 9000 Controller fences a broker that stops heartbeating

Spring for Apache Kafka defaults

Behavior Default
Offset commits AckMode.BATCH: after all records from a poll are processed; Kafka auto-commit is turned off
Error handler DefaultErrorHandler: 10 attempts with no delay, then log and skip
Dead letter destination DeadLetterPublishingRecoverer: <topic>-dlt, same partition (3.3+; <topic>.DLT before)
@RetryableTopic 3 attempts, topics suffixed -retry and -dlt
JSON (de)serializers JacksonJsonSerializer and JacksonJsonDeserializer in 4.x (JsonSerializer and JsonDeserializer are deprecated)

Delivery recipes

Goal Producer Consumer
At-most-once acks=0 or 1 Commit before processing
At-least-once acks=all, idempotence on Auto-commit off, commit after processing
Effectively once into a database acks=all, idempotence on Idempotent writes, or store offsets in the same database transaction
Exactly-once, Kafka to Kafka transactional.id, sendOffsetsToTransaction isolation.level=read_committed
Exactly-once in Kafka Streams processing.guarantee=exactly_once_v2 Handled by Streams
Database change plus event Transactional outbox and CDC Idempotent consumers

Command line

Run from /opt/kafka/bin in the container, adding --bootstrap-server localhost:9092 (and --command-config for secured clusters).

Topics
kafka-topics.sh --list
kafka-topics.sh --describe --topic orders
kafka-topics.sh --create --topic orders --partitions 12 --replication-factor 3 --config min.insync.replicas=2
kafka-topics.sh --alter --topic orders --partitions 24          # keys will move
kafka-topics.sh --describe --under-replicated-partitions
kafka-topics.sh --describe --under-min-isr-partitions
kafka-configs.sh --describe --entity-type topics --entity-name orders
kafka-configs.sh --alter --entity-type topics --entity-name orders --add-config retention.ms=259200000
kafka-get-offsets.sh --topic orders --time latest               # or earliest, or a timestamp in ms
Produce and consume
kafka-console-producer.sh --topic orders --reader-property parse.key=true --reader-property key.separator=:
kafka-console-consumer.sh --topic orders --from-beginning \
  --formatter-property print.key=true --formatter-property print.partition=true --formatter-property print.offset=true
kafka-console-consumer.sh --topic orders --partition 3 --offset 1200 --max-messages 5
kafka-console-share-consumer.sh --topic jobs --group workers
Consumer groups
kafka-consumer-groups.sh --list
kafka-consumer-groups.sh --describe --group billing              # lag per partition
kafka-consumer-groups.sh --describe --group billing --members --verbose
kafka-consumer-groups.sh --describe --group billing --state
kafka-consumer-groups.sh --group billing --topic orders --reset-offsets --to-datetime 2026-10-17T00:00:00.000 --dry-run
kafka-consumer-groups.sh --group billing --topic orders --reset-offsets --to-earliest --execute   # group must be empty
kafka-consumer-groups.sh --group billing --topic orders:3 --reset-offsets --shift-by 1 --execute  # skip one record
kafka-share-groups.sh --describe --group workers --members
Cluster
kafka-metadata-quorum.sh --bootstrap-server localhost:9092 describe --status
kafka-metadata-quorum.sh --bootstrap-server localhost:9092 describe --replication
kafka-features.sh --bootstrap-server localhost:9092 describe
kafka-log-dirs.sh --describe --topic-list orders
kafka-leader-election.sh --election-type preferred --all-topic-partitions
kafka-reassign-partitions.sh --reassignment-json-file plan.json --execute --throttle 10000000
kafka-reassign-partitions.sh --reassignment-json-file plan.json --verify   # also removes the throttle
kafka-transactions.sh --bootstrap-server localhost:9092 list
kafka-dump-log.sh --files /tmp/kraft-combined-logs/orders-0/00000000000000000000.log --print-data-log
Performance tests
kafka-producer-perf-test.sh --topic bench --num-records 1000000 --record-size 512 --throughput -1 \
  --command-property acks=all --command-property linger.ms=20 --command-property compression.type=lz4
kafka-consumer-perf-test.sh --topic bench --num-records 1000000 --group bench-reader

What happens when

Assume RF 3 and min.insync.replicas=2 unless stated.

Event Producers Consumers
One broker down acks=all writes continue after leaders move Continue after leaders move
Two brokers down acks=all gets NotEnoughReplicasException (retried until delivery.timeout.ms); acks=1 writes are accepted No new records visible: the high watermark does not advance while ISR is below min ISR
Leader dies right after an acks=1 write Write may be lost; the old leader truncates it on return Never saw it
All replicas down Partition offline Wait for an in-sync (or eligible) replica to return
Consumer crashes after processing, before commit Records reprocessed: duplicates
Consumer commits, then crashes before processing Records skipped: loss
Processing exceeds max.poll.interval.ms Member removed; partitions reassigned; its commit fails
Committed offset deleted by retention auto.offset.reset decides where to start
Group empty for 7 days Offsets expire; auto.offset.reset applies on return
Producer retries without idempotence Duplicates, and reordering if more than 1 request in flight Sees duplicates
Producer buffer full send() blocks up to max.block.ms, then fails with TimeoutException

Errors you will meet

Error Meaning What to do
NotEnoughReplicasException ISR below min.insync.replicas for acks=all Retriable; find out why replicas are down or lagging
NotLeaderOrFollowerException Client metadata is stale Retriable; the client refreshes metadata
TimeoutException (producer) Not sent within delivery.timeout.ms or max.block.ms Check broker health, network, and buffer pressure
RecordTooLargeException Record exceeds max.request.size or max.message.bytes Raise both limits, compress, or store the payload elsewhere
SerializationException Serializer failed Not retriable; fix data or schema
RecordDeserializationException Consumer cannot deserialize a record Poison pill: it carries partition and offset, so skip or dead-letter it (ErrorHandlingDeserializer in Spring)
CommitFailedException Commit after the member was removed from the group Shorten processing per poll or raise max.poll.interval.ms
RebalanceInProgressException Commit during a rebalance Poll again, then commit
ProducerFencedException Another producer took over the transactional.id Fatal: close this producer
OutOfOrderSequenceException Broker saw a sequence gap from an idempotent producer Fatal for the producer; investigate data loss on the broker side
UnknownTopicOrPartitionException Topic does not exist Create it; check the name and auto-creation settings
TopicAuthorizationException, GroupAuthorizationException ACL missing Grant the right operation to the principal
WakeupException You called consumer.wakeup() Expected during shutdown; close the consumer

Rules of thumb

  • Partitions: enough for peak throughput and consumer parallelism with growth headroom; changing the count later remaps keys. Use counts with many divisors (6, 12, 24, 48).
  • Replication: RF 3, min.insync.replicas=2, acks=all, unclean election off, replicas spread across zones.
  • Consumers per group: at most the partition count (except share groups).
  • Lag: alert on lag in time or on growth, not on a fixed record count.
  • Record size: keep records small (KBs); store large payloads in object storage and send a reference.
  • Controllers: 3 (or 5) KRaft controllers; brokers scale independently.
