Kafka in interviews

Where Kafka comes up in SDE-2 interviews, how to use it well in a design round, how to talk about your own Kafka work, and a bank of questions with answers to rehearse out loud.

On this page

  1. Where Kafka comes up
  2. Using Kafka in a design round
  3. Decode any prompt
  4. Talking about your own Kafka work
  5. Question bank: fundamentals
  6. Question bank: producers
  7. Question bank: consumers and groups
  8. Question bank: delivery and transactions
  9. Question bank: replication and storage
  10. Question bank: design and operations
  11. Question bank: streams and ecosystem
  12. Question bank: scenarios
  13. Red flags

Where Kafka comes up

  • System design rounds: any design with asynchronous work, fan-out, event-driven services, pipelines, or audit trails. You are expected to place Kafka well and defend the details, not just draw a box labelled "Kafka".
  • Deep-dive questions: "How does Kafka guarantee ordering?", "What happens when a broker dies?", "How do you get exactly-once?" These test whether you know the mechanism behind the claim.
  • Experience discussions: "Tell me about a system you built with Kafka" or "Describe an incident". Interviewers probe your decisions: keys, partitions, delivery semantics, failure handling, monitoring.
  • Coding rounds: rare. Occasionally a "design a message queue" or "implement a consumer with retries" exercise.

Using Kafka in a design round

Propose Kafka when you need durable, replayable, ordered (per key) streams consumed by several independent readers, or a buffer between producers and slower consumers. Prefer a simple queue or a direct call when you need request-response, per-message priority or delay, or tiny scale where Kafka's operational cost is not worth it.

Every time you draw Kafka, cover these five points in a sentence each:

Point Say
Topic and key "One topic of order events keyed by order_id, so each order's events stay in order."
Partitions "Peak 5,000 events/s; one consumer handles about 500/s, so at least 10; I will use 24 for growth."
Delivery semantics "acks=all, idempotent producer, at-least-once consumers that are idempotent by event ID."
Failures "Blocking retries for transient errors, a dead letter topic for poison records, alerts on lag in seconds."
Contract and retention "Avro with a schema registry, BACKWARD compatibility; 7 days retention, enough to replay after a bad deploy."
Interview signal

What separates answers: an SDE-2 answer names the key, the partition math, and the delivery guarantee, and handles duplicates. A senior answer also covers the dual-write problem (outbox), hot keys, rebalances, consumer lag in time, replay strategy, and the operational cost of each choice.

Decode any prompt

Most Kafka questions are a few recurring pressures in disguise. Train yourself to hear the signal and name the mechanism.

Signal in the prompt Pressure Name this
"Never lose a confirmed payment or order" Durability over write latency acks=all, RF 3, min.insync.replicas=2, unclean election off, outbox for database changes
"Events for the same X must stay in order" Per-entity ordering Key by X; idempotent producer; blocking retries or per-key parking for failures
"Never apply the same event twice" Effectively-once effects At-least-once commits plus idempotent writes (unique event ID, upserts, versions)
"Read from A, transform, write to B" Kafka-to-Kafka exactly-once Transactions with sendOffsetsToTransaction and read_committed, or Kafka Streams exactly_once_v2
"Write to the database and notify other services" Dual writes Transactional outbox with CDC or a poller
"Keep the latest state per entity", "rebuild a cache or index" Current state, replay Compacted topic keyed by entity ID; tombstones for deletes
"Calls an external API that sometimes fails" Head-of-line blocking Classify errors; retry topics and a DLT for some failures; pause and circuit breaker when the dependency is down
"One tenant or celebrity is half the traffic" Hot key Finer key if ordering allows; salting with two-stage aggregation; a separate lane for the big tenant
"Millions of events per second" Throughput Batching (linger.ms, batch.size), lz4 or zstd, partitions from per-partition and per-consumer rates
"Urgent messages must not wait behind bulk ones" Priority Separate topics and consumer pools per priority; Kafka has no message priority
"Run this in 10 minutes", "retry tomorrow" Delays Delay tiers or a scheduler with a store; Kafka has no per-message delay
"More workers than partitions; order does not matter" Queue semantics Share groups (Kafka 4.2+), or more partitions
"Consumers keep getting kicked out" Poll loop too slow Smaller max.poll.records, no blocking I/O in the loop, cooperative or KIP-848 rebalancing, static membership
"Must survive a region outage" Disaster recovery MirrorMaker 2 active-passive with translated offsets and idempotent consumers; stretch cluster only if zero loss beats latency
Guided designRapid drills: 60 seconds eachAnswer each before revealing
  1. 1
    Bank ledger with SMS alerts

    Every debit and credit must update the balance in order, never be lost or applied twice, and trigger an SMS. Key, durability, and consumers?

    Write your answer, then reveal

    Key by account_id so an account's entries stay ordered. Publish through an outbox from the ledger database; topic with RF 3 and min.insync.replicas=2, producer acks=all with idempotence. Two consumer groups (balance projector, SMS sender), both at-least-once and idempotent by entry ID, the SMS sender also by a notification ID.

  2. 2
    500,000 vehicle readings per second

    Cars send GPS and engine data every 5 seconds; alert within 3 seconds if engine temperature stays above a limit for three readings. Partitioning and processing?

    Write your answer, then reveal

    Key by vehicle_id so each car's readings are ordered and land in one task. Producers batch and compress (linger.ms around 20, lz4 or zstd). A Kafka Streams or Flink job keeps per-vehicle state in event time and emits alerts to an alerts topic; partitions sized from throughput per partition and per task.

  3. 3
    Price change to search and cache within a second

    A seller edits a price in PostgreSQL; search and Redis must follow. Why not write all three from the service, and what instead?

    Write your answer, then reveal

    Three writes can partly fail and leave systems out of sync. Use Debezium to stream row changes into a compacted topic keyed by product ID; one consumer group updates search with versioned upserts, another evicts cache keys. A new index is rebuilt by replaying the compacted topic.

  4. 4
    Webhooks to 10,000 merchants

    Some merchant endpoints are slow or down. What goes wrong with retrying inside the main poll loop, and what do you build?

    Write your answer, then reveal

    One dead endpoint blocks every merchant behind it on that partition and can exceed max.poll.interval.ms. Move failed deliveries to retry topics with growing delays and then a DLT, keep per-merchant rate limits and circuit breakers, and key by merchant so one merchant's webhooks stay ordered. A share group fits if ordering per merchant is not required.

Talking about your own Kafka work

Prepare two stories: one system you built or changed, and one incident. For each, be ready to answer:

  • Why Kafka and not a queue, a database table, or a direct call.
  • Topic and key design, partition count, and what you would change now.
  • Delivery guarantees: producer settings, commit strategy, and how duplicates are handled.
  • Failure handling: retries, dead letters, poison records, and what happens during a rebalance.
  • Observability: which metrics and alerts you used, and how you found the root cause.
  • Numbers: throughput, lag, latency, retention, number of consumers.

A useful shape for an incident: what users saw, how you detected it, what you checked first and why, the root cause, the fix, and what you changed so it cannot recur. Module 21 has incident walkthroughs to borrow the reasoning from.

Question bank: fundamentals

PracticeAnswer out loud, then reveal
  1. What is Kafka, in two sentences?
    Reveal

    A distributed, replicated, append-only log. Producers append records to partitioned topics, and any number of consumer groups read them independently at their own pace, from any retained position.

  2. How is Kafka different from a traditional message queue like RabbitMQ?
    Reveal

    A queue usually deletes a message once it is consumed and pushes messages to consumers. Kafka keeps records for a retention period regardless of consumption, consumers pull and track their own offsets, many groups can read the same data, and order is guaranteed per partition. Kafka 4.2+ also offers share groups for queue-style consumption.

  3. What guarantees ordering in Kafka?
    Reveal

    Records in one partition are stored and read in order. Records with the same key go to the same partition (while the partition count does not change), so ordering per key holds. There is no order across partitions.

  4. What is an offset?
    Reveal

    The position of a record within a partition, assigned by the partition leader when the record is appended. Consumers commit offsets to remember where they are.

  5. What is a consumer group?
    Reveal

    A set of consumers sharing a group.id. Each partition is assigned to one member, so the group splits the work; separate groups each get all the data.

  6. Why can't you have more active consumers than partitions in a group?
    Reveal

    Each partition goes to exactly one member of a consumer group, so extra members sit idle. Share groups are the exception: they hand out records, not partitions.

  7. What is KRaft?
    Reveal

    Kafka's built-in Raft-based metadata quorum. Controllers store cluster metadata in a replicated log and elect partition leaders. It replaced ZooKeeper, which was removed in Kafka 4.0.

  8. How long does Kafka keep data?
    Reveal

    Until retention removes it: by time (retention.ms, 7 days by default) or size (retention.bytes), deleting whole segments. Compacted topics keep the latest record per key instead.

Question bank: producers

PracticeAnswer out loud, then reveal
  1. What does acks control?
    Reveal

    When the leader answers a produce request: 0 never waits, 1 after the leader writes it, all after every in-sync replica has it. Combined with min.insync.replicas, acks=all decides how many copies exist before success.

  2. How does the idempotent producer prevent duplicates?
    Reveal

    The producer gets a producer ID and numbers each batch per partition. The leader remembers recent sequence numbers and discards a retried batch it already wrote, and rejects gaps, so retries cannot duplicate or reorder within a partition.

  3. What do batch.size and linger.ms do?
    Reveal

    Records are grouped per partition into batches up to batch.size bytes; linger.ms is how long the producer may wait to fill a batch. Bigger batches mean better throughput and compression, at a few milliseconds of latency.

  4. How does the default partitioner pick a partition?
    Reveal

    An explicit partition wins; otherwise a keyed record goes to murmur2(key bytes) % partitions; a keyless record sticks to one partition until a batch fills, then switches (adapting to slow brokers).

  5. What happens if you add partitions to a keyed topic?
    Reveal

    New records for many keys map to different partitions, so per-key ordering breaks across the change and key-based state (such as Streams stores) no longer lines up. Plan partition counts up front, or migrate to a new topic.

  6. Your producer gets TimeoutException. What do you check?
    Reveal

    Whether brokers are reachable and leaders exist (metadata), whether the ISR is healthy, whether the buffer is full because the producer outpaces the cluster, and whether delivery.timeout.ms is too short for the retry pattern.

  7. How would you handle a 10 MB message?
    Reveal

    Prefer storing the payload in object storage and sending a reference (claim check). If it must go through Kafka, raise max.request.size, the topic's max.message.bytes, and consumer fetch sizes, and use compression.

Question bank: consumers and groups

PracticeAnswer out loud, then reveal
  1. What triggers a rebalance?
    Reveal

    A member joining or leaving (including being removed after missing heartbeats or exceeding max.poll.interval.ms), a change in subscriptions, or a change in the partitions of subscribed topics (more partitions, or new topics matching a pattern).

  2. What is the difference between eager and cooperative rebalancing?
    Reveal

    Eager: every member gives up all partitions, then receives a new assignment, so the whole group stops. Cooperative: only the partitions that move are revoked, so others keep processing. The new consumer protocol (KIP-848) is incremental and driven by the broker.

  3. What is max.poll.interval.ms and why does it matter?
    Reveal

    The longest allowed gap between poll() calls (5 minutes by default). Exceed it and the member is removed from the group and its partitions are reassigned, causing duplicates and rebalance loops.

  4. How do you process records with a slow downstream without being kicked out?
    Reveal

    Fewer records per poll, batch the downstream writes, pause() partitions while waiting (still calling poll()), process in parallel while preserving per-key order, or scale out up to the partition count.

  5. What is static membership?
    Reveal

    Setting group.instance.id so a restarting consumer keeps its assignment if it returns within the session timeout, avoiding rebalances during rolling restarts.

  6. When would you use a share group?
    Reveal

    For independent jobs where you want more workers than partitions, per-record acknowledgement, and delivery counting, and where per-key order does not matter.

  7. How do you run a consumer that must process partitions in parallel but keep per-key order?
    Reveal

    Hand records to worker threads by hashing the key, so each key always goes to the same worker; commit an offset only when all records below it in that partition are done.

Question bank: delivery and transactions

PracticeAnswer out loud, then reveal
  1. Explain at-most-once, at-least-once, and exactly-once in terms of commits.
    Reveal

    At-most-once: commit before processing; a crash skips records. At-least-once: commit after processing; a crash reprocesses records. Exactly-once: offsets and outputs commit atomically (Kafka transactions), or processing is idempotent so repeats change nothing.

  2. Does Kafka give exactly-once delivery end to end?
    Reveal

    Within Kafka, yes: transactions make consume-process-produce atomic, and read_committed consumers see only committed data. Effects outside Kafka (a database, an email) need idempotency or the outbox pattern.

  3. How do Kafka transactions work at a high level?
    Reveal

    A producer with a transactional.id registers with a transaction coordinator, writes to partitions, adds the consumer offsets with sendOffsetsToTransaction, then commits. The coordinator writes commit or abort markers to every partition involved; read_committed consumers read up to the last stable offset and skip aborted records.

  4. What is zombie fencing?
    Reveal

    When a producer with the same transactional.id starts, the coordinator bumps the epoch, and requests from the old instance (a "zombie" after a pause or network split) are rejected with ProducerFencedException.

  5. What is the outbox pattern and why use it?
    Reveal

    Write the business change and an event row in one database transaction; a relay (CDC or a poller) publishes the event to Kafka. It removes the dual-write problem where a crash leaves the database and Kafka inconsistent.

  6. How do you make a consumer idempotent?
    Reveal

    Record processed event IDs (or use a natural unique key) in the same transaction as the side effect, with a unique constraint, and skip duplicates. Or design writes as upserts keyed by entity and version.

  7. A consumer must write to a database and commit offsets. How do you avoid duplicates?
    Reveal

    Either make writes idempotent and commit offsets after, or store the offsets in the same database transaction as the writes and seek to them on startup.

Question bank: replication and storage

PracticeAnswer out loud, then reveal
  1. What is the ISR?
    Reveal

    The in-sync replica set: the leader and followers that are caught up (not lagging more than replica.lag.time.max.ms). With acks=all, a write succeeds once all ISR members have it.

  2. What is the high watermark?
    Reveal

    The highest offset replicated to all ISR members. Consumers only read below it, so they never see a record that could be lost in a failover.

  3. With RF 3 and min.insync.replicas=2, what happens when two brokers fail?
    Reveal

    The ISR drops to 1, so acks=all writes fail with NotEnoughReplicasException and the high watermark stops advancing. Reads of already committed data continue. Availability is traded for durability.

  4. What is unclean leader election?
    Reveal

    Electing a replica that is not in the ISR when no in-sync replica is available. It restores availability but loses committed records the new leader lacks, so it is off by default.

  5. Why is Kafka fast?
    Reveal

    Sequential appends to segment files, heavy use of the page cache, batching and compression end to end, zero-copy transfer from page cache to socket, and partitions spreading load across brokers and disks.

  6. Does Kafka fsync every write?
    Reveal

    No, by default it relies on replication for durability and lets the OS flush. A record acknowledged with acks=all is in memory on several machines.

  7. What is log compaction?
    Reveal

    A cleanup policy that keeps at least the latest record for each key and removes older ones; a null value (tombstone) deletes a key. Used for state, changelogs, and __consumer_offsets.

  8. What is tiered storage?
    Reveal

    Moving older, closed segments to object storage while keeping recent data on broker disks, so retention can grow without adding brokers. Consumers read old data transparently.

Question bank: design and operations

PracticeAnswer out loud, then reveal
  1. How do you choose a partition key?
    Reveal

    The entity whose events must stay in order (an account, an order). Check its cardinality and skew: too few distinct keys or one dominant key creates hot partitions.

  2. How many partitions would you create?
    Reveal

    Enough for peak throughput divided by per-partition and per-consumer capacity, with growth headroom, since increasing later moves keys. Avoid thousands without need; each partition costs files, memory, and failover time.

  3. How do you handle a hot key?
    Reveal

    Find whether ordering for that key is truly needed. If not, salt the key. If yes, scale the consumer for that key (more efficient processing) or split the entity. For aggregations, pre-aggregate with salted keys and combine.

  4. How do you monitor consumer lag?
    Reveal

    From outside the consumer (Burrow, an exporter, or the broker's group offsets), per partition, and as time behind the head, alerting on growth or on age rather than a fixed record count.

  5. How do you replay data after a bug?
    Reveal

    Stop the consumer group, reset its offsets (--to-datetime), deploy the fix, restart. Processing must be idempotent. For data beyond retention, replay from an archive.

  6. How do you evolve an event schema safely?
    Reveal

    Use a schema registry with a compatibility rule (BACKWARD by default): add optional fields with defaults, never reuse or retype fields, and use a new topic for breaking changes.

  7. How would you replicate Kafka across regions?
    Reveal

    MirrorMaker 2 (or a managed equivalent) copies topics and translates consumer offsets to a standby cluster. Plan for duplicates on failover, which idempotent consumers absorb.

  8. How would you secure a Kafka cluster?
    Reveal

    TLS on listeners, authentication with mTLS or SASL (SCRAM or OAUTHBEARER), ACLs with least privilege per principal, quotas against noisy clients, and encryption at rest.

Question bank: streams and ecosystem

PracticeAnswer out loud, then reveal
  1. Kafka Streams or Flink?
    Reveal

    Kafka Streams is a library inside your service: Kafka in, Kafka out, no extra cluster, ideal for per-key stateful processing in Java services. Flink is a separate cluster with richer windowing, many sources and sinks, very large state, and SQL. Pick by where the data lives and who operates it.

  2. What is the difference between a KStream and a KTable?
    Reveal

    A KStream is a sequence of independent events; a KTable is the latest value per key, where each record is an update. Stream-table duality: a table is a stream compacted to the latest values; a table's changes form a stream.

  3. How does Kafka Streams keep state fault tolerant?
    Reveal

    State stores (RocksDB by default) are backed by compacted changelog topics. A restarted or moved task restores its store from the changelog; standby replicas shorten restore time.

  4. What is a grace period in windowing?
    Reveal

    How long a window keeps accepting late records after it ends. Records later than the grace period are dropped.

  5. What is Kafka Connect for?
    Reveal

    Moving data between Kafka and other systems with configuration instead of code: source connectors (databases, CDC with Debezium) and sink connectors (search, object storage, warehouses), with scaling, offsets, and dead letter queues built in.

  6. What does Debezium do?
    Reveal

    Reads a database's change log (for example the PostgreSQL WAL) and publishes every committed row change to Kafka, in commit order, keyed by primary key.

Question bank: scenarios

PracticeAnswer out loud, then reveal
  1. Lag is growing on one partition only. What do you suspect?
    Reveal

    A hot key or a poison record stuck in retries. Check bytes per partition and the consumer's error logs for that partition.

  2. Consumers rebalance every few minutes. Where do you look?
    Reveal

    Processing time per poll versus max.poll.interval.ms, long GC pauses, consumers crashing, rolling deploys without static membership, and the eager protocol stopping the whole group.

  3. Downstream reports duplicate payments. Kafka is involved. How do you investigate and fix?
    Reveal

    Find where duplicates enter: producer retries without idempotence, consumer reprocessing after rebalances or crashes, or upstream retries. Fix with idempotent producers and an idempotency key enforced by a unique constraint at the payment write.

  4. Messages seem lost. What could cause it?
    Reveal

    acks=1 or 0 with a leader failure, unclean election, consumer commits before processing, auto-commit with async processing, retention deleting data before slow consumers read it, auto.offset.reset=latest on a new group, or errors swallowed in producer callbacks.

  5. A broker's disk is almost full. What do you do?
    Reveal

    Find the largest topics and partitions, lower retention on topics that allow it, delete unused topics, check for stuck compaction, then add disk or brokers and rebalance partitions. Alert earlier next time.

  6. You need to change a topic's key. How?
    Reveal

    Create a new topic with the new key, dual-publish or republish with a bridge, migrate consumers, then retire the old topic. A key change in place breaks ordering and co-partitioning.

Red flags

Common mistakes interviewers notice

  • Drawing Kafka without naming the key, the partition count, or the delivery guarantee.
  • Claiming "exactly-once" for side effects outside Kafka without idempotency.
  • Assuming global ordering across partitions.
  • Using Kafka for request-response, per-message delays, or priority without saying how.
  • Ignoring duplicates on retries and rebalances.
  • Adding partitions later as if keys would not move.
  • Measuring lag only in records, or not monitoring it at all.

Glossary

Every Kafka term used in this handbook, in one or two lines. Use the search box to jump to a term.

A
acks
Producer setting for when the leader answers: 0 (no wait), 1 (leader wrote it), all (every in-sync replica has it). Default all.
Assignor
The strategy that maps partitions to group members, such as range, round robin, cooperative sticky, or the broker-side uniform and range assignors of the new protocol.
At-least-once
Every record is processed, possibly more than once. Commit after processing.
At-most-once
Every record is processed zero or one time. Commit before processing.
Auto commit
enable.auto.commit=true: the consumer commits the latest polled offsets every auto.commit.interval.ms (5 s) during poll().
auto.offset.reset
Where a group starts when it has no valid committed offset: latest (default), earliest, by_duration:<ISO 8601 duration>, or none.
B
Batch
A group of records for one partition sent and stored together. Compression and idempotence work per batch.
Bootstrap servers
The initial broker addresses a client uses to fetch cluster metadata. They need not be all brokers.
Broker
A Kafka server that stores partitions and serves produce and fetch requests.
C
Changelog topic
A compacted topic that backs a Kafka Streams state store so it can be restored.
Claim check
Storing a large payload elsewhere (object storage) and sending a reference through Kafka.
Classic protocol
The original consumer group protocol, where a group leader computes the assignment in the client. Still the client default in Kafka 4.x.
Cleanup policy
Topic setting cleanup.policy: delete (retention by time or size), compact (latest per key), or both.
Cluster
A set of brokers and controllers sharing metadata.
Co-partitioning
Two topics with the same key and partition count, so records with the same key land on the same partition number. Required for local joins.
Commit
Saving a consumer group's position for a partition in __consumer_offsets. The committed offset is the next record to read.
Compaction
Removing older records for a key while keeping at least the latest one. A null value (tombstone) deletes the key.
Connector
A Kafka Connect plugin that moves data from a system into Kafka (source) or from Kafka to a system (sink).
Consumer
A client that reads records by polling partitions.
Consumer group
Consumers sharing a group.id that split a topic's partitions between them; each partition goes to one member.
Consumer lag
How far a group is behind: log end offset minus committed offset, per partition. Best watched as time.
__consumer_offsets
The internal compacted topic (50 partitions by default) where consumer groups store committed offsets.
Controller
A KRaft node that stores cluster metadata and makes decisions such as leader elections. One is active at a time.
Cooperative rebalancing
Incremental rebalancing where only partitions that move are revoked, so the rest keep processing.
D
Dead letter topic (DLT)
A topic where records that cannot be processed are sent, with error details, for inspection and replay.
Debezium
A set of source connectors that turn database change logs into Kafka records (change data capture).
Delivery timeout
delivery.timeout.ms (2 min): the maximum time a producer spends trying to deliver a record, including retries.
Dual-write problem
Updating a database and Kafka separately, where a crash between the two leaves them inconsistent.
E
Eager rebalancing
Rebalancing where every member revokes all partitions before reassignment, pausing the whole group.
Eligible leader replicas (ELR)
Replicas that left the ISR while it was below min.insync.replicas and therefore still hold all committed data; they may be elected leader. Kafka 4.0+, on by default for new clusters since 4.1.
Epoch
A counter that increases on each leadership or ownership change (leader epoch, producer epoch, member epoch) and fences stale actors.
Event
A fact that something happened. Stored in Kafka as a record.
Exactly-once semantics (EOS)
Each record's effect happens once. In Kafka, via idempotent producers and transactions; outside Kafka, via idempotent processing.
F
Fetch
A request to read records from a partition starting at an offset. Followers and consumers both fetch.
Follower
A replica that copies a partition from its leader.
Follower fetching
Consumers reading from a nearby follower instead of the leader, using client.rack and a rack-aware replica selector.
G
Grace period
How long a time window accepts late records after it ends.
Group coordinator
The broker that manages a consumer group's membership and stores its offsets.
H
Heartbeat
A periodic message from a group member to the coordinator proving it is alive.
High watermark (HW)
The highest offset copied to all in-sync replicas. Consumers read only below it.
Hot partition
A partition receiving much more traffic than others, usually because of a dominant key.
I
Idempotent consumer
A consumer whose processing gives the same result when a record is processed more than once.
Idempotent producer
A producer that tags batches with a producer ID and sequence numbers, so brokers drop duplicates from retries. On by default.
In-sync replica set (ISR)
The leader plus followers that are caught up within replica.lag.time.max.ms.
Isolation level
Consumer setting: read_uncommitted (default) or read_committed, which hides aborted and open transactional records.
K
Key
Optional bytes attached to a record. Determines the partition and therefore ordering.
KIP
Kafka Improvement Proposal: the design document behind each change, such as KIP-848 (new consumer protocol) or KIP-932 (share groups).
KRaft
Kafka's Raft-based metadata mode. The only mode since Kafka 4.0.
KStream
In Kafka Streams, an unbounded stream of independent events.
KTable
In Kafka Streams, a table of the latest value per key, updated by each record.
L
Last stable offset (LSO)
The first offset that belongs to a still-open transaction. read_committed consumers read up to it.
Leader
The replica that handles produce requests (and usually fetches) for a partition.
Leader election
Choosing a new partition leader, normally from the ISR, when the current one fails, or to move leadership back to the preferred replica.
Linger
linger.ms: how long a producer waits to fill a batch. 5 ms by default since Kafka 4.0.
Listener
A broker endpoint (host, port, protocol). Advertised listeners are the addresses brokers tell clients to use.
Log
An ordered, append-only sequence of records. Each partition is a log.
Log end offset (LEO)
The offset the next appended record will get on a replica.
Log segment
One file of a partition's log, with its offset and time indexes. Retention deletes whole segments.
M
Max poll interval
max.poll.interval.ms (5 min): the longest allowed gap between poll() calls before a member is removed from its group.
Metadata
Information about topics, partitions, leaders, and brokers that clients fetch to route requests.
min.insync.replicas
The minimum ISR size for a partition to accept acks=all writes.
MirrorMaker 2
A Connect-based tool that replicates topics and consumer offsets between clusters.
murmur2
The hash the Java client's default partitioner applies to key bytes.
O
Offset
A record's position in a partition, assigned by the leader on append.
Outbox pattern
Writing an event row in the same database transaction as a business change, then publishing it with a relay such as CDC.
P
Page cache
Operating system memory caching file data. Kafka relies on it for fast reads and writes.
Partition
An ordered log that is a shard of a topic. The unit of parallelism, ordering, and replication.
Partitioner
Producer logic that chooses a partition for each record.
Poison record
A record that fails processing every time, blocking its partition if not handled.
Poll loop
The consumer's main loop: poll(), process records, commit, repeat.
Preferred leader
The first replica in a partition's assignment; leadership returns to it to balance load.
Producer
A client that writes records to topics.
Producer ID (PID)
An identifier the broker assigns to an idempotent or transactional producer.
R
Rack awareness
Placing a partition's replicas in different racks or zones so one failure does not take them all.
Read committed
See isolation level.
Reassignment
Moving partition replicas between brokers, for example onto new brokers.
Rebalance
Redistributing partitions among group members when membership or subscriptions change.
Record
The unit of data in Kafka: key, value, headers, timestamp, and (once stored) an offset.
Replication factor (RF)
The number of copies of each partition.
Retention
How long or how much data a topic keeps before deleting old segments.
Retry topic
A topic used to retry failed records later without blocking the main topic, at the cost of ordering.
S
Schema registry
A service that stores versioned schemas and checks compatibility; records carry a schema ID.
Segment
See log segment.
Sequence number
A per-partition counter on idempotent producer batches used to detect duplicates and gaps.
Serializer
Code that turns a key or value into bytes (deserializer: the reverse).
Session timeout
How long a member may go without heartbeats before the coordinator removes it (45 s).
Share group
A group type (production-ready in Kafka 4.2) where members receive individual records with locks and acknowledgements, allowing more consumers than partitions and no per-key ordering.
Sink connector
A connector that writes from Kafka to an external system.
Source connector
A connector that reads from an external system into Kafka.
State store
Local storage (RocksDB or in-memory) for a Kafka Streams task, backed by a changelog topic.
Static membership
Giving a consumer a group.instance.id so restarts within the session timeout do not trigger rebalances.
Sticky partitioner
The keyless partitioning behavior: stay on one partition until a batch fills, then switch.
T
Task
In Kafka Streams and Connect, the unit of work assigned to a thread or worker, tied to input partitions.
Tiered storage
Moving older log segments to remote object storage while recent data stays on local disks.
Tombstone
A record with a key and a null value; in a compacted topic it marks the key as deleted.
Topic
A named stream of records, split into partitions.
Transaction
A set of writes (and consumer offsets) across partitions that commit or abort together.
Transaction coordinator
The broker that manages a transactional producer's state and writes commit or abort markers.
__transaction_state
The internal topic where transaction coordinators store transaction state.
Transactional ID
A stable name for a transactional producer, used to fence older instances and finish their transactions.
U
Unclean leader election
Electing an out-of-sync replica when no in-sync one is available. Restores availability, loses data. Off by default.
W
Window
A time range for aggregations: tumbling (fixed, no overlap), hopping (fixed, overlapping), sliding, or session (gap-based).
Z
Zero-copy
Sending file data from the page cache to a socket without copying it through the application (sendfile). Not possible with TLS.
ZooKeeper
The external coordination service Kafka used for metadata before KRaft. Removed in Kafka 4.0.

Roadmap and revision

An 8-week plan at about one hour on weekdays plus one longer weekend session for labs and case studies. Stretch it to 12 weeks if your weekday time is shorter; the order matters more than the pace.

On this page

  1. A daily session
  2. Weekly plan
  3. Revision rules
  4. Mock interviews
  5. Using the handbook at work

A daily session

A fixed slot of 45 to 60 minutes works well:

Minutes Do
5 to 10 Clear the revision queue on the home page, or redo one quiz you missed last time
30 to 40 One or two lessons: "Try it first", read, step through the figure, say the idea out loud
5 to 10 Tick the lesson studied; at the end of a module, do its self-check quiz

Keep labs and case studies for the longer weekly session, where you have time to break things and design without rushing.

Weekly plan

Week Weekdays (about 1 hour each) Weekend (about 2 hours)
1 M1, M2, M3 Lab setup; labs for M2 and M3
2 M4, M5, M6 Labs for M4 to M6; play with the partition explorer
3 M7, M8, M9 Labs for M7 to M9
4 M10, M11, M12 Labs for M10 to M12; case study 1
5 M13, M14, M15 Labs for M13 to M15; case study 2
6 M16, M17, M18 Labs for M16 to M18; case study 3; first mock
7 M19, M20, M21 Labs for M19 and M20; incident drills in M21; case studies 4 and 5
8 Case studies 6, 7, 8; interview bank Case studies 9 and 10; readiness check

After week 8: a 50-minute mock, then the revision queue every session, one practice prompt from the tracker a week, and one lab redone from memory a week.

Revision rules

  • Spaced review: set a status after every case study and practice prompt. The queue brings designs back after 1, 2, 4, 10, or 30 days.
  • Redesign, do not reread: on review, close the page, set a timer, and draw the design from scratch. Then compare.
  • Redo labs from memory: once a week, run a past lab without reading its steps. If you cannot, the module is not done.
  • One-line misses: keep a running list of what you forgot ("no key named", "forgot rebalance duplicates"). Read it before every mock.
  • Mastery checklists: revisit them at the end of each phase; untick anything that is no longer true.

Mock interviews

When Format Focus
Week 6 40 minutes with a peer, a Starter case study you have not seen Five points for every Kafka box: key, partitions, delivery, failures, contract
Week 9 50 minutes, a Stretch prompt Deep dives, failure handling, trade-offs at senior depth
Then Every 1 to 2 weeks Rotate practice prompts; include one "tell me about your Kafka system" round

Using the handbook at work

  • Before creating a topic: walk the five points on the interview page and size it with the partition calculator.
  • Reviewing producer or consumer code: compare settings with the cheat sheets, and use each module's "Common mistakes" box as review questions.
  • On call: follow the method in Module 21 and the "What happens when" table on the cheat sheets.
  • Upgrading Kafka or Spring for Apache Kafka: search the handbook for "Version note" boxes; they list behavior that changed in recent releases.

Design practice tracker

All 10 case studies and 16 more practice prompts in one list. Set a status after each attempt; due designs come back in the revision queue on the home page.

Your designs

How to use practice prompts

Practice prompts have no write-up of their own. Each combines ideas from the case studies and modules listed under it. Attempt it with a 40-minute timer: requirements, estimates, topics and keys, the diagram, then the two hardest parts. Then reread the linked material to check your design, and set your status honestly.

Status When to choose it
Could not design it You could not get a coherent design without help
Designed with hints You needed to look something up for the core design
Designed independently Full design, estimates, and two deep dives on your own
Needs revision You did it before, but a redo went badly
Can teach it Done twice, weeks apart, and you can answer every follow-up

For every prompt, check your design against the five points: key, partitions, delivery guarantee, failure handling, and contract and retention.
